While gathered under a solitary tree, with a child's face concealed in a mother's dress to avoid the smoke, the mother expressed relief that neighbors had arrived and released the pig. The pig, a large white one, had escaped its pen near the barn, where it had been kept. It was observed running to safety. The father and James returned shortly after noon, and some neighbors arrived to offer sympathy. Despite appearing to be a fresh, clear day, the barn was in ruins. The hills were blackened in all directions, though the property's fields and the area up to the N.T. were spared because the fire did not cross the highway there. It was believed that the fire had crossed the highway only to burn the barn. Two small valleys converged at the northeast corner of the garden, forming a significant ravine that ran northward between the old and new fields.
styled: East, among which the prairie chickens at first played and danced were gone; And as we were huddled together under said lone tree (my own little face hidden in Mother's dress from the smoke) I heard Mother saying in ac- cents of relief: "Thanks be to God! some of the neighbors have come and let the pig out". It was a big white one and had broken out of the pen itself where it had been a contented prisoner right near the barn. We saw it running for safety. Papa and James got home shortly after Noon and some of the neighbors came to sympathise with us. It seemed a fresh clear day but our barn was in ruins and the hills were black in every direction, except our fields and up to the N.T. where the fire did not cross the highway. In fact, I do not think it crossed said highway except to burn our barn. Two slight vallies joined at the foot of theN.E. corner of the garden and formed quite a ravine running nothword between the old and the new fields.

neutral: Despite your significant past mistakes, which may or may not have been worse than my own, there is still hope that in the remaining years, you can compensate for lost time and achieve the ultimate success, the only accomplishment truly worthy of a rational individual's full effort. The duration of these remaining years is uncertain. This is hoped for, if circumstances permit, but the future is highly uncertain. It is possible that any of us could pass away tomorrow. If either of us lives ten years longer, it would exceed the typical lifespan for our family. Ultimately, the timing of death is irrelevant if one is prepared. Whether it occurs tomorrow or in fifty years, if that ultimate well-being is achieved, the timing is inconsequential.
styled: In fact, not only this, but notwithstanding your very sad blunderings in the past -- possibly worse than my own, possibly not so bad -- I still hope and pray that in the few years left us, you may do something to make up for lost time; something to save your soul and gain the one vic- tory, the one crown, the only triumph really worthy a rational creature's every effort. The "few years" did I say ??? Who can tell? We hope so, of course, if it be God's holy will; but O! How uncertain! . . it may be tomorrow they'll say of you or of me or of each of us: "He is gone." If either of us live ten years longer it will be passing the old-age mark for our clan. And after all, what's the difference if we only be ready? Nay, if it be tomorrow or fifty years hence, if we only save our immortal souls? What's the difference?

neutral: I hope you are well and finding contentment. I began writing to you on December 8th, which was the 42nd anniversary of my entry into the St. Bonaventure's order. However, as often occurs, I did not make much progress with my letter that day. So now, within the following week, I am trying again. I wanted to write this out of gratitude for joining this order, and particularly for the good fortune of quickly developing an affection for it, despite my initial reluctance and prejudice upon arriving. This morning, I prayed for your well-being and guidance. I am confident that despite the difficulties, challenges, setbacks, and occasional successes that all people experience, you will be protected from serious errors.
styled: God bless you and I hope you are well -- trying at least to be contented. I started to write you on the beautiful Feast of our Blessed Mother, the Immaculate Conception; being as it was the 42nd anniversary of the happy day of my vocation to St. Bonaventure's. Thanks be to God and the same His Blessed Immaculate Mother. As often happens, however, I did not get far with my letter that day; so now, before the octave passes, I'll try once more. This I've wanted to do out of gratitude for such a vocation to such an order and, I might say, especially for the grace of learning so quickly to love the Order -- notwithstanding my prejudice on coming hither as I did, half against my will. I offered my rosary this morning out in the crisp, moon-light air for your intentions and your guidance. I am confident that though, like the rest of us -- poor children of Eve -- you have your difficulties, your temptations, your falls even, and your occasional little triumphs, our dear Lord will keep you from serious blunderings.

neutral: It is difficult to respond to Maurice Joachim's proposition to write to his former diocese, specifically to a prelate he likely has not met and who may not be familiar with him. It is natural to hope for a positive reception, perhaps imagining a comfortable position in Wisconsin. However, this expectation is unrealistic. Given his age and experience, such aspirations should be considered outdated. This is particularly relevant considering his past long-standing desire to join a religious order or live a secluded life. Approximately 35 years ago, while employed in the mail service, he wrote on a particular date, outlining a plan: "This is my plan, and I want you to let me know what you think of it. I'll try it out for a year or so, and if it goes, then I'll join yours or some other religious community."
styled: But dear Father Maurice Joachim: I hardly know what to say or to think of your proposition to write back to your old diocese, to a prelate you've possibly never met and who has possibly never heard of Father Joachim. Naturally you would hope to be received with open arms, -- dreaming as you probably do, of some cozy little place just smiling across the Wisconsin hills at you. Ah dear Fr. Maurice Joachim! You may be sure, such would be only dreaming. Your age and your experience shoul rather exclude such dreams as belonging to the long ago. This we might think especially, considering your years of dreaming when and how you might get away from the world to a monastery. Think of it, dear Father Joachim Nearly five and thirty years back, while still in the mail service, you wrote on the feast that since has become your own name-day: 11 .. . This is my plan' and I want you to let me know what you think of it. 11 . . . .I'll try it out for a year or so and if it goes then I'll join yours or some other holy order.

neutral: A note was written to congratulate the recipient and send best wishes. Mary Casey called and was scheduled to visit that afternoon before returning to camp that night. Mary Casey's mother, Emma, had recently suffered a serious scald, and James Jr. had undergone an operation on his leg. Otherwise, conditions on the Coast appeared to be as usual. Edward had been written to a few days prior, as no word had been received from him in a long time. It was noted that he had very little time for himself, which he reportedly found satisfying. Best wishes were extended to the recipient and friends in "City of fine Schools, Villas & Terraces."
styled: Just a line while I have time to gratulate you and wish you every blessing. Mary Casey just phoned - is coming out this p.m. to have a little visit, before going back to-night to camp. .. Her mother Emma scalded herself recently rather badly and James Jr. had an operation oo his les. ... . otherwise things seem about as usual on the Coast. I wrote Fr. Edward a few days ago - have not bad word from him in a long time. I know he has very little time for himself - what quite pleases him, I think. God bless you now and all my old friends in "City of fine Schools, Villas & Terraces"

neutral: It may be beneficial to read it whenever you feel sad. My friends here offered to make copies to send to anyone I chose. Additionally, I found a description of my father's death, written shortly after he died. Wanting a copy before sending the original to the oldest family member, these friends also made copies of it. I am enclosing one of these copies. By the way, Christmas Eve will be the tenth anniversary of the writer's funeral. I believe a funeral service was held, with six of her brothers serving as pallbearers. You also buried two of those brothers just a month later.
styled: It will do you good to read it over whenever you be inclined to play with "the blues." Friends of ours here offered to make a number of copies to send to any- one I might wish. Besides this, I cam across a description of dear, old Father's death, written shortly after he died. Wishing to get a copy of it before I'd send the original to the oldest of the Family, these friends made copies of it too, one of which I am herewith enclosing. Incidentally, Christmas Eve will be the tenth anniversary of the writer's funeral. R.I.P. I believe you had the Mass, with six of her brothers pall-bearers -- two of whom you had the privilege, sad as it must have been, of laying to rest just a month later. R.I.P.

neutral: You have long wanted to be a missionary, and your brother, who is three years younger than you, has also wanted to be one. When should we start, and where should we go to find a place where our efforts will be beneficial to others and valued? Should we go to distant places, or should we believe that helping others effectively begins at home, starting with our own inner development? Considering that personal development is inherently valuable, there's no need to travel far for such work. After all, we each have only one self that we must care for. If we were to help everyone else in the world but neglect our own well-being, what would we gain?
styled: : You've long since wanted to be a real missionary. So has your brother whom you have led (according to age, three years in advance) wished to be indeed a missionary ... When are we to start? Whither shall we turn to find a field wherein our zeal will be profitable to souls and appreciated? Shall we go to the ends of the earth, or shall we, convinced that Charity, rightly ordered, begins at home? Shall we begin right in our own hearts? As, dear Maurice; if, "what we do for our own souls is 100% for the glory of God, then surely we don't need to go far for mission work. After all, we have just one soul -- and only -- that we must save. Should we in the end save everyone else in the whole world and not save our own soul, what would it profit us? . (What wretchedly poor work! Interrupted again and again: I'd do it all over had I another day. Deo Gratias! O Brother Dear! Why are we all so stupid? We are all alike in a way.

neutral: A letter from the author's eldest sister, Mrs. Ella (Casey) Traynor, details their shared father's final struggles and death. Ella (Casey) Traynor, who had provided the author's early education, later died and was buried on December 24, 1928.
styled: The following letter from my eldest sister, Mrs. Ella (Casey) Traynor, who taught me my ABCs and next to dear Mother my prayers, describes dear Father's last struggles and beautiful death. The writer herself has since passed away, having been burried Christmas Eve 1928. May their dear souls rest in the peace of the saints!

neutral: The writer stated that if a current endeavor failed, they would become a lay brother. If that also failed, they would marry, move West, and contribute as much as possible, emphasizing that they would never live a secular life. This was written from Prairie Avenue, Chicago. The recipient of the letter showed it to Father Bonaventure, who was the former Provincial and Father Superior in Yonkers, where the recipient was assigned for the subsequent 14 years. Father Bonaventure was pleased with the letter and commented, "He has good intentions. Tell him to go ahead." The next letter received was from the writer, who was back in college after a twenty-year break, this time in Berlin (now Kitchener), Ontario. The handwriting on the envelope indicated the sentiments expressed inside: "I have found the peace again I looked for so long, and in this I feel amply re- paid for the sacrifice it took to give up everything." This was described as a practical experience, demonstrating that willing sacrifice for a higher purpose is always a small sacrifice compared to the certain positive outcomes.
styled: If it don't go, I'll be a lay-brother. And if that fails, then by George I'll get married and go out West and be as useful to God and man as I can, a secular I'll never be." You wrote that from Prairie Avenue, Chicago. I showed your letter to dear, old Father Bonaventure, ex-Provincial at the time, and Fr. Superior in Yonkers, where I was stationed (for 14 years following). May his dear soul rest in peace. He was pleased with your letter and said: " ... He has good intentions. Tell him to go ahead .. " The next letter I received from you, you were back in college after twenty years vacation. This time in Berlin -- now Kitchener -- Ontario. Your handwriting on the envelope presaged your sentiments within: " ... I have found the peace again I looked for so long, and in this I feel amply re- paid for the sacrifice it took to give up everything." What a practical experience, -- a grace to convince you that sacrifice willingly made for God's sake is always a small sacrifice for results sure to follow. Deo Gratias! Dear Brother -- Dear Father M. J.

neutral: Wishing you well. I have been trying to contact you for weeks. I am sending you Jim's letter, which I received last Monday. Since I began writing this message, twelve people have arrived and are waiting. I wanted to inform you about the jubilee event held in Royal Oak. A large crowd attended. Approximately fifty individuals identified as priests, bishops, and sisters were present, including three Capuchins.
styled: God bless you and yours. I've been trying to get in touch you for weeks. Am sending you herewith Jim's letter received last Monday. There is since I started this card just a dozen people came in waiting. I wanted to tell you about the jubilee we had out in Royal Oak. There was surely a grand crowd . . about fifty priests -- bishops and sisters. (3 Capuchins)

neutral:
Individuals often become preoccupied with numerous external matters, thereby undervaluing the importance of a humble, inner focus. This perspective was understood and appreciated by some. If individuals were to fully utilize the opportunities for improvement available to everyone, they could experience rapid and significant personal transformation.

The following is an excerpt from a recently received letter. It is from a former prominent spiritual leader and writer, who appears to have experienced significant difficulties in recent years. The writer states, "I have truly realized my insignificance and powerlessness. All that remains is a fragile but persistent desire to maintain my resolve and continue, regardless of the difficulties." A copy of the rhyme-letter previously given to the former Provincial two years prior is also included.
styled: We worry our heads and our hearts about many things like Martha and almost totally undervalue the in- vitation -- most beautiful of all -- "learn of me because I am meek and humble of heart." Mary the Penitent understood it and Jesus praised her for her appreciation. . It seems to me that, were we only to correspond to God's graces, continually being showered down on everyone of us, we would be able to pass from being great sinners one day to be great saints the next. The following are a few lines from a letter received a day or two back. It is from a one-time leading religious and writer, who seemingly is having a purgatory of things these past few years. " ... to the good God who must sorrow even more than I do over this situation, "I have indeed come to know that I am nothing, I have nothing and can do nothing, and all that re- mains is a tiny flicker of a weak will 'to want' to remain faith- ful and persevere, no matter what the cost." I am enclosing a copy of the rhyme-letter you gave to Fr. ex-Provincial two years ago.

neutral: I received your letter yesterday. While it contained an underlying dissatisfaction, which I can hardly be surprised at or blame you for, I am very pleased. I am grateful for what, in my opinion, is more commendable than any success you have had or could have had in your professional work, such as missions, parishes, or teaching. I appreciate your tone of patient resignation, which both fosters and results from a humble attitude. Your current difficult circumstances have provided an opportunity for growth and development in these valued qualities. It seems to me a most hopeful indication if, despite your mistakes and successes over thirty-three years in your dedicated service – at the forefront of difficulties – and especially under your current trying circumstances, you can still express the sentiment that credit belongs elsewhere. We should attribute success to external factors and good fortune more than anything else.
styled: God bless you and yours -- including my poor self I hope. I received your welcome letter yesterday and, while there is a silent note therein of dis- satisfaction, that I can hardly be surprized at or blame you for, yet I am more than pleased and I thank God for what, in my opinion, must please Heaven better than any success you ever had -- or could have without it -- on missions, parishes or catechism teachings. Thank God for your tone of patient resignation, at once a great promoter and a fruit of Christian humility. God himself has provide in your present trying circumstances, a mill in His wisdom and in His mercy for your refinement in these virtues that pleas Him most. It seems to me a most hopeful indication if, notwithstanding your blunders as well as your successes for three and thirty years in the holy Priesthood -- in the brunt of the warfare, therefore -- and especially under your present trying circumstances, you can still sigh: "Non nobis Domine! non nobis ... ". Its God and His holy grace more than anything else that we ought thak. Blessed be His Holy Name!

neutral: One might imagine that a major institution could have been established and overseen by perfectly flawless beings, free from human errors and weaknesses. However, it is remarkable that this institution, currently managed by ordinary, fallible individuals – descendants of humble beginnings – has endured and thrived. Its continued existence, despite its human leadership, seems extraordinary. This observation could apply to almost any charitable organization. Therefore, our role should be to contribute in small, seemingly insignificant ways. Major contributions are, in a sense, less critical. There will always be individuals willing to undertake significant tasks, even if their efforts are ultimately flawed or unsuccessful. However, there is a unique value in attending to minor details, which might only be fully understood or appreciated by a higher consciousness. These include simple actions like sweeping, weeding, or offering a kind word – all seemingly minor. Yet, it is often said that "small details contribute to excellence, and excellence is never a small detail." Excellence represents the highest standard. From a comprehensive viewpoint, the entire world is composed of countless small elements.
styled: God could have founded His Church and left/under the supervision of angels, that have no human faults and weaknesses. But who can doubt that as it stands today, consisting of and under the supervision of poor sinners -- successors to ignorant fishermen -- that it is more of a "standing miracle" than in any other way think- able? Could not the same thing be said of practically every charitable institution? It seems to me that our task-our privilege -- ought to be just to help along in some trifling way. In a way, the big things are really not so important. There is always some one ready to take care of such -- even if, like Judas, they make a botch of it. But what a privilege to take care of trifles that only our guardian-angels enjoy and God himself can divinely appreciate! -- sweeping, pulling weeds, picking potato-bugs, etc. etc. How trifling! or suffering little mortifications, offering little ejaculatory prayers, dropping a word of sympathy, etc. all trifles. But "trifles make perfection and perfection is never a trifle. Perfection is divine. In God's sight -- who can doubt-the world itself is made up of trifles .

neutral:
About a year ago, on the occasion of his 60th anniversary of ordination, the renowned clergyman of Ironton, Ohio, Mr. Cotter, an outstanding lecturer and writer, recounted a story about his highly regarded sister, who had recently passed away. He said that when he had visited her after receiving much praise during his 50th anniversary celebration ten years prior, she earnestly and honestly stated that they should be grateful that for those fifty years, he had avoided any real scandal.

The passage then advises that one should be grateful for all experiences, both challenges and positive ones. It suggests not to criticize the institution's chaplain too harshly if he appears overly demanding, as his role is likely very stressful. It is clear that he must occasionally deal with difficult situations. Instead, one should offer support for him and everyone associated with the institution, as they all face challenges and have their imperfections. The passage concludes by questioning who is to blame.
styled: About a year ago, on occasion of his 60th anniversary as a priest the renowned Pastor of Ironton, Ohio-outstanding lecturer and writer -- Father Cotter, told of his saintly and venerated sister then recently deceased, that when he had come into her presence after just hearing all kinds of laudations on occasion of his jubilee ten years before, she earnestly and honestly exclaimed: "O James! How we ought to thank God that for these fifty years He has never per- mitted you to/any real scandal." So dear Brother, Fr. Joachim: let us be grateful to God for everything -- the knocks we get as well as the consolations. ... and do not blame the Father Chaplain too severely if he seem unduly exacting, etc. Of all positions he has one that in my opinion must at times be on his nerves. Who can doubt that at times, now and then at least, he must be up against delicat cases? Rather continue to pray for him and for all connected with the institution. They all have their difficulties and there is none without their defects. Who is to blame? ....

neutral:
About a year ago, on the occasion of his 60th anniversary of service as a religious leader, the well-known religious leader from Ironton, Ohio, Mr. Cotter—a notable writer and lecturer—spoke about his respected sister, who had recently passed away. He recounted that when he had come into her presence after hearing many praises during his 50th anniversary celebration ten years earlier, she honestly and earnestly exclaimed, "James, we should be thankful that for these fifty years you have never caused any real scandal!"

Therefore, do not blame the chaplain if he seems overly strict. If he were not a conscientious individual in his role, he would hardly be in such a demanding position. For who can doubt that at least occasionally, he handles sensitive situations? Instead, continue to support him and all those involved with the institution. They all face challenges, and none are without flaws. Who is responsible? The institution could have been established under the supervision of perfect beings, free from faults or weaknesses.
styled: not to us, but to Thy Name be the glory given !" About a year ago, on occasion of his 60th anniversary to the Priesthood, the re- nowned Pastor of Ironton, Ohio -- outstanding writer and lecturer -- Father Cotter, told of his saintly and venerated sister, then recently deceased, that when he had come into her presence after just hearing all kinds of laudations on occasion of his Jubilee ten years before, she exclaimed earnestly and honestly: "O James ! How we ought thank God that for these fifty years He has never permitted you to give any real scandal !" So, dear Brother Maurice, Fr. Joachim: do not blame poor Father Chaplain if he seems unduly exacting, etc. If he were not a conscientious priest he would hardly be in such an ex- tremely trying position. For who can doubt that at least now and then, he has delicate cases, etc? Rather continue to pray for him -- and for all concerned with the institution. They all have their difficulties and there is none of them without defects. Who is to blame? God could have established His Church under supervision of angels that have no faults or weaknesses.

neutral: It is clear that, in its current state, despite being run by imperfect individuals, the organization's continued existence and impact are remarkably successful, perhaps more so than any other approach. The same could be said for any philanthropic organization. Therefore, maintain your perseverance, patience, and acceptance. Be assured that all efforts are observed and will be met with abundant recompense. The principle holds true that those who act humbly will be elevated. It is a common, unfortunate experience that those who act arrogantly will face a downfall. We should be grateful for the ongoing opportunity to act modestly and earn recognition.
styled: But who can doubt that as it standsToday, consisting of and under the supervision of poor sinners -- successors to the "poor Fisher-men of Galilee", the Church is a more outstanding miracle than any other way? Quite the same might be said of any charitable institution. So keep up your prayers and patience and resignation for God's blessed sake; and be sure He is watching all and will never be outdone in generosity. Nor will He ever fail in what He assures : "He that humbleth himself shall be exalted." Who has not sadly experienced the opposite: "He that exalteth himself shall be humbled"? How can we ever thank the merciful God that we still have a chance to humble ourselves and to merit!

neutral:
I intended to write to you earlier today, but it is now 11 P.M. It is remarkable to consider the patience and positive experiences that have been granted.

Thirty-two years ago, on October 2, the writer, Father E'd, and Jim (who is now deceased) awoke in the Badlands of North Dakota. Jim observed a coyote climbing one of the distinctive geological formations and drew the others' attention to it. The passage of time since then seems brief. Many changes have occurred, and one anticipates further changes in the next sixteen years. There is a sense of being protected and guided, with a belief that, despite errors and poor judgment, circumstances will ultimately lead to the best outcome.

This afternoon, I received my own letter to Father E'd, which had been sent back from the Philippines via Detroit, Michigan. Father E'd should be aware of its contents by tomorrow. The writer has forgotten what was written. The letter will have been postmarked five months ago tomorrow.
styled: God bless you and yours. I meant to write you a letter to-day a number of times and now its 11 P.M. Well, how can we thank the Good God for all His patience with us and all the graces lavished upon each? ! Thirty-two yrs back Oct. 2 -- we Fr. E'd, Jim (R. I. P.) and I awoke in the "Bad-Lands of N. D." Jim's keen eye espied a kyote scrambling up one of the peculiar formations to which he called our attention . - How short it now seems! What changes since! But looking forward, what changes are ahead in half 32 years! ? Let us bless and adore the Providence that has kept us and have all in His hands who keep tally on the hairs of our heads. . . and the sighes and the breaths we take -- and notwithstanding our blunders and stupid- ity still plans on for our best. Only this P. M. I received, Via Detroit, Mich, my own letter to Fr. E'd, back from the Phil- ippines. He ought to know what's in it by tomorrow. I forget. Mail-marked five months tomorrow.

neutral: I have just written to J. O'Donnell and also replied to my sister-in-law. It appears that she and Florence are making a strong effort to cope and to live in a way that they believe will lead to happiness. Please try to send a note to J. O'Donnell. As I just wrote to him, and as is true for everyone, there is a force that consistently attempts to downplay and obscure the considerable advantages available to all of us.
styled: God bless you and yours. Have just written Fr. J. O'Donnell -- also answered cur poor sister-in-law. Thank God she and Florence too seem to be trying bravely to keep up -- following close (at least) to the straight narrow path -- the chalk-line to happiness. Try and drop a card to poor Fr. O'Donnell. In his case, as I just wrote him, like everybody else's, it is the enemy of our souls that is always trying to minimize and to hide the surpassing advantages by which everyone of us are surrounded. God help us!

neutral: When the author was seven years old and had five older siblings, three of whom were brothers, it was widely assumed, as if predetermined, that Maurice would become a priest. This belief was not limited to their immediate family and relatives; even neighboring children frequently discussed it, appearing to admire him as someone destined for this role. The conviction was so strong that, even then or perhaps earlier, someone began to consider if it were possible for a family to have two priests, with this individual readily considering himself to be the second. However, despite his promising childhood and early youth, which seemed to align with these expectations, the old proverb...
styled: Furthermore; when the writer was in his seventh year and there were three brothers among the five dear-ones ahead of him, it just seemed self - understood as though planned before his birth that Maurice was to be the Priest. Not only was this the case in our immediate family and relatives, but our neighboring children often spoke of it and seemed to revere him as so fortunately destined and chosen. So much was this true that some one even at that time and perhaps earlier, began to wonder if possibly there couldn't be two priests in a family -- hardly hesitating that he would be the other himself. However, promising and all as was his childhood and early youth to harmonize with such happy plannings, the old proverb

neutral: I received your letter yesterday. I hope I am included in your well-wishes. While I detect an unspoken dissatisfaction, which I understand and don't fault you for, I am very pleased. The progress you've made is, in my opinion, more valuable than your achievements in the Rocky Mountain Missions or in religious instruction in various settings. This progress stems from your ability to learn from a difficult, humbling experience. As the saying goes, "Without humiliation, there is no humility; without humility, there is no true virtue." It is commendable that, after thirty-three years in your religious vocation and enduring significant challenges, you continue to uphold your guiding principle, expressed as "Not to us!", which emphasizes humility and the attribution of success to factors beyond oneself. This sentiment is particularly relevant to your current situation, both in words and actions.
styled: God bless you and yours -- my poor self I hope included. I received your letter yesterday and, while there is a silent note therein of dissatisfaction that I can hardly be surprized at or blame you for, yet I am more than pleased and I thank God for the wonderful progress you've made in what must, in my opinion, please Heaven better than all your success on the Rockey-Mountain Missions or at catechism in parishes or hospitals, etc. In other words, your profiting by the outstanding opportunity God himself, in His wisdom and mercy has been providing for you in the mill of humiliation. -- "No humiliation, no humility; no humility, no real virtue." (S. Ber - nard) . It's God and His holy grace more than anything else we ought thank that you, after three and thirty years in the Holy Priesthood, in the brunt of the "warfare, therefore, you can still cling to your motto: "NON NOBIS DOMINE NON NOBIS !" This we may say especially under your present circumstances to say -- and to act what we proclaim to God: "Not to us O Lord!

neutral: The death of Father Maurice was announced to relatives and friends who were familiar with the challenges, disappointments, humiliations, ambitions, and occasional triumphs of his 81-plus years. However, even among these close acquaintances, and despite the commonality of such aspirations in their culture, few knew that his parents had shared the aspiration for one of their children to become a priest. This aspiration sustained their hopes from early in their marriage, which they viewed as a commitment to spiritual service.
styled: fact, -- though the ideal seems common the "Island of Saints" - - that our dear Parents NOTE. The above "End of the road .... " following the peaceful death of our dear Rev. Brother, is the announcement of the same happy event to near relatives and friends who would be naturally more or less acquainted with the ups and downs that poor dear Father Maurice was known to have gone through, and the more than ordinary disappointments, humiliations, ambitions and sometimes triumphs of his over 81 years. Even among such near and dear ones, however, -- though the ideal seems to be common in the "Island of Saints" -- comparatively few ever knew of the fact that our dear Parents had mutually dreamed of the privilege of being parent to a Priest in their family, which ideal would seem to have buoyed their hopes from the earliest years wherein they recognized holy matrimony as a state of life in which to serve God and help Him to save souls.

neutral: I re-addressed it and added a third airmail stamp. I hope you are able to find a situation that is more agreeable than what you have accepted for the past few years. However, M. Joachim, it is beneficial for us. I just located this, which I had left several days ago. It was intended to reach you by this Sunday; however, it is now 9:30 P.M. I returned half an hour ago from the senior care facility in Staten Island. Best wishes to you and Edw'd. These wishes are extended to all individuals I had in mind, particularly clergy.
styled: I just reddressed it and added a 3rd Air Stamp. I am praying the dear, Good God to guide you whither you'll find it more congenial than you resigned yourself to the past few years. Nevertheless dear Fr. M. Joachim, its good for us. I just found this as I left it several days ago. to reach you by this Sunday and here it is 9:30 P. M. got back half an hour back from old people's Home in Staten Island . . God's blessing to yourself and Fr. Edw'd -- Rt. to all I meant - just Rev.

neutral: He was born on November 10, 1867, was formally inducted into a religious role on June 9, 1911, and died on January 12, 1949. His 81 years, dedicated to combating what he perceived as universal moral and spiritual challenges, concluded with several months of peaceful decline leading to his death. Those close to him had hoped for and believed his death to be a peaceful transition to a promised afterlife, a state of ultimate fulfillment and connection. This afterlife was envisioned as a place of unimaginable wonder and profound experiences, beyond human comprehension.
styled: 3ORI NOV. 10, 1867; ORDAINED JUNE 9TH 1911; DIED JAN. 12TH 1949. HIS 81 years OF "WARFARE AGAINST THE ENEMIES OF OUR SOULS, THE UNBELIEVING WORLD, THE FLESH AND THE DEVIL - COMMON TO MANKIND - WERE CROWNED BY SEVERAL MONTES OF A PEACEFUL APPROACH TO A HAPPY DEATH. FOR THIS WE HAD PRAYED AND THIS WE DO CONFIDENTLY HOPE HIS DEATH WAS viz, A HAPPY TRANSISION TO THE HEAVEN-PROMISED ABODE WHERE GRATITUDE RIPETS INTO PERFET LOVE OF GOD AND NEIGHBOR: AND WHERE ACCORDING TO ST. PAUL: " .... EYE HATH NOT SEMET, EAR HATH NOT HEARD NOR HATH IT ENTERED INTO THE HEART OF MAN TO COCEIVE WHAT THINGS GOD HATH PREPARE FOR THEM THAT LOVE HIM. "

neutral: I hope you and your family are well. Although it is 11 p.m., I want to write a few words before retiring after what has been a busy and, for me, eventful day. For you, and for everyone who had direct involvement with the Eucharistic Congress in the Philippines, it must have been exceptionally eventful. However, we in Detroit received announcements via radio around 8 a.m. and heard the Pope's voice delivering a blessing. His concluding blessing appeared to be the Latin phrase: "In Nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti". I hope you can send us worthwhile details. Local press coverage, including Catholic publications, has been quite subdued regarding this significant event. I hope to hear that it exceeded the solemnity and impressiveness, including the grandeur, of the Congress held in Ireland, about which Cardinal Hayes reportedly stated, "It surpassed the unsurpassable."
styled: God bless you . I hope you are well - you and yours. Though it is just striking 11 p.m. I want to at least start you a few words before re- tiring after this busy day, and in a way even for me eventful day. For yourself of course, and for every one whose privilege it has been to be in immediate touch with the Eucharistic Congress out there in the Philippines it has been no doubt more than eventful. However, we here get the announce- ments over the radeo about 8 a.m. in Detroit and heard the Holy Father's own voice and benediction. His conclusion with benediction seemed to be really: ". in Nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti". I hope you may send us details worth while. The press here - even the Catholic part of it has been very tame so far about this great event. I hope to learn that it surpassed in solemnity and impressiveness even the grandeur, etc, of the Congress in Ireland, of which Cardinal Hayes is said to have remarked: "It surpassed the insurpassible".

neutral: A portion of the property, including Sugarloaf Mountain—described as one of the most beautiful along the Hudson—was sold to help fund the construction of a new monastery. Later that day, the individual went for a hike. The individual was only partially determined to climb the mountain and proceeded as they were. However, the air was so pleasant during the ascent, and the breezes and shade were so inviting, that the individual continued upward, moving through underbrush and across paths and roads until these features disappeared. Finally, after a significant climb through mostly sparse, almost trackless brush, the individual reached the rather uninviting summit and climbed a small evergreen tree to view the canopy of summit foliage. The scenery was grand, to a limited extent, but compared to previously experienced beautiful views, particularly those from Mount Saint Helen and the gentler hills of Trimbelle, the individual soon found the views monotonous and disappointing compared to expectations. Therefore, after a short time, the individual descended and began the descent down Sugarloaf Mountain.
styled: They soled quit a piece of it includ- ing the Sugar-loaf Mountain - one of the most beautiful along the Hudson, to help defray building of the new Monastery. After vespers I went for a hyke. Only half determined to climb the Mt., and feeling more like myself in the holy habit I just went as I was. How- ever, the air was so salubrious as I ascended and the breezes and shade so inviting that I pushed on and up through under brush and across paths and roads till I found none of these any more. Finally, after quite a climb through almost trackless brush, mostly not dense, I reached the rather unin- viting top and climbed a gentle evergreen to look out over the canoy (canopy) of sumit foliage. The scenry was grand, as far as it went, but in remembrance of the beautiful views, decade age so familiar to us, from Mt. Saint Helen and before that from the gentler hills of old Trimbelle, I soon found it monotnous and disapointing in hoped-for views. So I climed down after a little and started down the face of old Sugar-loaf.

neutral:
The route was believed to be totally unexplored. With the aid of a strong emergency staff and recollections of similar, though smaller, journeys from 60 or more years prior, the descent was made. There were some narrow escapes and a few harmless bumps on the vehicle's rear fenders.

The return to the monastery occurred close to supper-time, and the individual had a significant appetite. That evening included recreation, which was very enjoyable, and the individual slept very soundly, more so than in a long time.

The following day, Guardian, having additional business in New York, transported the individual by car. They crossed between Sugar-loaf and the now famous Mount of Atonement, then descended through the Highlands. The descent was indeed substantial. After descending numerous hills, the individual began to anticipate reaching level ground when they suddenly curved past a sign marked 'Hill'. The individual smiled as they quickly passed the sign and went over the top of the hill. The driver appeared to know every inch and bump of the road, as they continued to encounter inclines repeatedly.
styled: I think it was a totally unexplored route; but aided by a strong emergency staff, and dreamings of similar climb- ings - though on smaller scales - 60 or more years ago, I made the descent with some narow escapes and a few harmless bumps on rear fenders. Deo Gratias. It was close to supper-time when I got back to the monastery, and I need not tell you I had an appetite. We had recreation that evening which ... very happy and its a long time since I slept sounder than that night. Next day, finding he had some extra business in New York, Fr. Guardian brought me down by auto. We crossed over between Sugar-loaf and the now famous Mt. of Atonement and went down over the High-lands. It was quite a descent indeed. After we had gone down so many hills that I was beginning to think we were coming close to normally level ground we suddenly curved past a sign: "Hill". I had to smile as we dashed past it and over the top, the dri- ver seemingly knowing every inch and bump ahead till again and again we con- tinued to make inclines.

neutral: Having narrowly missed attending a previous significant event, I strongly desired to attend the 1937 event. If it had coincided more closely with your anniversary celebration, I might have been dispatched. However, I have not been eager to undertake such an expensive and unusual trip, unless an additional duty required my presence there. My being sent to assist Maurice with a celebration seemed appropriate at the time. Now, it appears to have been fortunate. In fact, I believe several positive outcomes resulted for me and others. I have a letter from Mary Kerrman, a chronically ill individual from Elizabeth Hospital in Elizabeth, New Jersey, which I want to include as a sample. Regarding requests for details about the Congress, I hope my example is not taken as a criterion. I am sure you expected a report about our visit to New York last June. In fact, I started more than once to provide a short summary of my ten-day trip on that occasion.
styled: Having barely missed going to that great event I almost dreamed of my going this one in '37. Had it been closer to the time of your jubilee I would possibly have been sent. I have not been anxious, however, to under- take such an expensive and extraordinary trip, - unless of course some ad- ditional duty should waft me thither. That I was sent to help Father Mau- rice to celebrate, seemed quite appropriate at the time. Now it seems to have been fortunate. In fact I believe quite a few blessings came as a con- sequence to myself & more. I have a letter from a certain ascetic invalid, Mary Kerrman of St. Elizabeth Hospital, Elizabeth New Jersey, I want to in- close ... well, just as a sample. Asking for details about the great Congress, I hope you may not think of taking as a criterion the example of the present writer. I am sure you expected some report about our visit in New York last June. As a matter of fact I started more than once to give you a short summary of my ten-day di- version, on that occasion.

neutral: M. Joachim had reportedly discussed the matter with a superior several months prior, and the superior had given approval. The journey began on Wednesday evening, June 3rd. The evening and night were clear, with a sunset and moonlight. The Niagara River was crossed approximately 13 miles above the Falls; even at that distance, the waters appeared to swirl rapidly, suggesting a powerful, uncontrolled force. Despite minimal sleep, no fatigue was felt when dawn revealed the descent into the Mohawk Valley. There were only one or two stops before reaching Albany. The journey continued down the Hudson River to Garrison, located directly opposite Westpoint Military Academy. Mass was conducted around 9 a.m. at the Monastery, located approximately one mile away. The conditions at the Monastery were sufficiently appealing that a decision was made to stay and rest for a day. The grounds were exceptionally spacious and notably grand. The original property was understood to be over 400 acres.
styled: Hoping that it may not be without interest, I'll try just briefly to give you an idea about the whole affair even though be- lated. Father M. Joachim seems to have spoken to Rev. Father Provincial about it some months before, and the latter told me it would be alright. I started off Wednesday evening June 3rd. The evening and night were ideal in sun-set and moon-light, we crossed the Niagara about 13 miles above the Falls but even at that the waters seemed to be swirling on to as if rushing to a tragedy. Though I slept very little I was not tired when the dawn re- vealed we were descending the Mchawk Valley stopping only once or twice before reaching Albany. Then down the Hudson to Garrison just across from Westpoint Military Academy. Walking to the Monastery about a mile below, I said holy Mass close to 9 a.m. Deo Gratias! I found things so inviting afterwords that I decided to rest there a day. The grounds are spacious to say the least and I might say almost dangerously grand. Originally there were, I believe over 400 acres.

neutral: One person involved was not entirely satisfied, but did not complain. Instead, he was grateful that things had gone as well as they did and hoped for improvement in the future. In addition to friends from Yonkers, Harlem, Brooklyn, and other places, two of our cousins, who were nuns from Waltham, Massachusetts, attended the formal religious service that day. In the subsequent days, the brothers visited their fellow members and friends in East New York, Harlem, Yonkers, Hoboken, New Jersey, and other locations. We also visited Thomas Ford, who was associated with the Irish World publication. He is the sole surviving son of the prominent founder, who was a significant figure in culture, patriotism, and religion. I had known all of them in previous years, along with their sister, who is also still alive. He appeared pleased by our visit. On Friday at noon, I traveled to Albany and then by bus to visit friends in Watervliet, located directly across from Troy. They took me back to Albany to catch the overnight train, "Wolverine." The train arrived in Detroit around 7 a.m. on Saturday. There is no need to inform you about the Provincial Chapter and the numerous subsequent changes.
styled: Just one in all con- cerned was not exactly satisfied that I knew, but neither did he complain. Rather he thanked God that it went as well as it did and hoped he might do better another time. Besides friends from Yonkers and Harlem and Brooklyn, etc, two of our cousins - nuns from Waltham, Mass., were at the Solemn Mass that day. The following days the Rev. brothers visited the brethren and friends together in East New York, Harlem, Yonkers, Hoboken, N.J., etc. We went also to see Thomas Ford of the Irish World. He is the only survivor of the sons of the great founder that old beacon-light of culture - of pa- triotism at once and of religion. I knew them all in former years together with their still surviving sister. He seemed pleased at our call. Friday noon I went to Albany and thence by bus to some friends in Watervleit just across from Troy. They took me back to Albany for the night "Wolverine" and that reached Detroit about 7 a.m. Saturday, Deo Grat! Of course I need not inform you of the Provincial Chapter and the many changes that followed.

neutral:
Around 11 a.m., the route passed through picturesque old Yonkers, which was mostly downhill with a few small uphill sections. The journey continued via the Western Driveway, past the Washington Bridge (over the Hudson), and over Canal Street, passing the "Office of the Irish World." The destination, the religious complex named Our Lady of Sorrows, was reached just before noon and the start of dinner.

It was only after dinner that day that information was received indicating Sol. was scheduled to deliver the address for the anniversary celebration. Fortunately, a week or so prior, a fellow diner had inquired about an invitation to deliver the anniversary address. This prior inquiry, combined with a memory of an unexpected speaker announcement (Bernard) at a 50th-anniversary event in Seattle, meant the task was not unwelcome, as the content had already been considered. It was considered a significant opportunity to return to the familiar speaker's platform, which had not been seen for nearly fifteen years, and to speak to both long-standing acquaintances and new ones. The anniversary event concluded, as all events do, and there appeared to be general satisfaction regarding its impact and execution.
styled: At about 11 a.m. we passed through picturesque old Yonkers and still down with, few little ups. Via the Western Driveway past the Washington Bridge (over the Hudson), and over Canal Street past "Office of the Irish World" we reached Our Lady of Sorrows Monastery just before the noon Angelus and dinner greeting. Only after dinner that day was I informed that Fr. Sol. was supposed to give the sermon of the jubilee solemnity. Luckily my next neighbor at table had asked me a week or so before: "Did you get an invitation to preach the jubilee sermon?", and remembering my surprise the morning before the Golden Jubilee in Seatle, by the announcement in church that "Father Bernard will give the sermon", I did not mind the task, having thought things over what to say. In fact I felt it quit a privilege even to get back again into the old pulpit that I had not seen for near fifteen years, and to address old friends & new. Well the jubilee passed, as do all things temporal, and seemingly everyone was satisfied as to its impressiveness, etc.

neutral: Following a profound personal ending, I aim to redirect my aspirations away from past hopes that are no longer attainable. Instead, I want to repeatedly focus on ideals that are neither shattered by reality nor left dormant and unfulfilled. The letter's length may be surprising. I hope its content is serious enough not to cause offense. It was completed Sunday night, having been started at 11 o'clock. It might not have been completed, like many others, had I not improved physically and avoided confinement for recovery. I had only a minor cold. I am assigned to the 5 o'clock service tomorrow, the first Sunday of Lent.
styled: and after the dear Angel of death, to lift my longings of heart and soul from such days "and dreamings never more to be", and to focus them again and again on ideals that are not" .. wrecked on the shores of the real", and neither, sleep like a dream in a grave". Well Dear Edward; you are no doubt surprized at the length of this letter. I hope it is grave enough not to scandalize. I hardly need say I finished it Sunday night after starting as the clock struck 11. I pro- bably had not finished and it would have gone as so many others, and I behaved myself a little better, physically, and not been sent ... a cell recuperating. Just a little cold Thank God. I'm posted for the 5 o'clock Mass tomorrow ( 1st Sunday of Lent) So I'll just say

neutral: Religious texts such as the Bible are considered divinely inspired by the Church, and millions have reportedly benefited from reading them, developing faith and devotion. Conversely, others have read these texts without benefit, or even to their own detriment. This outcome is attributed to an unsuited mindset or a lack of reverence, leading some to misinterpret the scriptures to their own harm. Some consider "The Mystical City of God" to be exceptionally inspiring, comparable to the Bible itself. Its introduction alone, if read with careful attention, is said to strongly suggest an extraordinary origin. The consistent opposition it has encountered from its inception, particularly from those who reject its message, is viewed as further proof of its value in spiritual guidance.
styled: We speak of the Holy Bible, the Holy Gospel, etc, because the Church has declared them to be inspired writings and because millions have profited from their perusal; have learned to believe in God and to love Him by devoutly reading about him therin. Others have read therin without profit; others again to their own detriment. Why so? How? Failure of disposition; Want of reverence. neutral: M. E.J. was transferred to Marathon, Wisconsin. After stopping for a few days en route and spending a few weeks at the new St. Anthony Monastery, he took a vacation of about a week. He spent this time primarily visiting old friends and places from his past, though these locations often differed from his memories. The speaker finds it sufficient to reflect on the significant changes that occurred in Trimbelle even before their departure, and have continued since, both there and around the Mt. St. Helen Home, which is located in the Saint Croix Valley.
styled: One of these was that Fr. M. E.J. was transferred to Marathon, Wis. After stoping here a few days on the way thither, and a few weeks in the new - St. Anthony Monastery - he seems to have quite enjoyed a week or so vacation. This he spent mostly visiting old friends, and scenes of long ago -- in the majority of cases of course, not the same as painted on memory's canvas. Well, if they only reminded him of ups and downs of our in- nocent days, congratulations. In a way I think I would like to have been with him; Though as a rule it suffices me to think back and consider the lonesome changes that were taking place in old Trimbelle even before we left, and that I know to have taken place since, both there and about the Mt. St. Helen Home - the little green garden of the Saint Croix Valley. It suffices me, I wanted to say, to think of these changes by the hand of time.

I recently learned from a clipping sent by Mrs. Doonan that I can now address you as Right Reverend Monsignor. Given this information and having been otherwise informed of your new title, I also want to offer my congratulations. However, I will discuss this further at a later time.

A few days later, a telegram arrived from the Monastery on West 31st Street, New York City, stating that Father wanted to be admitted to St. Elizabeth Hospital. He had not yet succeeded in gaining admission. Father Provincial had, in the meantime, traveled to Calvary, Wisconsin. Upon receiving the telegram, which was sent by special delivery, he wired the Father Guardian at the 31st Street location, instructing him to do everything possible to help Father gain admission to St. Elizabeth's or a similar facility. However, Father M.J. could not be located.
styled: God bless you and yours. But I learn from a clipping that Mrs. Doonan sent me recently that I may address you hereafter as Rt. Rev. Msgr. In that case and since I've been informed of the dignity otherwise I want to say God bless you again; and in as much as it probably is for the glory of His holy Name and that of our Blessed Mother Mary, Let me say also, Congratulations! About this, however, more another time. Well a few days later a telegram from the Monastery on West 31st St. N. Y. City to the efect that Fr. wanted to get into St. Elizabeth Hospital ... what to do, so far he had failed .... Father Provincial had gone to Calvary Wis., in the mean time and on reception of the telegram by special delivery, wired the Fr. Guard- ian in 31st St. to do all in his power to help Father to get into St. Elizabeth's or some other like it. Poor Fr. M.J., however, could not be located. ...

neutral: After experiencing repeated disappointments in the East, he traveled westward again, as a second message from Baltimore indicated less than a week after the first. In Baltimore, he sought treatment for his carbuncle at St. Agnes Hospital and subsequently asked the staff to arrange transport to the B. & O. Depot for a trip to Chicago. Instead, however, they sent him to a retreat, believing he was not in suitable condition to travel alone. In fact, considering the institution and his condition at the time and since, it is clear he could not have been placed in a more suitable location. It was later realized that the earlier suggestion was to pray the "Coronation" rather than simply read it.
styled: Heart-sick, as I imagine he must have been, at disa- pointment after disapointment, in the East, he had turned his steps again westward, as a second communication from Baltimore indicated hardly a week after the former. In Baltimore he had gone to St. Agnes Hospital for treatment on his carbuncle and had afterwards requested the authorities to get him to the B. & O. Depot for Chicago. Instead, however, they had sent him out to said retreat, conscientiously no doubt - providentially I trust - convinced that he was in no fit condition to be traveling a- lone. Indeed the more we have learned about that institution and the more I've considered his condition both at the time and since, the more too am I convinced that he could hardly landed in a better or a more providential place. At all events we at the Monastery here looked opon his going thither as an answer to prayer and as an evi- dence that he was in God's guidance. Only later on it dawned on my mind that my simple proposition - as said above - to pray, rather than simply read, the "Coronation".

neutral: This letter is described as having a humorous, brotherly tone, being both poetic and earnest, and offering comfort. Edward Casey, a missionary in the Philippines, wrote to his elder brother, Maurice Casey, who was then in Yonkers, New York. Maurice had resumed his studies after a twenty-year break, pursuing the same path as his younger brother, and was ordained a year before him. After eighteen years of pastoral and missionary work, Maurice joined the Capuchin Order, taking the name Joachim. The letter contains an example using "K-C", which the brothers understood as a familiar equivalent for "Casey".
styled: NOTE: With a tinge of fraternal humor, the following letter -- at once poetic, yet decidedly earnest -- will be found a relief for any color of the "blues" (in season). A missionary in the Philippines, Rev. Edward Casey, writes an elder brother, Rev. Maurice Casey, at the time in Yonkers, N. Y. The latter, having resumed studying after twenty years vacation continued with the younger and was ordained just a year before him. Then after eighteen years of pastoral and missionary work joined the Capuchin Order as Fr. Joachim. The "K" - "C" used as an example, is at the same time familiar to the brothers as an equivalent of Casey.

neutral: A swift resolution to the situation is desired. M. J. departed from the order approximately two years ago, following the emergence of concerning signs of unrest. Both you and I offered him serious and practical advice at that time. Several months passed before his final departure. The reasons for his mental state and its development are difficult to ascertain. He had been suffering for a considerable period from a severe carbuncle on the back of his neck, a condition potentially capable of causing significant mental distress, regardless of whether it was a cause or an effect of other issues. Although the local doctor found no definitive mental health issues, it appeared that little could be done to assist him or manage his situation within the Monastery. Consequently, he was sent to a hospital in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin, or a similar institution, where his condition was suspected to be hardening of the brain arteries or a related ailment.
styled: God grant it may come to that soon -- "Deo Volente." I am not sure if I told you before of my dismay at same poor, dear Fr. M. J. 's defection, as it has seemed now close to two years, viz., since his unrest began to show itself threatening. You wrote him at the time yourself, earnest, practical lines of advice. I tried to do so too. Well, months went on before the real break came. What was in his mind, and how it was there, is not easy to say. He had been suffering for quite some time from a fearful carbuncle on the back of his neck - whether a cause or an effect of something else - enough to set many a man crazy. At all events, while the local doctor found nothing positively wrong with his mind, there seemed to be little or nothing to be done for him or with him in the Monastery. They sent him, there- fore, to the hospital in Fond du Lac, Wis., or some other, where his case was believed to be hardening of the brain-arteries or something of that nature.

neutral: However, as his father often repeated, human plans do not always come to fruition. Maurice's health failed, and he returned home from the Seminary, which was a disappointment to his family. Worse than that, in his own words, he considered himself "a misfit, a personal failure—a sadly misfit and personal failure." Around that time, his mother's hair began to show signs of graying, and his father's sighs would lead to a quiet reflection: "If I had to start life over again, I'd be a priest." Years and decades passed. It would have been extraordinary not to feel discouraged under such circumstances. However, this was not the first challenge he had encountered, and it was far from being the last he would endure. He quickly adjusted to what seemed like the next best option. He decided to encourage others to pursue religious vocations, and in this way potentially influence someone to take his place in the ministry, serving in roles such as a priest, confessor, or missionary.
styled: Alas! however, as dear Father was wont to repeat, the proverb: "Man proposes-God disposes." Poor, dear Maurice's health failed and he came home from the Seminary a family disappointment and worse than that in his own words: "a misfit, a personal failure - - a sadly misfit and personal failure." Ah! It was about that time that silver began to tell its story in Mother's hair and Father's sighs would bring a gentle Soliloquy: "If I had to start life over again, I'd be a priest." . . Winters and summers slipped away. Years and decacs rolled by. Never to be discouraged under such circumstances would surely be more than human. But this was by no means the first knock he had met, and God, if "those whom God loves He tries," it was far from being the last he was to wether. It did not take too long to adjust himself to what seemed next best. He would promote vocations in others at least and in this way possibly in- fluence someone to take his place at the Altar, in the confessional, on the missions.

neutral:
I hope you are well. Your silence suggests you are as busy as I am, with time passing quickly, which often leaves me feeling unproductive and that I'm not making much progress. For instance, I have many letters I should write but send very few, despite my desire to communicate personally and the expectations of others.

However, my health has been good; generally, working 18 hours a day does not feel burdensome. The Monastery has experienced very few colds and little other sickness this year. I hope we can learn to appreciate the favorable circumstances we experience.

We have positive news from Joachim, as the enclosed copy of his letter will confirm. According to it, he is planning to resume a significant religious service soon.
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope you are well and that the silence you maintain is only an indication that your time, like my own, flies, whither I hardly know; so that it seems almost continually blaming me for doing nothing and getting nowhere. There are so many letters, e. g. I ought to write and still so few I get off, as I would like to do personally, and as is often expected. Thanks be to God, however, my health has been good; so that, as a rule 18 hours a day hardly seems to weigh me down at all. Again, "Deo Gratias." We've had hardly any colds in the Monastery this year and very little sickness otherwise. I just hope that we may some day learn to appreciate His graces and be grateful to God. Thanks be to God, we have good word from Father Joachim, as the en- closed copy of his letter will convince you. According to it, you will see that he is figuring on saying Holy Mass again before long.

neutral: Due to an apparent lack of understanding of his condition, the hospital(s) seemed to minimize the seriousness of his situation and discharged him without further assistance. Again, his voice was so unfamiliar that even when his identity was confirmed by the speaker, I could not recognize his voice. The senior leader dispatched me to assess his situation and determine what assistance could be provided. We had dinner with Coughlin and his household. Afterward, the three of us held a confidential conference for approximately half an hour. Coughlin was very practical and earnest, speaking with the intensity of someone addressing a large audience. Following his request, M. J.

Well, instead of speeding up my efforts to finish the book, I decided to start over again and to read it with due reverence from the beginning. Without a word about it to anyone, I felt that our Blessed Mother would know what I was doing and why. . . . I could hardly help being anxious. I I try not to be. Rather, on the contrary, am trying to foster con- fidence in the wisdom and good ness of God and the powerful inter- cession of our Blessed Mother Mary. "Deo Gratias." Relocating to the current location has provided significant relief from the persistent difficulties and strain experienced over twenty years at the previous office in Detroit. Although the work hours may be comparable, the change in environment is beneficial. At the current location, correspondence consumes most of the time. Previously, much of that work was delegated. While still encountering challenging situations that require resolution or alleviation, the overall strain and tension are considerably less pressing.
styled: However, he seemed promising and pleased when I suggested that with his coaching us just a little that difficulty could probably be minimized. This especially since he had assured me that he himself is there in the Chancery practically every day. Your coming in May or June therefore would probably be oppor- tune. For that matter he did not make any suggestions when we should come, except that he said he would be away the week of April 11th, since he is expected in Milwaukee for the Consecration of a new Bishop. I did not ask him but I understand its to be Msgr. Meyers - new Bishop of Superior. Yes, my coming hither to St. Michael's has been a decided re- lief to me from the continued drain and strain of difficulties brought to the office for twenty years at St. Bonaventure's in Detroit. I do have perhaps as long hours but its a change. Here its correspondence takes most of my time. There, I simply had to leave most of that to others; and while I meet with pathetic cases to solve or try to aleviate the strain and tension is by no means so pressing.

To summarize this page, I would like you to note two problems I have been working on without satisfactory progress. I acknowledge my delay in thanking you, but I am doing so now.

Therefore, although I should have thanked you earlier for your support and interest in the Seraphic Mass Association and for the welfare of those in distress, I will do so now. However, this time, I will prepare the certificates as appropriate.

I hope you can easily overlook my omissions and errors in the above. With best regards to Maurice Joachim, Klein, and Harrington, and any mutual acquaintances you may encounter, I hope to continue to be of service to you and your valuable work.

P.S. To E'd: I have reconsidered and prepared the enclosed card.
styled: In brief conclusion of this page, I wish you would make a special memento for a couple of problems I have been working on without the progress I'd be encouraged to see. "Better late than never", Answered Joe Ferbush working on the roof of the "new granery" down on the Burkhardt farm when I called him to supper, lamenting tardiness. So, while to have thanked you in the beginning for your charitable interest and faith in the Seraphic Mass Association together with the welfare of our dear ones in estrangement from the ways of peace .... I'll do so now; while, this time at least, I shall prepare certificates according- ly, etc. Hoping that you may, without too much trouble supply my skip- ping and slipping in the course of the above and with best regards and God's blessing to Father Maurice Joachim, Father Klein, and Father Harrington and all our friends you may chance to meet, I hope to remain, of service to you and your good work etc, P.S. Dear Monsignor E'd. I thought it over and have made out the inclosed card ....
