neutral: The passage expresses a hopeful belief that more of the original sixteen individuals, including their parents, have died and are now in an afterlife. These deceased individuals are seen as examples to follow in maintaining one's beliefs, praying for others, and resisting worldly temptations, with the ultimate goal of achieving a divine vision. Mary Ann was the first to die, followed a week later by Martha, both described as innocent children. Others died subsequently. Their endurance during their final struggles and their apparent strong faith in God lead to the belief that all of them have achieved a favorable outcome in the afterlife. It is also believed that many deceased relatives and neighbors are interceding for the living and requesting prayers from them. This situation is interpreted as an example of the spiritual connection between the living and the deceased.
styled: How grateful we ought to be that we can confidently hope that we have another, another of our original sixteen -- with dear Father and Mother -- waving us from beyond the grave to follow their footsteps in keeping the faith, in praying for one another as among the INTERESTS OF THE SACRED HEART and striving manfully against the world, the flesh and the devil for the one great prize of the final BEATIFIC VISION. Mary Ann was the first to cross the border into eternity and saintly little Martha a week later -- innocent children -- and the others following after, judging from their patience in their final struggles and the seemingly brightness of their faith in God, give great hope that so far every one of them have made the Great Grade, have saved their souls -- the one thing necessary -- and with so many of our dear ones of kin and neighbors are praying for us and asking our prayers. Ah !.. What else is this than just a little side-view of the great Communion of the Saints? Thanks and praises and Glory be to God!

neutral: The individual, Austin, preferred that name. Information regarding his final days was desired. Austin sent a letter from the hospital, seemingly after his first operation. He appeared composed and reflective about his future, and it was evident he knew he had cancer. In the letter, Austin stated his observation that cancer was rarely cured, particularly by surgery. He also expressed a reliance on spiritual support for his well-being. He mentioned receiving religious rites at 6 a.m. on the morning of his surgery and again on the second day, expressing gratitude for these experiences. The narrator noted that Austin's expressed reliance on spiritual support appeared to be fulfilled on a particular religious observance. Austin had previously requested prayers for Pat, even before his illness. The narrator believed Austin had been praying for reconciliation involving Pat, and that this reconciliation was achieved.
styled: Gus - Austin rather, since he prefered and as I told him, so much more like the real name of the great doctor of the Church. I would like to have details of his last days. He wrote me quite a touching letter from the hospital apparently after his first operation, seemingly quite cool and philosophical about what might come -- and certainly with beautiful faith. He evidently knew that he had cancer. Just a few of his words: "I have observed that very seldom is cancer cured ... at least by surgery. "I am relying on the Sacred Heart to come to my rescue . " . .. "I was privileged to receive our Lord at 6 a.m. the morning they opened me; and again on the 2nd day (1st Friday) , Thanks and praise to the Sacred Heart." How beautifully condescending that the Merciful Sacred H't actually did come to his rescue on His own blessed Feast! He had written me a number of times to pray for Pat., even before he was sick. I am sure he was praying for his -- their reconsiliation, etc. and how beautifully did it not come about!

neutral: I am grateful for all developments. The way things unfold, like all events, is profound and intricate. I have just read your interesting message, which I had been expecting for some time. I was perhaps a little concerned that I hadn't heard from you recently from Brooklyn. I am also grateful for your good health and that of Maurice J. I am hopeful for positive developments for us in the future, always anticipating the best outcomes, provided we do not interfere with those outcomes through our own actions. You will likely be pleased to learn that I have finally initiated steps to facilitate your meeting with Bishop Molloy. I had a pleasant visit with his auxiliary, Bishop Carney, last Friday. He appears to be a modest, friendly, young leader and expressed significant interest in your work for religious schools in the Philippines. I had heard that meeting Bishop Molloy is often difficult, so I was not surprised when I subtly brought up that point.
styled: God bless you and all. Thanks be to the Good God for all things. His ways like all His works are so deep, so divine. I just read your interesting communication, which for some time I have been more or less expecting - possibly with a tinge of a gentle ear-pull at your not having recently heard / Br'klin. Thank God again for yourself and Fr. Maurice J's good health and for whatever His great plans may materialize for us in the near and distant future - always planning for our best - " .. if we only don't spoil His plans by ours" . Well, I am sure you will be pleased to know that I did finally wake up and take at least some steps toward your seeing Bishop Molloy. I had a very nice little visit with his auxeliary last Friday, Bishop Carney. He seems to be quite a modest, friendly, young Prelate and showed a decided interest in your work for religious schools in the Philippines. I had heard before that it is not too easy to see His Excellency Bishop Molloy and therefore, it did not surprise me when 1 intimated something to that effect.

neutral: My availability will depend on your program arrangements. I have not heard recently from anyone in the western region. Hopefully, this indicates that things are going smoothly there. I believe I owe you two letters since January. The problem is that I frequently postpone answering letters until I can respond thoroughly, and soon they get buried and are often forgotten. My apologies.
styled: So I'll be more or less depending on your arrangements for a program, etc. I have not heard just lately from any one in the farther west. Please God it's indicative of smoothe sailing out that way. Thanks be to God and our Bl. Mother Mary and all the Communion of Saints. P. S. I believe I owe you a couple letters since January. The trouble is -- too often -- I put letters aside till I can answer them properly and the 1st thing I know they're snowed under and often forgotten. Please pardon.

neutral: I hope you are well. After writing a card to M. E. Joachim this morning, I felt I should also send you a few lines. Approximately one year ago at this time, we were traveling through Santa Barbara as we approached Los Angeles. Considering our friends along the coast, it was a privilege. I will tell you about the remainder of my trip after Owen and I left you on the bus for Mt. Anges1. I arrived in Seattle that evening, then in Spokane at 6:30 p.m., in St. Paul on Tuesday at 7:15 a.m., and again in St. Paul on Thursday at 10:30 p.m. as scheduled. I reached Chicago around 6:30 p.m. on Friday, and Detroit on Saturday at 4:30 p.m. The following morning, I attended a service at the Convent. I arrived in New York on Monday morning and Brooklyn on Monday afternoon. Since leaving Los Angeles, I only missed two religious services. You buried the body of .
styled: I sure hope you are well. I wrote a card to Fr. M. E. Joachim this morning and it's been on my mind all day that I should send you also a few lines. You can guess about the time if I say that just a year about this time you and I were passing through beautifully picturesque little Sta. Barbara, as nearing Los Angeles. Thanks be to God -- and our dear ones adown the Coast, - was it not quite a privilege, all in all? Some day, D. v., I'll tell you of the rest of my trip after I and poor, dear Owen left you on the bus for Mt. Anges1. Suffice now to say that I arrived in Seattle that p.m. at 6:30 in Spokane, Tuesday at 7:15 a.m. in St. Paul Thurs. 10:30 p.m. on schedule; in Chicago about 6:30 p.m. Friday: Detroit Sat. at 4:30 p.m. Convent Mass next a.m .; New York and Brooklyn Monday a.m. and p.m. respectively. From Los Angeles Only missed two holy Masses, Deo gratias. Well, you burried the mortal remains of poor dear .

neutral: I hope you are in good health. We are well here in St. Felix. After a cold and wet spring, including black frost on the 8th, the weather has become ideal. I was pleased to receive a very positive letter from M. Joachim last week, one of the best in a long time. He seems to be back to his usual self. Several weeks ago, I informed him that I had already received permission to take a trip to Chicago and St. Paul, among other places, at my discretion, with the arrangements to be made by you and him. I believe he mentioned sending you a copy of that letter. We expect the Provincial from Detroit shortly; he is just back from Guam and several other Pacific islands. I anticipate no difficulty in obtaining permission to also go to Superior, as M. Joachim proposes. I would appreciate any suggestions that might enhance the appeal of the proposal. I will likely receive approximately a week off for the trip.
styled: I hope this finds you in the best of health and hopes. Thanks be to God we are quite well down here in St. Felix. After a cold and wet spring -- even black frost on the 8th the weather has turned quite ideal. Deo Gr. I was certainly pleased to receive a very bright letter from Fr. M. Joachim last week, about the best in a long time. It really looks like his old self once more. Thanks be to God "a billion." I wrote him several weeks ago that I had already permis - sion to go on a trip to Chicago and St. Paul, etc. at my choice and leaving the arrangements to yourself and him. I believe he said he sent you a copy of said letter. Well, We expect V. Rev. Fr. Provincial down from Detroit shortly -- just back from Guam and several other islands in the Pacific, and I anticipate no difficulty in obtaining permission to go also to Superior as M. J. proposes. I would be glad to have any suggestions that might heighten interests relative to the proposition. I'll probably get a week or so off for the trip.

neutral: I hope my delay in responding to your letters from early December is not a problem. I am currently trying to catch up, having written three letters consecutively. I had hoped to acquire one of the items referred to as 'Begone S.' I recall having a couple in Brooklyn, but I am uncertain if they were included or if I can find them now among my other belongings. Until just before Christmas, I was consistently falling behind in my correspondence, despite occasional assistance from others. Currently, Michael, a former assistant from Pitt Street I. Y. who is now involved in outreach work, helps me when he is not away. However, I will try to obtain a copy of that booklet for you; I believe I have one somewhere. I am sending this letter via expedited airmail, hoping it will arrive before the regular mail letter I sent yesterday, which did not include a name or comment. Regarding the $20 check dated December 10th: Since I was unsure how you wished for it to be used, I have used the funds to register your specific request with a group dedicated to spiritual observances for the deceased, identified by the reference 310. This allocation is temporary, pending any further instructions from you.
styled: Hoping that my tardiness in answering your letters early in December may not scandalize, I am trying these few days to makd up for lost time - three in-a-row. I hoped to get one of those "Begone S." I know I had a couple of them in Brooklyn, but whether or not they put them in or if I can find them now among other things I am not certain. Till shortly before Christmas I was continually getting behind in my correspondence; though others helped me now and then. Now, thank God Fr.Michael, one of my former altar boys from Pitt Street I. Y. and now one of our missionaries helps me when not away. However, I am going to try and get a copy of that booklet for you. I must have one somewhere I am trying to get this off Air-special so as if possible to overtake the one I mailed you yesterday without name of comment regular mail. As to that $20. check, of Dec. 10th: not knowing what you might want me to do with it, I am enroling the Poor Holy Souls for your intion. - at least till further instructed, - i.e. 310.

neutral: This note, which was intended to begin on the evening of the 4th, is now concluding. The enclosed letter from Miss Ryan in New York outlines the ongoing hope of encouraging relatives to embrace a particular religious devotion by reading and praying from the book 'Autobiography of God's eternally chosen Queen of the Universe,' also known as 'The Mystical City of God.' Miss Ryan would appreciate a message of appreciation and encouragement, possibly a verse. She had been a successful businesswoman prior to a major conflict. In 1942, an order was issued by the government in Washington to discard all unused prints and cuts unless they were redeemed. The redemption fee for 'The Mystical City of God' prints was $500.00. The situation was further complicated by a religious authority, under whose jurisdiction the prints were stored, prohibiting their retrieval. However, Miss Ryan, who is characterized by a strong spiritual devotion...
styled: I just felt I'd have to bring the note I meant to start, on evening of the 4th to an end. I hope it has not bored you. The inclosed letter from Miss Ryan in New York will give an idea of what my hopes were -- still are -- of converting our wayward family and clan to seraphic love of God and our Bl. Mother Mary, by having them read and pray the wonderful, all-outstanding "Autobiography of God's eternally chosen Queen of the Universe", the "Mystical City of God". Dear Edward: I think Miss Ryan would appreciate a line from you, of appreciation and of encouragement. Better a verse. She had been quite a successful business-lady before the War. I think it was in 1942 that quite an unexpected order came from Washington to "scrap" all prints and cuts not in actual use unless redeemed, etc. The redemption-fee on the Mystical City of God prints was quite an item; $500.00 I believe; and with a bishop in whose jurisdiction these prints were stored forbidding the rescue, it certainly looked dark for them. However, Miss R. who seems to be specially devoted to the Holy Ghost ...

neutral: The local superior, after a brief discussion, provisionally suggested that I could begin on June 1st or 2nd. I believe that would be quite early, unless there was a specific reason for it. If there was an assignment to complete somewhere before or, preferably, after the anniversary, arrangements could be made. A meeting of the leadership council is being held at the St. Bonaventure's facility for the next three or four days. I understand that immediately afterward, the regional superior, having traveled many thousands of miles, plans to come here for a rest, which I presume is intended as a private period of respite for him. There is a possibility that I might be transferred back to Detroit or elsewhere, though I consider it highly improbable. I have no concern whatsoever about whether I remain here or am transferred. It is, after all, fundamentally the same. It is an immense privilege to know with certainty that one is acting in accordance with divine purpose by adhering to the regulations and complying with instructions. Unfortunately, it is difficult for any of us to fully appreciate such privileges.
styled: Rev. Fr. Guardian, after a little consultation just noted -- tentatively -- that I could start June 1st or 2nd. Of course I think that would be rather early, unless there were a purpose for it. If we had a mission to do somewhere before the anniversary or possibly preferably after, we could arrange accordingly. They are having a meeting in Saint Bonaventure's these three or four days, of the Definitorium and I understand that right thereafter Father Provincial after many thousand miles travel is figuring on coming down here for a rest. -- a sort of private retreat for himself I presume. There is a possibility that I be sent back there to Detroit or elsewhere, though I hardly think it at all probable. I have not the least worry about whether I re- main here or be transferred. It is after all, essentially quite the same. It is such a surpassing privilege to know definitely that one is doing God's holy will by keeping the rule and obeying. Sorry to say, if we can use the word, it is so little possible for any of us to appreciate such privileges.

neutral: Everyone on the Coast appears to be doing well. This situation is a cause for considerable gratitude. Also enclosed is a letter from Brother Pat. He also appears to be well and maintains a positive disposition. This correspondence was intended to be sent yesterday morning, as had been communicated to Grace. Apologies for the delay.
styled: Otherwise every one seems to be holding their own on the Coast. How can we ever be thankful as we ought to be! Glory be to God. Inclosed is also a letter from poor, dear Brother Pat. He too seems well and, glad to see, still retains a coloring of favorable humor. I should have had this off yesterday morning, as I told Grace I would and by all means meant to do. ... Please pardon.

neutral: I apologize for the delay in responding to your correspondence. Fortunately, I have recently been engaged in practical exercises suitable for a Capuchin novice. Four weeks ago, we traveled to Milwaukee for a celebration honoring Father Stephen Eckert, whose Dominican brother, Brother Michael, you must know. From Notre Dame... Afterwards, I was transported by ambulance to St. Michael's Hospital. From there, after two days, I was moved to St. Felix - St. Joseph Hospital in Fort Wayne for two weeks (16 days). I am now back at the Novitiate. I am grateful for my recovery. They considered me a critical patient, but I am now able to bend my knee and eat, which is a genuine improvement. Now I need to catch up on correspondence and other matters. I certainly sympathize with you and your associate. Best wishes to everyone, including the staff at St. Joseph Hospital, where I received very supportive and compassionate encouragement. I always leave with renewed memories of St. Thomas. I wish Father Cashman well and acknowledge all the excellent work.
styled: God bless you and yours. Pardon my tardiness in complying with demands of -- correspondence. Thanks be to God I've had some really practical exercises recently that befit a capuchin novitiate ..... Four weeks ago we drove over to Milwaukee for a celebration in honor of Fr. Stephen Eckert, whose Dominicad (Dominican brother) Br. Michael you must have .... . From Notre Dame .... Afterwards they ambulanced me to St. Michael's Hospital - thence after two days to St. Felix - St. Joseph Hospital Ft. Wayne for two long weeks (16 days) and now again back to the Novitiate .... Deo Gratias. They seem to think they had pretty critical patient I can genuflect again .... and can eat - "no foolin." Now to catch up a little with letters, etc .... God help us ... I surely sympathize with you and your practical associate .. . . Best wishes to all ...... including down to the personnel of St. Joseph Hospital where I met such really fraternal and sister- like encouragement !.... I always bring away with me newly awakened memories from St. Thomas. God bless Fr. Cashman ... and all the great work:

neutral:
I hope you and your family are well. We are doing well here. We've had a very mild winter, with very little snow and practically no colds. Despite this, there has been a lot of rain, and early in the week, sleet and freezing rain caused shrubs and trees in many places to be weighed down to the point of breaking.

The enclosed telegram arrived two nights ago, and Grace phoned yesterday morning to provide more details and asked me to inform you about the situation. Bernard Sr. had been in Eureka on official business and was quite occupied Thursday evening, leading him to neglect a natural bodily function. Consequently, he had to go to the hospital for treatment. Grace did not seem to think it was very serious comparatively. We hope, of course, that it was not serious. However, it is wise to hope that no serious consequences arise from such experiences.
styled: God bless you and yours -- Aye and -- including this poor plodder. I surely hope you keep well. Thanks be to God we are well down here. We've had a very mild Winter, hardly any snow to speak of and practically no colds. All this, not- withstanding quite a lot of rain and early in the week a visita- tion of sleet and freezing rain that in quite a few places shrubs and trees were loaded down to breaking down. The inclosed telegram came the night before last and Grace phoned yesterday morning giving more particulars and asking that I let you know about the situation. Bernard, Sr. had been out on some official busines in Eureka, was quite occupied Thursday evening so that he neglected some kind of a natural call to which he was not as promptly obedient as Grandmother Nature often has to insist on. So he had to go to the hospital for treatment. Grace did not seem to think it very serious coparatively. We hope of course that it was not serious. However, they are right -- we do right rather -- to pray that nothing serious come of such experiences.

neutral: A message was received yesterday for Jimmy Ryan, who is approximately 80 years old and was situated beside Kate. A letter was also received yesterday from Pat, which indicated Pat was busy and hopeful. Mildred Conley called from Chicago a short time ago, providing details about Neil and Genevieve's trip to Europe.
styled: I got a mes- I hope it may in some way break sage of yesterday to Jimmy Ryan. the ice for what we hope the holy Ghost may deign to promp you to do. Jimmy must be now about 80. He was next to Kate . I rec- eived a very interesting letter from Br. Pat yesterday. . Quite busy and hopeful. Thank be to God. Mildred Conley phoned a few minutes ago from Chicago quite some details about Neil and Gene- vieve's going to Europe.

neutral: December 26. I had intended to contact you before Christmas, as I also planned to contact several other individuals. Owen is preparing to return to the West; he was here Monday night. He appears to be doing well. He will go to Chicago first. Everyone here at St. Felix has been well recently, with only a few exceptions. Owen is about to seal his letter and suggested that I include mine with his. I had hoped you would visit upon your return from your engagements in New York. I am pleased to hear of their success.
styled: Dec. 26 - God bless you Father E'd - Rt. Rev Msg. rather. I meant to reach you before the beautiful Feast Xmas as indeed was on my mind in regards to quite some others. Br. Owen is about to start back for the West - been here Monday night. He seems to hold his own, Deo Gr. - back to Chicago first. Thanks be to God We've all been well here at the St. Felix lately. with few exceptions. Now O. B. J. (Owen) comes along and is about to seal his letter. So suggests that I just put it in with his. . . I did hope to have you call on your return or your return from your missions in New York. Thank God for the success. ·

neutral: Few people understood the significance of Fr. Maurice's twenty years of humiliation. Even fewer knew of the at least twelve years of disappointment and humiliation that led to his calm and perfect acceptance. This was evident during his time at the Mt. Hope Sanatorium, and particularly at the moment of his death, which occurred peacefully during prayer. This marked a significant change, a transition.
styled: ~ and the prayers and sighs there offered for vocations and, as we may surely hope, reinforced and reechced in Purgatory or and indeed even in Heaven - Fr. M. E. J. still active. Comparatively very few ever tried to fathom the meaning of those twenty years of humiliation to Fr. Maurice. And still fewer I think ever knew of the, at-least-dozen-yrs dispointment and humiliations where- by she merciful Divine Wisdom deigned to chisel and to emery him down to such calmly perfect acceptance of God's holy designs - as manifested both in the Mt. Hope San. and especially as you were privileged to see him, during rosary, slumber into Eternity; -- the "change", the transition -- "Tuis enim fidelibus Domine Vita Mutatur non taliture." .. Oremus pro invicem ...

neutral: I have just seen the photo you sent of M. E. Joachim's tombstone. I am currently using a chair as a writing desk, with my feet elevated. I have not officiated at Mass since last Thursday. The skin burns I wrote to you about last week (if that letter was received) caused the eczema to flare up again, after Dr. Stan Casey treated the burns. He referred me to a skin specialist in Fort Wayne, Dr. McNairy, who emphasizes keeping one's feet elevated during treatment. I would have officiated at Mass yesterday, but the Guardian advised me to adhere to the doctor's orders. This will likely mean a week or so before I am fully recovered. It gives me comparatively little pain or itch, so the time does not pass as painfully as it might otherwise. Regarding the aforementioned tombstone, it is fortunate that we were able to acquire such a respectable memorial. It is extremely brief, of course, but it is unknown how many individuals might be inspired to dedicate their lives to spiritual service, or have their commitment to such a path solidified, by its simple inscription. The simple inscription itself holds significant potential.
styled: I just read the photo you sent me of our dear Father M. E. Joachim's tomb-marker and, sitting here with my two feet on another chair am using it as a writing desk. Deo gratias. I've not said holy Mass since last Thursday. The skin-burns I wrote you about last week (if it got off), started the eczema activity again - after I'd had a Dr. Stan Casey treat the former. He sent me to a skin- specialist in Ft. Wayne, Dr. McNairy, who stresses with treatment, "feet up." I would have offered holy Mass yesterday but Fr. Guardian thought better keep to Dr.'s orders. So that will probably mean a week or so before I'm on my feet again properly. Thanks be to God is gives me comparatively little pain or itch; so that time does not hang so painfully as it might otherwise. As for above-said "marker", I think we should be grateful indeed that the good God enabled us to procure such a creditable "memorial. Extremely brief of course, but even so, who knows how many a vocation its simple reading may be destined to awaken, to encourage, to anchor. Ah ! "Its simple reading' ?

neutral: I began writing a letter to you on Monday, intending it to be substantial. I haven't been able to finish it, and my response to your proposal regarding the Gregorian Masses should have already reached you. I regret that I must decline this generous proposal. This is due to the rule that members of the Order are typically only able to allocate two requests for religious services per month. All other requests for religious services are left to the discretion and allocation of the local Superior. However, I have enrolled Grace multiple times in the Seraphic Mass Association, which I believe provides significant benefit each time. Indeed, based on reports of positive outcomes received from it, it is difficult to find a comparable alternative. Somehow, I did not learn of Grace's death until after my High Mass on Sunday, April 12.
styled: My dear Brother Edward. Rt. Rev. Monsignore: God bless you these days of grace. I started Monday with the intention of writing you a letter as I hoped would be worthwhile. I have not been able to finish it and my answer to your proposition about the Gregorian Masses ought to be already on the way thither. In a way I regret I'll have to be a disappointment in this really generous proposition You will understand from the fact that as members of the Order we have as a rule only the disposal of two holy Mass intentions per month. Otherwise all intentions for holy Masses are life (left) to the disposal and appointment of the local Superior. I have enrolled poor, dear Grace, however, anumber of times in the Seraphic Mass -Association, which in my conviction, means, each time an emmense benefit. In fact, judging from the reports of favors as received there therefrem, it is not easy to find a comparason. Deo gratias! Some how I did not receive word of Grace's death till after my High-Mass on Sunday April 12.

neutral: This text was written by Monsignor E. F. Casey to his youngest brother, Father M. J., whom E. F. Casey was older than by approximately fifteen months. However, Father M. J. is also identified as their second eldest brother and is now the eldest living. Owen was the youngest of ten brothers. Three sisters were among his nine older brothers. Three more siblings followed Owen; these three are still living and are now grandmothers. The text briefly mentions the mother's death, which followed a ten-day struggle. Monsignor E. F. Casey was rescued from the Japanese prison camp at Los Baños, along with two bishops, 150 priests, and 125 nuns, among over 2,000 prisoners. Early on the morning of February 23, 1943, the day when the Japanese appeared to be planning a mass execution of the prisoners, they were rescued by the MacArthur Forces.
styled: The above was written by the present Rt. Rev. Msgr. E'd F. Casey to his youngest brother, whom he had preceeded by birth about fifteen months, Father M. J., about whom the writer is concer ned, is their second eldest brother -- now the eldest living. Owen was the youngest of ten brothers with three sister among his nine brothers ahead of him and three more immediately following. These three are still living -- now grandmas. The writer briefly touches on dear Mother's beautiful death. May she rest with saints in Heaven. Thanks be to God for the great grace He provided her, for the ten-day fearful, yet glorious struggle, that preceeded her wonderful victory in a Happy Death P. S. The writer of the above, Rt. Rev. Edw'd, was rescued from the Jap. Prison Los Bonos. with two bishops, 150 priest and one hundred twenty-five nuns among over 2000 prisoners. Very early the morning of February 23rd, 1943 the day on which the desperate Japps would seem to have been planing a whole-sale masacre of them; they were rescued by the MacArthur Forces.

neutral:
A new phase may begin after May 2nd. A message card was unexpectedly discovered in the machine when a recording was initiated. The individual was reportedly more surprised than disappointed about the cancellation of the trip to Milwaukee and reacted positively to both developments.

Nerius, the Vice-Postulator for the canonization process, likely found insufficient time to hold another conference before departing for Europe and Rome. A General Chapter meeting is scheduled in Rome, commencing on the 18th with a three-day period of prayer for guidance.

There is a general preference for Clement of Milwaukee to remain in his position. However, Clement himself has already sent some of his belongings back to the U.S., as he is known to have a tendency to withdraw from responsibilities. A letter received last week was noted as interesting.
styled: P. S. ? Perhaps rather a new start for above May 2nd. It was not without surprise that I found the foregoing card in the machine when I went with this to start my "Te Deum, (afterwards inserting the "10:15 P. M., etc.) Incidently, I was probably more surprised than disapoin- at not going to Milwaukee. Thank the Lord, I was able to smile at the profference of both. The Vice-Postulator of the cause, V. Rev. Nerius, O. M. Cap. probably found the time too short before start- ing off for Europe and Rome to hold another conference. There is to be a General Chapter in Rome - starting with a triduum of prayer to the Holy Ghost on the 18th for God's holy Grace and guidance. Of course we'd all like to see Fr. Clement of Milwauke retained, D. v. - excepting Fr. Clement himself who has already sent some of baggage back ahead of him to U. S. . . He is known to be rather of a retiring disposition - from responsabilities. Many thanks for your interesting letter last week.

neutral: I missed this morning's scheduled contact, but I hope to reach you soon to arrange a convenient meeting. I am confident that this will be as significant as a formal meeting, and I will send them a letter before you make contact. Barbara Bedolfe phoned, and Wallace wrote about his first participation in significant religious ceremonies two weeks ago. I believe it was on August 2nd.
styled: Well, I did miss this a.m.'s pick-up, but I hope to reach you soon enough to make it conveni- ent for you/ see them in the near future. In a way I am confident that it will be close at least to as good as a "parish apointment," I shall try to reach them with a letter ahead of you. . Barbara Bedolfe phoned, and Wallace himself wrote about his first confession and Holy Communion two weeks ago. Deo Gr! I believe it was on August 2nd.

neutral: Wishing well to everyone, including friends and even adversaries. More than six weeks ago, after reading your letter, I immediately began to respond. I've only just started, and already a new period has arrived, indicating the rapid passage of time. Despite having experienced weather conducive to illness over the past three months, we have so far only had one case of that epidemic. I just returned from Detroit, where I had been since Wednesday, and found three complete sets of the Mystical City of God in our quarters. These were left by Wallace Bedolfe, who stayed here overnight about a week ago. Miss Doris Panyard of 1705 Peck Street, Muskegan, Michigan, just called to inform me that he requested four sets, one for himself. This promising 23-year-old had undergone a formal initiation ceremony, as had his elder brother Bob and sister Barbara. Grace has likely informed you about them. This refers to an aerial view of the St. Felix Victory Noll facility, which is located to the distant rear-left, overlooking the Wabash River. This facility also serves as the headquarters of the Missionary Catechists. We believe this photograph was taken by a local minister who is known to have a hobby in photography.
styled: God Bless us all - Yourself and myself and all our friends and honest enemies if such there be. More than six weeks ago, having readyour letter I started to respond at once . . . God help us! I just got started and here we have Sexigesima. Thanks be to God! though we've had quite a little grippe-weather the last three months, we so far, have had but one case of that epidemic. Up in Detroit since Wednesday, I just returned . . finding 3 full sets of the Mystical City of God in our Cell (% Wallace Bedolfe who was here over night about a week ago) Miss Doris Panyard of 1705 Peck Street Muskegan, Michigan just phoned me that he requested four sets -- one for himself. Deo gratias! -- a promising 23 yr. oldster who was baptised as was his elder Br. Bob and Sister Barbara. No doubt Grace has told you about them Air View. St. Felix Friary - Victory Noll overlooking the Wabash in distant rear --- left. Headq's of the Missionary Catechists. We think this snapped by a local Minister who is said to have a hobby in such.

neutral: This message is sent promptly so you can take advantage of a proposal. This proposal has been considered since your letter from White Plains, which mentioned your plans to be in the Green Bay Diocese during August. You may recall Mr. Philip Obrien of Chicago, who is currently at his summer farm fifteen miles outside Bailey's Harbor, Wisconsin. His wife, Eleanor, was contacted last night. They had expected you to contact them earlier this summer before they departed Chicago. They are now expecting you to contact them and to stay with them for at least a few days before the end of the month. Their telephone number is 15 R. 34 at Waseda Farm, Bailey's Harbor, Wisconsin. They request that you reverse the charges when calling. They will make arrangements for your visit.
styled: I want to reach you with this as soon as possible so that it be convenient for you to profit by a little proposition - up my sleeve since your interesting let- ter from White Plains, in reference to your betsg plans to be in the Green Bay Diocese during August. You probably remember me telling you about Mr. Philip Obrien of Chicago - just now on his summer-far ?if- teen miles out of Bailey's Harbor, Wisconsin, I called his amiable Wife Eleanor last nite - a little like Mrs. Tom Tobin of fifty years ago. ... They were expecting you to call on them earlier in the Summer before they left Chicago. Now they will be expecting you to get in touch with them and to stay with them at least a few days before the Month slips by. Their telephone - please don't disapoint us, then & - is: 15 R. 34. Waseda Farm Bailey's Harbor, Wisconsin. "3€ sure and have him reverse charges. We will see to his coming." P.M.

neutral:
Congratulations on your article published in "Priest." It is unfortunate that it could not be published in numerous other publications.

Beatrice McCahill visited from Chicago, at 7612 N. Ashland. She had previously pledged $100 to your Seminary, contingent on receiving a specific favor. The promised item is enclosed. I am pleased to provide this unexpected item. I am attempting to send it today.

I feel I am accomplishing very little, despite the significant amount of work that needs to be done. I frequently struggle to determine what to prioritize.
styled: Congratulations on your practical Write in the "Priest." Too bad you could'nt have it in a hundred publications. Miss Beatrice McCahill was over from Chicago, 7612 N. Ashland. She promised a $100 for your Seminary some time ago if she got a certain favor. . Here with you'll find same. Delighted to give the surprise. I am trying to get it off To-Day. God help us! I hardly seem to be getting anything done - any- yet so much to be done. I am often at my wits' end what to do first. · God bless us all.

neutral: Her serious health problems began more than a year before her husband's death. She had stomach cancer. The verses were written while he was in college, and she was considering joining a religious order. She was survived by three sons, one daughter, and approximately ten grandchildren.
styled: Her real struggling had started sometime before, her dear husband's death, which occured more than a year earlier. Hers - stomach cancer. P.S. The verses were written while he was still in college and as yet she was still dreaming of going to the convent. She left three sons, a daughter and about ten grand children.

neutral: A call was received regarding the matter while the author was conducting a service. The caller stated they would contact again later, but no further communication occurred at that time. Mr. Porter did not recall the caller's name, but Thomas Brady sent a telegram that evening. A request had fortunately been submitted for a special religious service for Mr. Sol's specific intention, and the following day, a regularly scheduled service was held. The author was pleased to conduct both services in memory of Grace Agatha. The author expressed profound satisfaction regarding this death, viewing it as another positive instance among others that have occurred without exception. It appears the author's parents continue their evening prayers, which include specific requests for a peaceful death and a positive final assessment. The author hopes that those remaining continue to uphold the principle of spiritual unity among individuals. The author concluded with a well-wish to the recipient.
styled: Some one phoned about it while I was on the Altar saying they would call later and that was the end of it. Brother Porter was not particular about the name of the caller but Thomas Brady wired that evening. Luckyly someone had sent in a request for a special holy Mass for Fr. Sol's Intent., and the following day I had a regular Missam propriam. I was happy to offer them both for poor, dear, Grace Agatha R. I. P. After all, how can we ever be grateful as we ought to be, for another so hopeful and beautiful death added to the happy list so far without exception. Glory and thanks be to God! Re - quiescant I.P. It would just seem that dear Mother and Father are keeping up their happy old night-prayers for -- "and for a happy death and a favorable judgement." I hope we all -- still left behind in this exile -- keep up on our part too that beautiful so beautiful feature of Communion of Saints. God bless you again Father - -

neutral: The sender reports having been unwell for approximately one week but has been able to officiate Mass. The sender anticipates seeing Crisi regarding the Mercy Hall Hospital case in Detroit in the near future. Crisi's opponents have been relentless in disseminating falsehoods.
styled: I hope this finds you well. I've not been too well now for a good week. But thank God I've been able to say holy Mass. We hope to see the Crisi in the Mercy Hall Hospital case, Detroit very soon. Her Enemies have hesitated at nothing to put over their lies.

neutral: It is almost time for the scheduled daily activities. I intend to respond to the above tonight if possible. Perhaps I should have mentioned earlier the practice of seeking assistance in what seem to be hopeless situations. Anyway, I believe some nearby notes will be encouraging. I decided against including a postscript, hoping instead to provide a more substantial addition. Another letter from my niece Clement provides an update on the operation. Let us continue to maintain hope, confidence, and gratitude, prioritizing the most important aspects. Since the trainees departed, I have had the opportunity to assist Rudolph with their daily duty each morning. I genuinely enjoy it, but it makes managing other responsibilities difficult.
styled: It is nearly time for office - Matins - Lauds - I want to answer the above Tonight if I can I perhaps should have told the secret before - of having prayers heard in "hopeless cases." Any how I think a few little notes near by will be interestingly Encouring - over. I had to cross proposed P.S. off. - can only hope to do something better than just a P.S. Another letter from same niece Clement informs of the operation - Let us continue praying and trusting and thanking - God first of course and then all else Since the novices are gone I've been having - so far - the privilege of serving Fr. Rudolph's Mass every morning. . I really enjoy it but - but - One hardly knows how to get around . ·

neutral: The absence of news yesterday from Margaret and Frank reinforced our confidence regarding a positive outcome for her serious cancer operation, one that would surprise the doctors. I hope her friends will express sincere gratitude. It is remarkable how circumstances align for those who maintain trust. We are very fortunate and deeply grateful. Though relatively unnoted and quiet, we had the privilege of celebrating a diamond jubilee within the Order, wearing the traditional habit of Saint Frances. This event occurred on Monday, January 14, during a formal religious service. It was considered exceptionally beautiful, despite the simple circumstances. I had arrived at the novitiate on Christmas Eve, six months before the seven other students who joined me the following July. All of those students have since passed away, as has their senior, Father Damasus, at the age of 90.
styled: Thanks be to God! In receiving no news yesterday -- from Margaret and Frank, we were confirmed in our confidence and in God that He would surprise the doctors in regard to her threatening carcinoma operation. I hope that all her friends may -- grateful to God offer a few holy communions in earnest thanksgiving. How wonder -- in all His designs with all who confide in Him. How fortunite! -- How humbly grateful we ought to be! Deo Gratias! A Million! Thanks be to God, though comparatively unnoted and quiet God granted us the gracious privilege to celebrate a happy diamond jubilee in the Order and in the holy habit if Saint Frances. This took place Monday, January 14, at solemn high Mass. I would hardly know how it could have been more beautiful, under the simple circumstances. ... I had come to the holy novitiate Christmas Eve. and six months ahead of the seven other students who joined me the following July. They are all gone on to Heaven now, we hope, with their senior of all, Father Damasus, in his 90th year .

neutral:
These unsettled days present a duality: on one hand, there are threatening predictions, and on the other, there are instances of profound wisdom, power, and boundless goodness. The negative predictions are attributed to a lack of spiritual belief and worldly preoccupations. Few can claim to be exempt from this inclination. This also explains a natural tendency to heed even baseless predictions and to fear for oneself personally, as well as for humanity in general, given its flawed nature.

Incidentally, approximately twelve years prior, a Jewish Rabbi named Rosenwasser visited the office at St. Bonaventure Monastery. He expressed concern about the increasing prevalence of atheism, specifically emphasizing its rise "among the rising Jewish generation." Father S. politely invited him into an instruction room. The narrative then describes something being written on a piece of tissue paper, but the text is incomplete at this point, mentioning "the Rev. Rabbi's index" in an unfinished draft. A note indicates that this informal communication was written a few days after the death of Mrs. Grace Brady on April 10, 1953.
styled: God bless you My Dear Rt. Rev. Brother Edward. God bless you and yours these unsettled days - at once - days of threatening forebodings and of manifestations of God's/Wisdom and Power merciful Goodness without end or & limit; the former on the part of irrelition and worldly-inclined humanity. And God help us! Who can presume to claim exemption from that stupid in- clination? . .. Hence too, our natural tendency to listen to even vain forebodings and to fear for ourselves personally as well as for crazy - be- cause sinful - humanity in general? Incidently, it was about twelve years ago that a certain (Jewish) Rabbi Rosenwasser came the Office here in the St. Bonaventure Monastery, lamenting the prevalence of atheism - most especially he stressed; " ... among the rising Jewish generation". Fr. S. politely invited him into an instruction room. Then, without a word on a piece of tissue-paper - the Rev. Rabbi's index (Unfinished Draft) NOTE: This informal. . . came a few days after the happy death of our dear Sister, Mrs. Grace Brady, last Easter Friday, 4/10/53.

The other person was described as patient and joyful until their death. The speaker expressed a hope for the other person's peaceful rest and a glorious future beyond death. The speaker then apologized for the digression. They stated that today marked sixty years and sixty days since their own investment, expressing gratitude for this milestone. The speaker then suggested it was likely their fault that the celebration...

May he be privileged to await in the peace of the saints, the inconceivable glory of the Gen. Ressurection. Pl. pardon the digresxion: To-day Deo Gratias, it is sixty years and sixty days I was invested. It was probably my fault that the cdldbfzgion (celebration)

neutral: Maurice Joachim's Jubilee in New York was scheduled to occur one year before Edward's. The author was sent to assist with the celebration, which lasted approximately one week to ten days and was described as very pleasant. This event occurred approximately 12 years after the author's 20-year stay in New York. Maurice Joachim had, in about 7 years, established a significant number of connections in the same three locations where the author had previously worked. Several relatives, including two women in religious orders, traveled from Boston and other places to attend a significant religious service, which was the main event of the celebration and proceeded smoothly. In the subsequent days, visits were made to various institutional residences in the East, as well as to friends in New Jersey. Soon after the celebration, the members of the author's religious province held a chapter or convention to elect new leaders and address other provincial matters. These chapters are typically held every three years, and participants are expected to be prepared for potential changes. It was considered fortunate that Maurice Joachim...
styled: Maurice Joachim's Jubilee in New York. It was suppose to take place just a year ahead of Fr . Edward's. Anyhow, they sent me thither to help him celebrate and, Thank God, we had a very pleasant celebration of about a week or ten days. Thanks be to God. It was about 12 years since my 20 year sojourn in the Empire State, and Fr. M. J. had, in about 7 years, made quite some friends in the same three stations where I had been located ahead of him. A number of our cousins from Boston and elsewhere, including two nuns, attended the solemn Mass as the climax of the celebration, which, Thank God, "went off without a hitch." The following days we visited our different houses in the East, and besides some friends in N. J. Shortly after that celebration the Fathers of our Province held a chapter or convention, for election of new superiors and other affairs of the Province. Such chapters, as a rule, are held every 3 years, and everyone is supposed to be ready for a change, if such come. Fortunately, it seemed to me, and providen- tially, Fr. M.

neutral: At the 1913 Golden Wedding celebration, as people recalled memories of the River Bank and old Trimbelle, someone expressed a wish to return to those times. The mother, sighing as if remembering the difficulties of those days which seemed to outweigh the pleasant experiences, whispered an exclamation expressing relief that the period was over. Subsequently, the speaker often considered that exclamation profound.
styled: Probably you remember when, at the Golden Wedding in 1913 we were all musing over scenes and events on the River Bank and in old Trimbelle someone remarked: "Wouldn't it be nice if we could go back there again!", dear Mother, gently sighing as if revisioning the trials of those days, outweighing the beauties and pleasures -- half whispered an exclamation: "Thanks be to God, I'm glad it's over !" Many a time since I've thought: How beautiful was that little exclamation, how really Christian!

neutral: Reflecting on his Jubilee celebration and the three-part vacation it provided, we agreed it would be a suitable topic for a short written account. This account would acknowledge the fortunate circumstances and express appreciation to all those, both long-standing and new, for the many acts of kindness they showed, and for the gratitude we all felt. Details of the preparations for that celebration, particularly the earlier stages, are not necessary or expected here. As the senior family member, since Ella's death, you are aware of those details, having observed each of our lives longer and perhaps with more interest than anyone else currently alive. The same could also be said for Pat, and, with a shorter recollection of earlier life, for the others: Guss and Owen, and the three sisters—Margaret, Grace, and Mayme—who are now grandmothers. I am not certain if I ever wrote to you about Fr.
styled: Musing together over the celebration of his Jubilee, and the triple vacation it occasioned us, we agreed that it were theme enough for a little treatise of some kind, whereby to praise the wonderful ways of God's providence, and at the same time, offer an expression of appreciation to the many dear ones -- old and new -- and for the gratitude we all experienced at so many manifestations of kindness at their hands. Details of preparations for that celebration, at least the more remote, will hardly be necessary or expected here. As the Senior of the family -- since dear Ella passed away -- you know those details; having watched the career of each of us longer and perhaps with more interest than anyone else breathing to- day. Something the same might be said also to poor, dear Brother Pat, and, for that matter, though of course with shorter scope of vision back to earlier spring-time of life, to each of the others -- Guss and Owen, and the one-time three little sisters -- now we might say Grandmas -- Margaret, Grace and Mayme. I am not certain if I ever wrote you of Fr.

neutral: Edward was present at the Monastery for nearly two months, until June 18th. Having returned from the Philippines, he had been engaged in activities to promote his religion in Asia for over 12 months prior to his stay. He appeared to enjoy his stay at the Bonaventure facility. Shortly after departing Detroit and returning to his headquarters in St. Paul, he was informed by a senior religious official in the Philippines that he is expected to return there in September. It is possible he may not be able to visit this location again before his journey westward.
styled: God bless you and all yours -- and sure including my poor self in every blessing I can get or give. Thanks be to God for the Faith and for all His blessings. I had Fr. Edward with me at the Monastary nearly 2 months to June 18th. Back from the Philippines, as you know, he was doing real missionary work for religion in the "Far East" something over the 12 months he was here. He seemed to enjoy his stay at St. Bonaventure's. I certainly did. Shortly after leaving Detroit and back to his headquarters in St. Paul, he received information from his Bishop in the Philippines that he is expected back there in September. It is possible that he may not be able to get this way again before his voyage west- ward.

neutral: Joachim was transferred to one of the largest monasteries, St. Anthony's in Marathon, Wisconsin. Before going there, he received permission to take a vacation of about a week to visit old friends and places. Notably, he visited Prescott, where he and another person were born, and 'Big River,' where they first attended religious services and instruction at St. Mary's. The other person was six years older than him. Subsequently, Maurice wrote to the narrator shortly after his arrival at St. Anthony's, mentioning the upcoming Diamond Jubilee celebration in Prescott, where the two individuals were born and underwent a religious ceremony, and a probable invitation for them to attend. Prior to this, they had not anticipated Edward's return from the Islands for his Jubilee the following June. Several months later, after the conclusion of the religious conference in Manila, they learned of his return.
styled: Joachim on this occasion was transferred to one of our largest monastaries, i. e., that of St. Anthony at Marathon, Wisconsin. Before going thither, however, he got permission to take a week or so vacation to visit old friends and places -- notably, in Prescott where we two were born, and "Big River," where we first went to Holy Mass, and to catechism classes, viz., in dear old St. Mary's. Thanks be to God! What colorful memories the mention of these places must awaken in you! They do in me at least and sure you were six when I was born. What a world of experience that meant in advance of the baby !... At all events, Fr. Maurice wrote me shortly after his arrival at St. Antos, of the coming Diamond Jubilee in Prescott, where we were born and baptized, etc., and of a probably invitation that we should attend. Up to this, we had hardly dreamed of Fr. Edward's coming back from the Islands for his Jubilee the following June. Only several months later when the excitement of the Eucharistic Congress at Manila was over, did we learn of his coming.

neutral: The speaker only learned of the individual's arrival in May, as he was approaching the location. Shortly thereafter, the Pastor of St. Joseph's in Prescott invited the speaker and others to the Jubilee and appointed the speaker to deliver the Jubilee sermon, also informing the speaker that Edward would be the presiding official. The speaker thanked him for the opportunity, explaining that while they never desired to return to any former location from which they had been moved, they acknowledged a natural inclination to do so, a tendency observed in many people who yearn for past circumstances. It was noted that this natural inclination is common to all.
styled: In fact, it was only when he was nearing our shores, in May, that I learned of his actual coming. Not long afterwards, the Pastor of St. Joseph's, in Prescott, not only invited us to the said Jubilee, but about as much as appointed me to give the Jubilee sermon; informing me at the same time that Fr. Edward was to be the Celebrant. Of course I thanked him for the privilege, because, while I never long to go back to any old place from which Divine Providence has seen good to remove me, yet I must acknowledge that I have a natural inclination that way -- like the Israelites in the desert naturally yearned (many of them) to go back to Egypt. No doubt, we are all naturally that way 1 inclined.

neutral: The brevity of life's joys and difficulties is considered in comparison to ultimate future gains. These experiences primarily serve either to sustain individuals until life's conclusion, or to detach them from excessive worldly attachments and self-interest, thereby freeing them from common illusions encountered in existence. Ryan, in his work "Son of the Mystic," refers to walking "in the world with the worldly," suggesting the futility of achieving true inner peace without dedication to a higher purpose and cultivating trust in it. He elaborates with the full quote: "I walked in the world with the worldly, I craved what the world never gave."
styled: Pardon for such a digression. I'll never get started. Than too, and this belongs to the same digression, I think of how short in comparison with eternal rewards are the pleasures, as well as the trials of this "exile." After all, what do they either or all amount to, except inasmuch as they buoy us up till the Merciful Father calls us Home, or wean us from inordinate love of the world, and of our- selves -- from deceptions so common this side of Heaven. walked in the world with the worldly", writes Fr. Ryan in his "Son of the Mystic", indicating something of the vanity of figuring on real peace of soul except in God's service and fostering confidence in Him: "I walked in the world with the worldly, I craved what the world never gave.

neutral: The narrator typically finds comfort and copes with a longing for past times and experiences by recalling the significant changes that had already occurred in their childhood home before they departed. These scenes included the "burned hills," the "Big Ravine," prairie fires, and the "little Poplars." The Poplars were described as bright and beautiful during spring and the day, but lonely in the evening. It was in this area that the recipient, on their way home one evening (likely near nightfall), encountered an animal they later identified as a lynx. Before becoming truly scared, the recipient, mistaking the animal for the narrator, called out, "Is that you Barney?" This action was subsequently interpreted as having bluffed the animal. Neither the recipient nor the animal responded verbally. However, the animal's action of leaping into the thicket and allowing Jimmy Casey to pass was considered the most appropriate response given the situation. Jimmy Casey then ran away very quickly, covering the distance over hills and hollows to reach home. The recipient was estimated to be about 13 years old at that time.
styled: For my part, I usually con- sole myself and overcome such "hunger of the heart for days and dreamings never more to be," by thinking of the lonesome changes that were already taking place before we left those scenes of our childhood -- scenes of the "burned hills", of the "Big Ravine," of the prairie-fires, etc; and of the "little Poplars", so bright, so beautiful in Spring, and during the day, yet so lonely in the evening; where you, on your way home on a certain evening, (must have been almost night), met a lynx, as you concluded afterwards it must have been, and before you were really scared, must have bluffed it, when, taking it for me, you called out: "Is that you Barney?" Of course, neither of us answered, except, on its part, which was perhaps the best answer we could give under the circum- stances, when it leaped into the ticket and let Jimmy Casey pass. It is not hard to reckon the amount of grass that grew, or that didn't grow, under his feet till Jimmy was over the hill and home over big and little hollows. You must have been about 13 at the time.

neutral: On August 11th, I departed from St. Bonaventure's Monastery in Detroit. My plan was to catch the first train to Chicago, then continue to Marathon, Wisconsin, that same day. In Marathon, I intended to meet Maurice, and the following day, we were to travel together to St. Paul, where Edward was expecting us. I arrived at the station on time but did not board the train. Although I initially viewed this as a personal error, three weeks later, after my first visit to Marathon, I realized that missing the train that morning had saved me 130 miles (twice 65 miles) on the initial part of my trip.
styled: And I said: In the world each ideal that sines like a star on life's wave is wrecked on the shores of the real and sleeps like a dream in a grave." Quite in the same spirit too, Moor beautifully tunes in: "Poor wanderers of a stormy day, from wave to wave we're driven; And fancy's flash and reason's ray serve but to light the troubled way ; -- There's nothing calm but Heaven. " Well to get started at last: I left St. Bonaventure's Monastery, Detroit, August 11th, planning to catch the first train to Chi- cago, thence to Marathon, Wis. same day, where I'd meet Fr. Maurice and go with him next day to St. Paul where Fr. Edward was expecting us. I was in time for the train o.k. but for- tunately failed to catch it. The Dear Lord had planned other- wise: though at the time it did seem to me as the result of nothing less than stupidity on my part. It was only three weeks later, having been to Marathon for the first time, I realized that missing the train that morning saved me twice 65 miles on starting out.

neutral: This saved approximately 300 miles and, coincidentally, allowed for beneficial and unforeseen connections that would have been difficult to establish otherwise. Instead of going to Marathon, I traveled to Milwaukee after having dinner in Chicago with an old friend, John Gorman, and his family. They met me at the station and insisted we go to a nearby hotel for dinner. Although I had not felt hungry and hadn't considered eating, I realized that nearly 12 hours sustained only by a cup of coffee and a small slice of bread had made me very hungry once we sat down to a generously provisioned table. That night, we had an enjoyable social evening at the St. Francis monastery, which I had first visited 40 years prior on my way to the novitiate. The next morning, after the service, I contacted an individual by telephone.
styled: Altogether it saved me about 300 miles and, as if all prearranged, enabled me to make happy and unexpected con- nections which I would hardly have found possible to make other - wise. Thanks be to God! Instead of to Marathon, I went to Milwaukee, after a very pleasant little repast in Chicago with an old friend, John Gorman and family, who met me at the depot and insisted on us going to a nearby hotel and having dinner. I had not felt particularly hungry at all -- in fact I'd not thought of eating -- but found that close to 12 hours on a cup of coffee and a small slice of bread had provided quite a vacancy when we sat down to a well spread table. How mindful of my need was the Good God to inspire my friend so charitably! We had a real friendly recreation that night in the first monastery (S. Francis) I had visited 40 years before, on my way to the privileged Noviciate. After Holy Mass next morning I got in touch by long distance telephone with Fr.

neutral:
The vehicle was crowded, and the narrator's beard, worn for over 40 years, made them somewhat noticeable. Any doubt about their conspicuousness was settled by Father M. Joachim's joyful exclamation. As they entered the lobby, each carrying luggage, he stopped in surprise and, in a clear voice that seemed expected from an older man, exclaimed, "Look at all the sisters!"

Shortly after, while crossing the Mississippi River near LaCrosse, a friendly-looking priest was pointing out scenic views downstream when the narrator whispered to him, "Look upstream." This caused the priest to forget the scenery. He approached their front seat, offered his hand, and asked, "Are you not Maurice Casey?" The narrator replied, as Father M. J.'s hand went up to meet his, "This is Father Maurice." Everyone's attention turned to the two men. They had studied together 30 years prior and had not met since their ordination.
styled: The coach was well filled, and the beard I carried -- had carried more than 40 years -- made me no doubt, at least a little conspicuous. Well, if there had been any misgivings in that direction, Fr. M. Joachim positively settled it with one happy exclamation. As we entered through the vestibule, each with a grip, he stopped as in astonishment and in a clear voice that everyone seemed expecting from one of the gray-beards, called out: "Glory be to God! Look at all the sisters." Crossing the Mississippi (at LaCrosse) , shortly after, said friendly looking priest was calling attention to beauties down the River when I called to him in a half whisper: "Father ; Look upstream. " With that, he seemed to forget the scenery altogether and, coming up to our front seat offered me his hand, asking: "Are you not Fr. Maurice Casey?" "Why!" I answered, as Fr. M. J.'s hand raised to meet his, "This is Father Maurice." All attention seemed on the two of them. They had studied together 30 years before and had not met since ordination.

neutral: The narrator had an agreement with Joachim to meet at New Lisbon, Wisconsin, on the westbound Hiawatha train. This arrangement allowed the narrator until 2:00 PM to visit various properties in Milwaukee belonging to their community and meet all its members, rather than departing on the Omaha train at 10:00 AM. Around 4:00 PM, the train made its second stop at New Lisbon, where Joachim had arrived by bus from Marathon, located 65 miles to the north. In Milwaukee, a friendly-looking clergyman boarded the train just before the narrator. He had visited the central institution of a religious order near St. Francis Seminary and, as the narrator later discovered, was escorting a staff of approximately 20 female religious educators to manage his school in an unspecified location in Minnesota. Additionally, several other individuals from religious orders were present. Until the train departed New Lisbon, the narrator was uncertain whether the other passengers perceived them as a respected religious leader or some other idealized figure.
styled: Maurice -- Joachim rather -- and had an under - standing with him to join me at New Lisbon (Wis.) on the west- bound Hiawatha. That gave me till 2 P.M. to visit our different houses in Milwaukee and meet all the Brethern, instead of hurrying away on the Omaha at 10 A. M. At about 4 o'clock we made our second stop at said New L. where Fr. M. J. had arrived by bus from Marathon 65 miles to the north. At Milwaukee a friendly looking priest had boarded the train immediately ahead of me. He had been out to the Mother-house near St. Francis Seminary and, as I learned later, was bringing a whole staff of teaching nuns to take charge of his school some place in Minnesota -- about 20 of them it seemed to me. Besides this there were several other religious. Till we were pulling out of New Lisbon I had felt in doubt as to whether or no they'd been taking me for a venerable rabbi, or for something else more or less ideal.

neutral: The journey proceeded along the Minnesota side, passing through Redwing, where in 1880 Solanus first saw railroad cars, and Hastings, where the mother had worked as a girl. Then, across and around the widening of the river, the sun set over the hills as the journey continued toward St. Paul and into the Union Depot. At the Union Depot, Edward was met, marking the first meeting since his return from the Philippines. A phone call was made to Mike Costello, a former acquaintance from 60 years prior. Costello had also been a cellmate ten years later, when the speaker was a laborer and Costello a boiler-maker at Stillwater Penitentiary. Their dormitory, however, was located outside the prison walls, suggesting a special influence or favor. Costello is currently a sergeant on the St. Paul Police Force. Mildred, with the assistance of the Conley family, had arranged a reception. The reception, hosted by Mildred and the Conley family, was described as ideally pleasant.
styled: Before we knew it, we were speeding up the Minnesota side on through Redwing, where in 1880 Father Solanus saw railroad cars the first time, and Hastings, where Mother worked as a girl, till across and around the beautiful widening in the River, we watched the great red sun dip to the hills while we glided toward St. Paul and into the Union Depot. Here we met Fr. Edward -- first time since his return from the Philippines. We phoned to your boy-friend of 60 years ago, Mike Costello, and my bed-fellow 10 years later when I was a "roust-a-bout" and he a boiler-maker in the Stillwater Penitentiary. Our dormitory, however, was outside the walls, so we had a "pull" of some kind. Mike is now a sergeant on the St. Paul Police Force. Your Mildred had arranged with her friends, the Conley family, to give us (as indeed they did together with herself) an ideally pleasant little reception.

neutral:
Having completed their morning religious services, Joachim and the author, serving as deacon and sub-deacon respectively, were prepared to assist Father Edward at the main ceremony. Bishop Reverman attended officially, and Father Weber, who is now Monsignor and Vicar General, delivered the address. The Jubilee service and subsequent receptions proceeded without issue.

The first reception occurred immediately after the church ceremony, with a significant number of friends gathering in the school hall to greet the honoree and his clerical colleagues. The second reception was a dinner and program for approximately fifty or more friends at a hotel on Tower Avenue. Attendees included many of Father Edward's classmates from Sacred Heart School, along with relatives and old friends of the participants from locations such as Burkhardt and Detroit.

The author and Joachim made several visits over the course of that evening, the following day, and Tuesday. Although not official church duties, these visits were regarded as having a missionary character. On Monday morning, Father Joachim and the author officiated each other's services in St. [The original passage ends abruptly here].
styled: Joachim and I having offered our Holy Masses earlier, were ready as deacon and sub-deacon, to assist Fr. Edward at the Solemnity proper. The Rt. Rev. Bishop Reverman attended in state, and Fr. Weber (now Rt. Rev. Msgr.) gave the sermon. The latter is now Vicar General and looks very well. Thanks be to God, everything went off smoothly, both at the Jubilee Mass itself, and at the receptions. The first of these took place immediately after the solemnity in church, when quite a procession of friends came to the school-hall to greet the Celebrant and his Reverend Brothers. The other con- sisted of a gathering of about fifty or more friends for dinner, and a program in a hotel down on Tower Ave. Besides a goodly number of Fr. Edward's class-mates from Sacred Heart School, a number of our cousins and other relatives and old friends from Burkhardt, Detroit, etc. attended. We made quite a number of visits -- taking altogether -- that evening, next day and Tuesday. These visits, though not exactly canonical had more or less the nature of missionary work. Monday A. M. Fr. Joachim and I served each other's Masses in St.

neutral:
Edward and a companion entered the Roberts Estate via its old entrance. They found Emma, who had been modest and winsome in her school days and later when Father S. assisted her father with spring farm work. She appeared to be alone, yet gently contented and friendly, and was now slightly older than fifteen. Anna, the older of the two, was perhaps more ambitious; she married and became a respected grandmother. One of her four sons became a professor at Cornell University. Her husband had died a few years prior, and the latest information indicated that the two were once again together on the farm.

The next destination was the Diehl-Germain home, where they were also surprised. Anna was now an elderly woman, and Joe was, literally, an elderly man. From there, they proceeded across the old bridge to Father Edward's childhood friend, William Ryan, and his wife, Agnes, who lived in Andy Tobin's former residence.

Leaving the others there, Father S. walked to the Baker residence. After a brief visit with the elderly woman and Mary, he then walked to the formerly beautiful Drydam. Meanwhile, the others arrived and took a longer hike.
styled: Edward and I climbed the old entrance to the Roberts Estate. We found, I'm inclined to say, poor little Emma, so modest and winsome in school-days and later when Fr. S. helped her Father with the Spring work. She seemed quite alone though gently con- tented and friendly, but of course a little more now than fif- teen. The older of the two, Anna, perhaps more ambitious, married and became a venerated grandma. One of her four sons, I believe, became a professor at Cornell. Her husband died a few years since and the last I heard the two were again together on the farm. Next stop was at the Diehl-Germain home. They, too, were surprised. Anna is the old lady now, and Joe, the old man, quite literally. Thence down across the old bridge and over to Fr. Edward's childhood chum, William Ryan, and wife Agnes, living in Andy Tobin's old house. Leaving the others there, Fr. S. hiked over to Baker's and after a short visit with the dear old lady and Mary, strolled down to the one-time beauti- ful Drydam. In the meantime, the others came and took a longer hike.

neutral: The old mill at Burkhardt appeared to be severely damaged or inactive. It had been inactive since World War I. Mrs. Baker, estimated to be close to 85, appeared to be in good health. Mary no longer possessed her youthful appearance but maintained a hopeful and friendly smile. Alice was quite ill during the visit. After seeing Alice, they departed for New Richmond, where they had a pleasant visit with Andy Tobin and family. After supper, they left New Richmond and stopped to visit Anna Ryan and her brother John, who lived just outside the city toward Boardman. There they met Scott Tobin, a former acquaintance, and his wife Jane (Henry). They then returned to Monsignor Owens for a service the following day. The chauffeur and associate, provided by Sister Mary Kathleen (Doonan) for the day, continued on to St. Paul and the Orphanage.
styled: The old mill at Burkhardt would seem to have been shell shocked or something like that. It has not moved since the war No. 1 and seems to impart a sort of spirit of its own to the whole vicinity. Mrs. Baker seems to hold her own remarkably well. I think she is close to 85. Mary, like the rest of us, has lost her child-like and youthful brightness, but still retains a hopeful and friendly smile. Poor dear Alice was quite ill at the time of our visit. We each gave her our blessing and started for New Richmond, where we had a congenial visit with Andy Tobin and family. Leaving there after supper, we stopped to see Anna Ryan and her brother John, just outside the city toward Boardman. Her we found Scott Tobin, my one-time boy- friend, and wife Jane (Henry) . Thence we sped back to Monsignor Owens to offer Holy Mass next day -- Feast of my dear Patron St. Bernard. Our chauffeur and associate whom Sister Mary Kathleen (Doonan) had sent us for the whole day, went on to St. Paul and the Orphanage. God bless them all.

neutral: She had a significant surprise planned. After supper, she connected you with us from Seattle via a long-distance phone call. We all spoke with you, Pat, Emma, and Guss—for me, it was the first time since the Golden Wedding anniversary twenty-five years prior. We found suitable accommodation at the College of St. Thomas, where Edward had served as Rector before resigning to go to Australia and the Philippines. The next day, after breakfast, we made some calls. M. J. and I were at the community's residence. Around 2 P.M., we departed via Sault Ste. Marie, arriving in Superior between 5:30 and 6 o'clock. At the station, we were pleased to meet our old friend Ed Sampson and his wife, who were waiting to take us to the church residence at 12th and John Streets. She had called me a day or two before I left Detroit, informing me that they were starting their vacation and might see us in Superior. The next day's celebration was a happy one.
styled: She had a decidedly- choice little surprise "up her sleeve," when, after supper, she brought you to us from Seattle on the "long distance", and we all talked with yourself and Pat, and Emma and Guss -- on my part the first time since the Golden Wedding twenty-five years before. We found ideal quarters in the College of St. Thomas, where Fr. Edward had been Rector before his resignation prior to going to Australia and the Philippines. We made some calls next day after Holy Mass and Breakfast -- Fr. M. J. and I serving each other in turn at the Convent -- and about 2 P.M. left via Sault Ste. Marie to reach Superior about 5:30 -6 o'clock. To our pleasant surprise, whom did we meet at the depot but our old friend Ed Sampson, and his wife, waiting to convey us to the Parish House on 12th and John Sts. She had phoned me a day or two before I left Detroit that they were starting off on their vacation and possibly would see us in Superior. The celebration next day, Feast of the Assumption, was a happy one. Fr. M.

neutral:
The author again officiated at a Mass, held at midnight with three priests, at the same location where the author first attended a Mass.

On Christmas Eve in 1881, a group traveled ten miles in vehicles, including those belonging to the Ryans and new sleighs. The temperature was 18 degrees below zero Fahrenheit at the start of the journey and dropped to 22 degrees below zero Fahrenheit before their return. The ceremonies were impressive.

A school now stands at the location where, in 1886 or 1887, the author's father, Maurice, Mr. Ryan, Matt and Peter Welsh, and Jim Pachingham began construction for Father Kelly. Father Kelly was very pleased and insisted they have dinner at Reilly's. He was visibly moved, shedding tears of appreciation.
