Later that morning, they hiked up the bluff to the south, which offered a view of the city, the St. Croix River, Stillwater, the new State Prison layout, and Mt. St. Helen in the distance to the right.
styled: I had the privilege once more of offering the Holy Sacrifice where for the first time I had attended a solemn Mass -- three priests -- and that at Midnight. It was Christmas Eve in 1881 when with Ryans' roadsters and our new sleighs a real load of us started in the ten miles when it was 18 below zero, and before we got home it was 22 below. The ceremonies were beautifully inspiring. Thanks be to God! They have a fine school now where in 1886 or 1887 Papa and Maurice and Mr. Ryan, Matt and Peter Welsh and young Jim Pachingham broke ground for dear Fr. Kelly. How happy he was, insisting that we come down to Reilly's and have a good dinner. Tears of appreciation filled his eyes, more expressive than any words he could have uttered. Later in the morning we went for a hike, climbing the bluff to the south whence is a surprisingly beautiful view, not only of the city itself and the St. Croix River, but of Stillwater and the new State Prison layout, with Mt. St. Helen in the distance to the right.

neutral: St. Joseph's Convent is located near the East end. There has been a significant change over the past 50 years. The speaker noted that members of the convent community were surprised to learn that, 50 years prior, only two or three individuals from the community were transported daily by trolley car to and from school. The speaker estimated the current number of individuals in the convent to be approximately thirty. One individual present recalled that earlier period. The speaker administered a religious rite to another individual who was ill and appeared to be near death. Later that afternoon, the speaker and companions performed a religious rite for a ten-year-old granddaughter of Teacher Aggie Murphy Oteir at the "Steel Plant," and for some others. The speaker observed little change in her appearance over twenty-six years, since she had attended M. Joachim's first religious service. Afterward, they crossed the St. Louis River to Duluth, where they met old friends from Hudson. Tuesday was short and busy due to their scheduled departure for St. Paul around 2 PM. They arrived via St. Cloud and Minneapolis between 5:30 and 6 PM. The train was modern. August.
styled: Joseph's Convent, down near the East end. What a change in 50 years! They wondered when I told them that I used to carry them on the trolley-cars as they went daily back and forth to school -- only two or three in the whole community. Now they must number about thirty in that Convent, as seemed to me. One of them present remembered those pioneer days. To another, now an invalid seemingly just waiting to take off for Heaven I had the privilege of giving Holy Communion. Deo Gratias. That P. M. we went to bless a little ten year old grand- daughter of Teacher Aggie Murphy Oteir in the "Steel Plant", and some others. I was surprised at the seemingly little change in her appearance in twenty-six years, when she attended Fr. M. Joachim's first Holy Mass. Thence we crossed over St. Louis River to Duluth where we found some old friends from Hudson. Tuesday was short and busy, from the fact that we were to leave for St. Paul about 2 P.m. We arrived via St. Cloud and Minneapolis about 5:30-6 P.m. It was an up-to-date train. Aug.

neutral:
On Thursday the 19th, a visit was made to Stillwater, including St. Michael's Church, School, and Convent. The facilities were maintained in excellent condition. The surroundings and views from established vantage points were considered to be potentially as appealing to the younger generation as they had been to the narrator fifty or sixty years prior. The narrator expressed a desire to have spent more time in the church building itself, which appeared to be unchanged.

The group then traveled down Third Avenue and Chestnut Street, a steep thoroughfare where the narrator had learned to operate trolley cars in 1887. At the base of Chestnut Street, the group crossed a new bridge, which was now free of tolls and lacked a draw mechanism, standing approximately ten feet higher than the previous drawbridge.

Traveling through Wisconsin scenery that was recognized by the narrator, the group had dinner and a pleasant meeting with Monsignor Owens. Monsignor Owens had been ordained one year prior to Fr. Maurice J. and had served as Master of Ceremonies at Fr. Maurice J.'s initial religious service. However, Monsignor Owens was observed to be in poor health due to a form of rheumatism.

Subsequently, the group traveled rapidly along a route familiar to the narrator from earlier times, especially during periods of regular religious observance, towards Burkhardt, Boardman, and New Richmond. The other members of the group waited under maple trees for the first designated stop, while Father...
styled: 19th, Thursday, we went over to Stillwater and visited St. Michael's Church, School and Convent. Things are kept in excellent condition. Dear old St. Michael's! The surroundings and views from familiar vantage points are perhaps as beautiful to the younger generation as they were to me fifty or sixty years ago; but to me! Only in the beautiful old Church itself, seemingly unchanged, could I have lingered longer. We sped down Third Avenue and steep Chestnut St., where in 1887 I learned to run the trolley-cars. At the foot of Chestnut, as of old, we crossed on the new bridge, now without toll or a draw and perhaps ten feet higher than was the old draw-bridge. Going down through Wisconsin scenery that still seemed familiar, we had dinner and a congenial visit with Monsignor Owens, who was ordained just a year ahead of Fr. Maurice J. and Master of Ceremonies at his First Holy Mass. We found him, however, in bad shape with some kind of rheumatism. Afterwards we speeded out the old road so familiar in younger, to church-going days to Burkhardt, Boardman and New Richmond. The others waited under the maples for our first stop while Fr.

neutral:
The speaker gradually recognized the hill they were standing on as one they had frequently dreamed about since leaving Yonkers, without understanding its significance. The top of the hill was park-like, featuring a single grave and a flagpole. They looked down at a point where descending would be dangerous, and then went down the west side of the hill.

Upon returning to the Rectory, they found Monsignor Owens, who had been there for several weeks due to rheumatism, sitting with his feet elevated on a chair. He appeared to be feeling better when he joined them for dinner. Afterwards, he put on his shoes and drove them to St. Paul.

The following evening (Saturday), Dean Conley transported them via Hudson and River Falls to Prescott. There, they met old friends who took them to the Rectory, where preparations were underway for the Jubilee celebration scheduled for the following day.
styled: I gradually recognized the hill on which we stood as one I had dreamed about, off and on, ever since I had left Yonkers, without knowing what it could all mean. It is quite park-like on top with a single grave and a flagpole, etc. We said the rosary together for the living and the dead as we peered down where it would be dangerous to des - cend, and went down the West side. On our return to the Rectory, we found Fr. Owens -- Pardon! Rt. Rev. Monsignor -- where he'd been most of the time for some weeks with rheumatism sitting with two helpless feet on a chair in front of him. We each blessed them in turn, someone remarking that a triple blessing ought to help some way. Well, Thanks be to God, he seemed better as he came to dinner with us and, afterwards, put on his shoes and "shot us over" to St. Paul. Next evening (Saturday) , Dean Conley brought us via Hudson and River Falls to Prescott, where we met some old friends who took us to the Rectory, where they were preparing for the Jubilee celebration next day. The Rev.

neutral: Following a visit to the Betsels, a group proceeded to the Bowers home for a prayer service. The family's eldest child, who had drowned in Chicago a day or two prior on their seventh birthday, was awaiting burial there. Further details about this would be provided later. It should be mentioned that Mr. Bowers was not Catholic, though he reportedly had received some religious instruction and appeared favorably inclined. The mother was related to the O'Brien family and, consequently, hoped that the group would stay for the funeral, potentially lead the service, and preside over the Mass. The group agreed to this, with Maurice and Edward making the necessary arrangements. The writer preferred to defer to their decisions and follow whatever they might decide. The prayer service was well-attended, and many present were reportedly positively affected. Between 2 and 3 P.M., upon returning from the Bowers home, a proposal was made for what was considered a positive activity for the day. The plan was to go to "The Bluff".
styled: Besides visiting the Betsels, we went over and said the rosary at a certain Bowers home, whose oldest was laid out awaiting burial -drowned in Chicago a day or two before, on his seventh birthday. More about this late. Suffice it to say here that Mr. Bowers was not a Catholic, though I believe had taken instructions to some extent and seemed well disposed. The mother belonged some way to the O'Brien family and, consequently, seemed to hope that we might stay for the funeral and possibly conduct it, and offer the Mass. This we consented to do -- I ought to say, they arranged to do -- Maurice and Edward. I wished simply to leave everything to them and passively fall in line with what- ever they might wish to decide on -- begging the Good God to guide them, and us all, for the best. There was quite a crowd at the Rosary recital, and I believe, quite some edified. Returning from the Bowers, between 2 and 3 P.M., what seemed to the writer a happy feature of the day's program, was proposed. We were to go to "The Bluff".

neutral: The late Judge Smith of the Superior Court represented one side, and a young lawyer named Wilson represented the other. The travelers waited until the senior judge returned before proceeding. A fifteen-year-old girl directed them to follow the main road until they reached Highway 'E', which would lead them to River Road. They departed at high speed, passing several properties, including Toohey's, O'Brien's, and Donovan's. Some of these properties still stand, while others have disappeared. Upon descending the old sand hill towards Big River Bottoms, they forgot their instructions and followed the road that led down the old river bed. The river itself no longer exists. After traveling approximately half a mile, they discovered that instead of leading them to the River, their chosen road led them in a zig-zag path up another hill and across a plateau-like section. They eventually descended to another cross-road marked 'E', at which point they were confident they would reach the Bluff.
styled: The late Judge Smith of Superior represented one side as opposed to a clever young lawyer named Wilson. However, we just waited until the senior judge returned before proceeding ... . . . Ha! Ha ! A modest little girl of about fifteen directed us to fol - low the main road until we came to a Highway "E", which would bring us right down to the River Road. Off we went, high speed, past Toohey's old place, and O'Brien's and Donovan's etc. Some of them (old places) still stand. Some have disappeared. Coming down the old sand hill to Big River Bottoms, we forgot our instruc- tions and followed the road down that old river bed. The river itself is a thing of past history. We only made about a half- mile when we found that instead of leading us to the River, our self-chosen road led us zig-zag up another hill -- scenery worth while -- and over a beautiful plateau-like section, till coming down to another cross-road, marked "E" we felt at ease again, knowing that now we'd reach the Bluff.

neutral: Paul was determined to perform a religious service, even though the only other train to Chicago that day was due in 30 minutes, and the speaker intended to reach Detroit by Saturday morning. It had been raining since they departed Seattle on Tuesday evening, with snow encountered while crossing parts of the Rocky Mountains. Now, swirling clouds twisted around the skyscrapers of the Twin Cities. The Union Depot in St. Paul had been destroyed by fire two days prior, and the area remained chaotic and disorganized. Sergeant Costello, whom the speaker knew, was present and greeted the speaker briefly, as both were occupied. He was prepared for the impending storm, and the speaker had so far managed to avoid the rain or was unaffected by it. The religious service was performed, and two trains were delayed. Under these circumstances, the speaker hesitated briefly, but there was no time for extended consideration. Having no umbrella, the speaker returned to their train, which was about to depart.
styled: Paul, deter - mined to say Holy Mass, even if the only train for Chicago that day, besides "our own" was due in 30 minutes, and I wanted to make Detroit next morning (Saturday). It had been raining ever since we left Seattle, (Tuesday evening), snowing, however, while crossing some of the Rocky Mountains: and now swirling clouds were actually twisting around the "Twin Cities" sky- scrapers. The Union Depot in St. Paul had been burned to the ground the day before yesterday, and, as yet, order and con- fusion were still wrangling for mastery. Your above referred to barefoot boy-friend -- now Sergeant Costello -- was on the scene, and gave me a warm greeting, mutually brief, however, for he was busy and I was in a hurry. He was prepared for the threatened storm and, as yet, I was able to dodge the drops or ignore them. HOLY MASS OFFERED -- TWO TRAINS HELD -- THANKS BE TO GOD Under such circumstances, I surely did hesitate: briefly, however, for there was really no time for deliberation. Having no umbrella, I started back to our train about to start off.

neutral: Although not noted at the time, the valley through which Highway E runs is the same as what was previously known as Manion's Ravine. It was understood that this location preceded the Bluff. The town was eventually reached, though its status as a town was questionable. The group left the highway, crossed the railroad, and searched the entire town without finding any place to eat lunch. Fortunately, the group was not very hungry; otherwise, the lack of food options would have been a significant disappointment. A prominent beer sign was visible, but this offer was not appealing. Approximately ten minutes later, the group returned to the highway, intending to see the old farm and the previously familiar hills and valleys. Diamond Bluff had not been seen before, but it had been imagined as a substantial town located at the mouth of the Trimbelle River.
styled: Though no remark was made about it at the time, the beautiful valley down which said Highway "E" runs, is none other than what we used to know as "Manion's Ravine". I knew we had to come to that before we'd reach the Bluff. Well, we did reach the town at last, if it could any longer be called a town. We left the highway, crossed the railroad, did the whole place up and down, without finding any indication of where one might find a lunch. It was good that we were not very hungry, otherwise it would probably have been a story of "sour grapes". There was one, quite a BEER sign but we hardly appreciated such an invitation. In about ten minutes we were back on the highway, now bent on seeing the old farm and once familiar hills and valleys, etc. As a child I had never seen Diamond Bluff, but I had pic- tured it as quite a town at the mouth of the beautiful Trimbelle.

neutral: A clergyman from St. Mary's, Big River, met the narrator and a colleague, accompanying them to lead a religious service the next morning. A clergyman named Maurice conducted the first service at 6:30 AM and delivered a brief, moving address. Attendance was good, and many participated in a religious rite. The St. Mary's building, still beautiful and well-maintained, had been expanded on both sides since the narrator's last visit sixty years prior. It could now comfortably accommodate approximately 800 people. A clergyman returned from his duties. Soon after, the narrator and colleagues were in Prescott, preparing for a major religious service. A high-ranking religious leader, Bishop Griffen, was present with his assistant, along with an unprecedented number of attendees. The attendees included many long-time acquaintances, particularly their children and grandchildren. Many members of the Manion family and their relatives greeted the narrator and colleagues after the proceedings. The oldest among them was 93-year-old Wm. Betsel. Mrs. Betsel was 87 years old, blind, and an invalid. She appeared very appreciative of the visit and expressions of goodwill. Wm. Betsel, also known as "Bill Betsel," was known for driving horses during the harvest season.
styled: Pastor from St. Mary's, Big River, met us there and took Fr. M. J. and myself out with him to offer Holy Mass next morning. Fr. Maurice said the first Mass -- 6:30, and gave a touching little sermon. The attendance was good, and quite a few Holy Communions. The same old St. Mary's, beautiful and well kept as ever, has been built out on both sides since we were there sixty years back, so that it would nicely accommodate probably eight hun- dred. The Rev. Pastor came back from his mission and in a very short time we were in Prescott, vesting for the Solemn Mass, His Excellency, Bishop Griffen, attending with his chaplain and a record congregation. Among these, of course, were many old friends, and, more especially, children and grandchildren of such. Quite a number of the Manions, and relatives, came to greet us after services, and the senior of them all -- the 93 year old Wm. Betsel. Mrs. Betsel was 87 and a blind invalid. She seemed quite appreciative of our visit and blessings. You re- member "Bill Betsel" who always drove the horses in threshing time.

neutral: The location was known to have a few stores, including one started by the Smith children's father, and was a former steamboat stop. However, the current visit was disappointing. After traveling approximately a quarter-mile, a road appeared to the left, identified as the southern end of what was previously known as "the Main Road." At this point, a fortunate encounter occurred with a handsome, rustic youth driving dairy cows. The group stopped and inquired about the location of the Trimbelle's mouth. The youth pointed downriver towards a cliff, indicating it was approximately two miles further, beyond a prominent landform. The journey then continued. This prompted a recollection of an event 25 years earlier, which had seemed mysterious at the time. This involved taking what some friends considered a risk while returning from the Golden Jubilee in Seattle, by disembarking at St.
styled: I knew it had a store or two and that the Smith childrens' father had started another one, and that the steamboats used to stop there, but today's visit was to me rather a disappointment. We had gone perhaps eighty rods when we came to a road leading up to the left, which must have been the southern end of what we once upon a time called "the Main Road :. Here Good Providence would have us meet another Raphael. It was a handsome, rustic youth, driving some milch cows -- a happy sight in itself. We stopped beside him. "Where is the mouth of the Trimbelle" I asked. Pointing down the river to one of the many beautiful cliffs, he answered: "It's just behind yonder mountain-head, two miles further on your way." "God bless you, Boy" and on we sped. Then I remembered what had struck me as a sort of mystery passing down that way 25 years before. I had taken quite a risk, as some of my friends thought, when, coming back from the Golden Jubilee, in Seattle. I got off at St.

neutral: The understanding was that the destination was Trimbelle, and this plan was realized. The group traveled on the old wagon road, choosing it over going half a mile north to the Elsworth Highway or south to the Mississippi River. They began to question their choice of route for the 13-mile down-the-river trip when, turning onto a well-used road to the right, a neat little white house appeared through the trees. Maurice exclaimed, "Aunt Mary's old house!" His neighbor confirmed this. Edward exited the vehicle and inquired about directions to the River Road leading to Diamond Bluff. S. also approached the door, wanting to see the place where he had spent time fifty-nine years earlier. During that two-week visit, he had attended a court case in Prescott and sat in Judge Ross's chair while court was in session, not understanding at the time why the court seemed amused.
styled: To him, that seemed to mean self-understoodly, "and to Trimbellle", and so it came. Fortunately, we took the old wagon road, rather than going a half mile north ot the Elsworth Highway, or down to that, following the course of the "Father of Waters". We were begin- ning to think we had made a mistake in not taking the latter for the 13 mile down-the-river trip, when, turning on a fairly trod road to the right, a neat little white house loomed through the trees (small bushes at my visit in 1878) and Fr. Maurice ex- claimed "Aunt Mary's old house!" "Sure enough" responded his neighbor. Fr. Edward got out and inquited how to reach the River Road down to Diamond Bluff. Fr. S. also went to the door, wish- ing to look in at least where nine and fifty years before he had spent happy days. Incidentally. it was during that visit of two weeks that he attended a court case in Prescott and took Judge Ross' chair while court was in session, hardly appreciating at that time why the court seemed amused.

neutral: Observing that the rain was not substantial, I decided, regardless of the weather or train schedule, to go to St. Mary's, where Edward was an assistant priest, and conduct a religious service, trusting in a favorable outcome. I had planned to catch the 'Milwaukee' train, scheduled to arrive from Seattle an hour after our own train on the Northern Pacific line. However, we had lost thirty of those sixty minutes between Minneapolis and the damaged train station. The housekeeper at St. Mary's expressed surprise at my early return from the religious ceremony. The senior priest was away on a visit to a sick person, and I reached the sacristy just in time for the concluding remarks and final benediction of the 8 o'clock service. The young minister was also surprised by my early arrival, and even more so upon learning of my intention to conduct a religious service and still catch a train to Chicago that day. He remarked, glancing at his watch, "If you were to leave for the station now, you might catch a train." Nevertheless, I proceeded with the religious service and also expressed brief gratitude.
styled: then, again, seeing that it was not actually raining to speak of, I determined -- rain or shine -- train or no train, to go over to St. Mary's where Fr. Edward was assistant, and say Holy Mass and leave the rest to God. I had figured on catching the "Mil - waukee" scheduled to arrive from Seattle just an hour behind us, on the "N. P." but, we had lost thirty of those sixty minutes be- tween Minneapolis and the burned depot. The house-keeper at St. Mary's wondered that I was back so soon from the Solemnity. The Rt. Rev. Pastor was out on a sick- call, and I got to the Sacristy just in time for the last "Dominus Vobiscum", and final blessing of the 8 o'clock Mass. The young celebrant, too, was surprised at my early appearance; doubly so, on learning of my purpose to say Holy Mass and, even then, catch a train that day for Chicago. "If you were to start for the depot now, you might catch a train", he said, glancing at his watch, but, Thanks be to God, I said Holy Mass and made a short thanksgiving too.

neutral: The narrator believed that offering the Mass would be beneficial and that a higher power could easily delay any desired train. The narrator requested this outcome. The narrator did not recall being anxious about connections in Chicago, though acknowledged it was likely, given the slow travel through rain and a severe thunderstorm. Just before LaCrosse, they passed a burning farmhouse, which appeared to have been struck by lightning during the storm. Nearing Chicago, five hours late, the narrator asked the baggage-master about possible connections to Detroit. The baggage-master informed them that the last train for Detroit was scheduled for around 6 P.M., and it was then nearly 10:30 P.M. Furthermore, that train was scheduled to depart from a station requiring a twenty-minute trolley ride from the Burlington station.
styled: I had reckoned, at all events, that it would please the Divine Lover of our poor souls and be good for mine especially to offer that Holy Mass; and that it would be a very easy thing for the Great God and Governor of the Universe to hold any train He might wish me to take. I hardly need to say that I asked HIM. Adored be His Holy Name! Now and forever. I do not remember that I was anxious about connections in Chicago, I probably was, more or less, seeing that we had to go so slowly in the rain, and for a time, through a fearful thun- derstorm. Just before reaching LaCrosse, we passed what seemed a victim of lightning, a burning farmhouse in the storm. Nearing the big city, five hours late, I asked the baggage- master about possible connections to Detroit. "The last train for Detroit is scheduled for some time about 6 P.M., and now it is nearly 10:30". Besides, that train was supposed to leave from a station about a twenty minute trolley ride from that of the "Burlington".

neutral: A wish was expressed for the well-being of the Alihueians and their elders. This was because, in the context of what was seen as a widespread and threatening global increase in atheism, they were cultivating religion, which the speaker considered the only practical solution.
styled: As it was, I just wished it on them: "God bless you little Alihueians ! -- you and your dear elders; because in the face of the fearfully threatening avalanche of atheism, inundating the world these days, you are fostering at least something of the only practical remedy: RELIGION

neutral: It was about two miles below the Bluff. They had a custom of performing a specific devotional prayer at the beginning of their longer journeys. On this day, however, after traveling approximately twenty miles over hills and through valleys, and now heading rapidly towards the aforementioned mountain, Maurice observed, "We have not performed our customary prayer. Barney, it is your turn to lead." Barney agreed and began the prayer. The question might arise as to how such a prayer could be performed without distractions in those circumstances. The speaker admitted not knowing the secret to achieving this. Instead, a different question could be posed: "Do such distractions genuinely displease the divine being?" The speaker's opinion was that they do not. Instead, the speaker would offer reassurance, similar to what is given to those overly concerned with religious exactitude: "No, the divine entity is not unreasonable."
styled: Now I remembered my conclusion at that time; that it was about two miles below the Bluff. Pardon such digression. We had been making it a sort of rule to say the Rosary starting out on our longer trips. Today, however, we had gone a good twenty miles over hills and through beautiful valleys, and now speeding for said mountain-head, Fr. Maurice remarked: "Say, we've not said our Rosary. (Father) Barney it's your turn to lead . " "Okay" and the later started: "In the name You may wonder how we could pray under such circumstances. without distractions, etc. Well, I am not going to tell you the secret today, for the simple reason I do not know it my- self. Rather, we might ask: "Do such distractions really dis- please the Good God?" For myself, I do not think they do. Rather, I would answer, as I have occasion now and then to assure scrupulous souls: "No, Jesus is no crank.

neutral: After breakfast, I quickly took a trolley for the approximately half-mile journey to the station. I asked an employee, who was signaling a train as it backed into the station, if there was a train to Chicago that day. He confirmed there was, indicating the arriving train. Immediately, the train stopped, and I boarded. The 'Burlington' then departed at full speed, three hours late, with its first scheduled stop at Point Douglas. The journey passed areas significant to my early experiences with nature, including a section of the Mississippi River approximately four miles downstream from where I had played on its shore. It crossed the mouth of the St. Croix River and proceeded past Prescott.
styled: After breakfast, needless to say, no heavy one -- I lost no time in catching a trolley and getting over the half-mile or so to the station. "Is there any train for Chicago today?" I asked what seemed to be an official just waving a train backing in to stop. "Yes" he answered courteously "Here is one now". He hardly finished speaking, when, stopped was the train; on I stepped: and off went the "Burlington" at full speed; three hours late, its first stop at Point Douglas. I need not tell you what that meant to me. It took me past where I first saw the beauties of God's visible creation, down the Mississippi, where I played in the sand of its beautiful shore some four miles below; having crossed the mouth of the beautiful St. Croix and shot past Prescott where five of us had received Baptism. I certainly was not a tenth as grateful as I ought to have been, but I hope to be more so some day.

neutral: A wait for a transfer, occurring about halfway through the journey, felt long in the misty night air. However, an announcement was made via megaphone immediately upon his arrival: "All aboard! and Detroit." This timing was fortunate. He anticipated they would wait for him to obtain his clergy-fare ticket, and they did. This allowed him to conduct a morning service at St. Bonaventure's, and, as a sacristan, it was essential for him to reach Yonkers, N.Y., for the dedication of the new Sacred Heart Church the following day. A digression follows regarding a particular observation. At that time, as on other occasions, there was disappointment at the absence of the Trimbelle, which typically graces Diamond Bluff. Despite an intense storm during a previous journey, careful observation eventually led to the identification of what was believed to be the desired small stream.
styled: Waiting for a transfer about half way over, it took me at least that, in the misty night air. How wonderful, however, and Thanks be to God; almost as though waiting for poor Father S., up went the megaphone the moment he entered: "All aboard! and Detroit. "All aboard" -- "Well, God bless them" he though -- "They'll wait now till I get my clergy-fare ticket." So they did. God bless them again. Now I could say Holy Mass at St. Bonaventure's in the morning, and what to me was imperative as Sacristan, I could reach Yonkers, N. Y. for the dedication of the new Sacred Heart Church next day. Thanks be to God, a million! Pardon this digression -- longer than it ought to be already -- but you'll be curious about the referred to mystery. Well, then as now, I was disappointed at no appearance of our beauti- ful Trimbelle, gracing Diamond Bluff, etc. However, notwith- standing the terrific storm that raged at the time of our passage that other trip, I had watched sharply and finally had the satis- faction of seeing what I concluded must be no other than the delightful little stream I looked for.

neutral: At 3:00 AM, a call was received. Upon being informed that an elderly person was dying, I inquired if the message was a telegram. I immediately wondered if it was from Seattle. I expressed gratitude. It is now the evening of July 14th, St. Bonaventure's Day. I attempted multiple times yesterday and again this morning to finish the preceding text and send it, but it is still not sent. I am still hoping that James will be spared. A chapter meeting began early this morning, including the election of a new Provincial and definitors. It will likely last a week or more. Nearly fifty priests and brothers are attending. On July 15th, I conducted a private service, which I dedicated specifically to the guidance of the meeting and for Brother James. Your letter is being sent to Maurice. He appears to be doing well. I will likely visit him soon.
styled: This at 3 O'C A.M. a call came and I asked, when they said, "an elderly person is dying", "is it a telegram ... ". I was at once wondering if it were from Seattle. ... I said: "Deo Gratias." It is now after vespers July 14th - Our dear St. Bonaventure's Day. I started a number of times yesterday and again this morning to finish the above and get it off and still it is not gore. I am still hoping it be God's will to spare our poor dear James. We are having "chapter here started early this A.M. - Election of a new Provincial and definitors, etc. It will probably be a week or more before its all over. We have close to fifty priests besides brothers attending .... . July 15. I had a "free Mass" Today which I offered quite specially for God's guidance of the Chapter and for dear Brother James. Am sending your letter on to Fr. Maurice. He seems doing well. Will probably go down to see him before long .... God's grace to all!

neutral: I informed Mrs. Baker and Mary about your difficulties, noting that you were managing. Therefore, continue to persevere for as long as you are able. However, avoid anxiety; ultimately, it will be a significant achievement simply to have accepted the circumstances.
styled: I wrote Mrs. Baker and Mary of your difficulties but that you were keeping up. So do keep up as long as the dear Good God wills. But of course avoid anxiety - what glory that will be for each of us in eternity, just, in the end to have been able to say "Thou knowest O Jesus! Thy will be done."

neutral: Despite an awareness of universal human fallibility, as the group rounded the mountain, a strong, shared reaction occurred. Edward, upon seeing the Trimbelle and the stunning, ancient landscape for the first time, simply exclaimed, "This is beautiful!" Soon, the group arrived in Alihue, which was still neat and orderly, but, like its surroundings, appeared smaller than it had sixty years prior. The village had been known for frequent religious revival meetings, and the group's religious background differed from the predominant Methodist and Lutheran communities there. Perhaps a dozen children played on the green near a modest, separate building, appearing to wait for a religious education class. They stopped and gazed at the group, likely wondering about the two older men in unfamiliar attire. A prayer ritual was still underway; otherwise, a greeting or benevolent gesture would likely have been offered to the children.
styled: He knows that we are not angels, but poor sinners ; every one of us." At all events, as we rounded said mountain-head, such a distraction (which was probably common to four of us) came out in positive form. Father Edward, seeing the Trimbelle for the first time, and the exquisite landscape there for untold ages praising the Creator ahead of us, exclaimed simply and unqualifiedly: "This is beautiful!" Soon we were in what I recognized as Alihue, still neat and prim, but, like everything around, it seemed smaller than it was sixty years ago. You remember, of course, the frequent "revivals" in that little village when we were possibly their nearest Catholic neigh- bors, -- methodists, lutherans, etc., -- mostly honest, good Christians, as far as they knew. Perhaps a dozen children played on the green near a modest building apart as if waiting for some kind of sunday-school. They stopped and gazed our way, wondering, no doubt, at the two grey- beards in such never-before-seen garb. I was still leading the Rosary, or I think I would have greeted them with a blessing of some kind.

neutral:
Although some friends, both in the hospital and outside, believed my condition was a near-miss for pneumonia, I personally never felt there was an immediate danger of collapse. I considered it to be about ten days of the most severe hardship I had ever endured, and since I survived it without complaint, I am grateful for the significant experience.

Now, having recently received an encouraging letter from M. Joachim, which indicated a significant change in his attitude and a desire to return to the community, and while you are still present and able to appreciate my work, I am beginning to conclude the description I started before M.J. became ill. This description covers Edward's anniversary celebration and our trip to "The Bluff" and old Trimbelle.
styled: While a number of my friends, both in the Hospital and outside seem to have considered my case "a close call to pneumonia, etc, I never felt that there was any immediate danger of colapse. Thanks be to God. To me it seemed about ten days of the really severest penance that the poor sinner Solanus had ever done and, therefore, since by God's grace he lived through it without complaint we have every reason to thank Heaven for the wonderful exper- ience. Deo Gratias. Now dear James :- since I received a hopeful letter from Fr. M. Joachim a few days ago, indicating a decided change in his attitude - a yearning to come back to the Monastery; and while you are still with us and able to appreciate, as I trust you will my little efforts, I am starting a conclusion to the description started before Fr. M.J. got sick; of Fr. Ed'wd's Jubilee and on that occasion our trip to "The Bluff" and old Trimbelle.

neutral: I hope things are well for you and your family. I am grateful for existence and for the specific beliefs that provide hope regarding the ultimate purpose of life. I just read your interesting and awaited letter; thank you very much. I feel for Jim and wish I could be there to cheer him up, console him, and perhaps playfully challenge him, as I have had the opportunity to do for several others in similar situations. Perhaps Jim is correct that S. visited him. It's possible that some beneficial influence provided him with the comfort I wish I could offer. Regardless, I think of him frequently every day. I am grateful for the shared beliefs and mutual appreciation that are fostered in environments of genuine conviction. I am thankful for everything. It has been a week since your letter arrived, and I began to answer it immediately. It has been on my mind continually.
styled: God bless you and yours. Blessed be God for having created us and given us the true faith in His Redemption - and hope thereby in the final purpose of our existance, to know Him our Blessed Begin- ning, our Life and our All. Deo Gratias! ! ! I just read your interesting - awaited - letter for which many thanks. Poor, dear Jim: I sure would like to be with him; to cheer him and console and to "kid" him and wake him up - as I've had the privilege to do, thank God for quite a few in condition similar to his. Well after all maybe Jim is right in saying Fr. S. was there to see him. Possibly at least his Guarding Angel did the trick and gave him the consolation I surely would like to give. At all events I am there in spirit not a few times every day. Thank God for the faith and the mutual appreciation - fostered wherever real religion is found. Praised be the Lord for everything !.... It is a week now since your letter came and I started to answer at once. Its been on my mind continually.

neutral: I hope you continue to improve physically, mentally, and in overall well-being, as Mildred's recent report suggests you have been. You and I should be grateful that we are still alive. I say 'we' because, while all people should be thankful, you and I have particular reason to be grateful this year. I hardly need to remind you of the narrow escapes you have had over the last ten months. Perhaps I should instead describe your threatening experiences and conditions as difficult battles that you ultimately won, demonstrating your resilience. However, I also had a significant experience of a similar nature beginning around September 10th last year, with a severe case of the flu and a varicose condition in my ankle.
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope you continue improving in body, mind and spirit, as last report from Mildred recently indicates you've been doing. Thanks be to God. How grateful we ought to be you and I that we are still "among the living"; still pilgrims able to merit for eternity, trying to follow thither at least in sight of the dearly de- serving, Divine Master. We, I say, because while it is something that at all event and everywhere as rational creatures men should do, you and I have special cause for thanking the Good God this year. I hardly need remind you of the marrow escapes you have had dur- ing the last ten months. Perhaps I ought rather refer to your threaten- ing experiences and conditions as someway pithed battles and, by the grace of God your victories; since you persevere in the Holy Faith. But I too had quite an experience in similar direction beginning last September about the 10th, with a severe case of "flue", together with a sort of vericose condition of ankle.

neutral: The venue at Joseph, overlooking the Mississippi River from a height of approximately 400 feet, was filled to capacity. Maurice J. and the narrator had traveled to St. Mary's Big River the previous night. Dean Conley, who was later identified as a future nephew-in-law and the third son of Br. Jim, had driven them there from St. Paul, via River Falls and Hudson. They had conducted religious services at that old St. Mary's, a place where the older individuals had first attended religious services and received religious instruction, and where Maurice had received his first communion. They led the first scheduled service, while the local pastor traveled to his mission, located several miles away. The pastor delivered a sermon. Following their post-service activities, the pastor returned and quickly drove them along the Prescott-Elsworth Highway. Soon, they were in the St. Joseph's sacristy, preparing for formal services.
styled: Joseph looking down the rear on the Mississippi about 400 feet below, was filled to capa- city. Fr. Maurice J. and I had gone out to St. Mary's Big River the night before; Dean Conley having driven us down from St. Paul via River Falls, and Hudson. (Hardly necessary now to say who same D.C. was. It might've added somewhat to the already exquisit pleasure of the trip had we recognized in him what we only surmised at the time, a future nephew-in-law and ... Br. Jim's third son). We had offered our holy Masses out at said old St. Mary's where we older ones first went to holy Mass and to Catechism instructions, down to Maurice receiving First Holy Communion. We took the first scheduled Mass while the Rev. Pastor went to his mission several miles distant. I was inclined to envy him the privilege but felt that it was coming to him rather than to his younger brother but I quite enjoyed his nice little sermon. After our thanksgiving, etc, the pastor having returned reshot us down the Prescott-Elsworth Highway and before we knew it we were in the St. Joseph's sacristy vesting for solemn services, Rt. Rev.

neutral: The recipient's letter was read on November 17 and again this morning, and it was appreciated. The description of the trips to Burkhardt, provided by the recipient's father, was also appreciated. The omission of details regarding Trimbelle was noted. A reminder will be issued, as he had indicated an intention to continue. Mary is well and visits or calls occasionally.
styled: I hope you are well. I quite enjoyed your letter when I read it on Nov. 17 and again This A.M. when it came to my notice. Also did enjoy your dear Dad's discription of your trips to Burkhardt. Sorry he left out all about old Trimbelle. No doubt I ought to re- mind him as he proposed to continue ..... God bless you and yours. Mary is well; drops in or phones occasionally.

neutral: I received your welcome card dated the fourth and am pleased to hear you are well and doing well. Monsignor Edward and Brother Owen arrived here on the evening of January 25th. Grace traveled by plane from San Francisco ahead of them and surprised them upon their arrival at Grand Central Depot. They all arrived together at the Monastery around 8:00 PM on Saturday, the 25th. Grace called from Edward Sampson's location, and her telegram announcing her arrival was received by mail on Monday morning. The celebration, which included a Solemn Mass, was impressive. However, there was insufficient space for half of the attendees. I am sending a few cards that convey more information concisely than lengthy letters could. I am grateful for the opportunity and for all the arrangements, and acknowledge the contributions of all involved in the program.
styled: I just read your welcome card of the fourth and thank God you are well to write and get along so well. "Yes Msgr. Edw'd and Br. Owen joined us here the night of Jan. 25th. Grace "beat them to it" by plain from San Francisco and sur- prised them on their arrival in the Grand Central Depot - all coming together to the Monastery about 8 o'cl. Saturday 25th P.M. ) Grace phoned from E'd Sampson's and the telegram of her coming arrived Monday a.m. in the mail. The celebration - Solemn Mass, etc. was quite impressive as seemed to me. Only there not room for one half of the crowd that had come. I am sending you a few little cards that tell more in a few words that many letters might express. Thanks be to God for the privilege and for every detail and God bless our Guardian Angels - visible and invisible - each and all - for their part in the program . -

neutral: Bishop Griffin was present. Solanus had been appointed to deliver the sermon either several months earlier or at approximately the same time as the sermon was scheduled. It was his first time speaking in the presence of a Bishop, and the speaker barely recalled if the sermon was satisfactory. From his own perspective, it did not meet his expectations. It was perhaps fortunate that he did not foresee the significant disappointment that awaited him before the service concluded: only the officiating minister received communion. Apart from this, the event proceeded smoothly. However, a large crowd was waiting outside after the service. Numerous individuals from the Mangan family were present, each accompanied by their family. The speaker recognized Tim and one or two other individuals. Among the many others present was the eldest among them, Bill Betzel, who would now be 98 years old if still alive. At that time, he was 93 years old. His wife, who was blind and an invalid at 87 years old, expressed a desire to see the visitors. Consequently, after dinner, the visitors went to see her. She wept when the visitors offered their blessing.
styled: Bishop Griffin present. Fr. Solanus had been appointed several months before or about the same as appointed to give the sermon. It was his first time before a Bishop and I hardly remember if it was satisfactory. For himself it was far from what it ought to have been. Perhaps it was fortunate that he did not forsee what caused him quite a dissapointment before the Mass was over - No one except the Rev. Celebrant received Holy Communion: .... Otherwise everything went off without a hitch. Deo Gratias. But what a crowd waiting outside after the celebration in Church! One Mangan after an- other each with a family. Tim. and one or two of the others I recog- nized. And among the many others the senior of them all, now the 98 year-old Bill Betzel, if he still lives. He was 93 then, and his wife who was blind and an invalid 87 years-old wished to see us. So after dinner we visited her and she wept when we gave her cur blessing.

neutral: Although there is ample work here, no task requires immediate completion, allowing me to postpone it until tomorrow. This serves a dual purpose: to provide you with some entertainment and to offer myself a form of recreation. I believe I provided a copy of the aforementioned initial description to Mary and Helena, who are cousins, when they visited me a few years ago while traveling to Montreal, Quebec, and other locations. Regardless, when I return to St. Bonaventure's, I will try to send you a copy, as I am certain someone made multiple copies for me, apparently hoping I would complete it as a substantial document even then. It is probably acceptable to review some of the previously created description. Therefore, I will begin with the sequence of activities following the Solemn Jubilee ceremony in Prescott, Wisconsin. On Sunday, August 22, the first celebration had taken place on August 15 in Superior, 165 miles to the north. Evidently, the well-maintained small church of St.
styled: Besides; while I find plenty of work to do here, nothing is so urgent that I cannot let it go till another day, for a sort of a double purpose; viz, to aford you a little entertain- ment and myself a form of recreation. - If I am not mistaken, I gave a copy of the above referred- to started-description to Mary and Helena when these two cousins were visiting me on their way to Montreal, Quebec, etc, a few years back. At all events when I get back to St. Bonaventure's I shall try and send you a copy of the same; for I am sure someone made a number of copies for me, seemingly anxious that even at that time I should finish it up as a worth-while whole. It will hardly be objectionable if we review a little of the description made before. So I'll start with our course of activity after the Solemn Mass of the Jubilee in Prescott (Wis.). Sunday August 22, the Octave of the Assumption, on which feast itself we had the first celebration in Superior, 165 miles to the N. Needless to say the neat little Church of St.

neutral: Dear Emma, even though your current condition might make time seem monotonous, this presents an excellent opportunity to deliver a compelling message. The best message one can deliver: One might ask, 'How?' or 'On what subject?' On April 22, 1949, I will answer that question by telling you about a former classmate who turned 84 on January 10th. Approximately six months prior, his vision deteriorated to the point where he could no longer perform his religious duties. Everyone was aware of this, and we knew he would not welcome such a decision. However, I was assigned the task of delivering the difficult news. I asked him, 'Father Damasus, what about that message?' 'What message?' he inquired. We were all somewhat anticipating signs of disappointment from him, because not only was his vision seriously declining, but his hearing was as well. I replied, 'Father D.'
styled: My Dear Sister Emma: - God bless you this joyful season of Eastertide and this even though in your condition the time must seem monotonous all the better chance to give a good sermon. The very best sermon one can give: - "How?" some one may ask, or on what subject! April 22 1949, Dear Emma: again; I am going to answer the above question by telling you of a dear class-mate of mine who was 84 last January 10th. About six months ago his sight became so poor that he had to give up saying holy Mass entirely. We all knew it: and oucourse we knew he would not like to hear such a decision. However, I was sort of deligated to break the unfavorable item. I asked him: " ... Well Father Damasus: How about that Sermon ?" "What sermon?" he enquired. We were all more or less anticipating indications of disapointment, etc. on his part; because not only was his sight failing seriously but his rearing likewise. I said: "Well Fr. D.

neutral: The sender hopes the recipient is well. The sender indicates having made several attempts to begin this correspondence; the current time is 10:15 P.M. The sender recently spoke with Mary. Mary expressed strong hope that the recipient would succeed in arranging a trip East for Mother and Dad Jim. The sender believes this trip would provide them, particularly Jim, with renewed vitality and well-being for an estimated ten years. The sender requested that the recipient convey this sentiment to Mother and Dad Jim. The sender has long intended to write to them and currently has approximately sixty letters requiring a response. Annie O'Brien is celebrating her fiftieth wedding anniversary. The sender remembers Annie O'Brien distinctly, having known her prior to her marriage. The sender intends to hold them in remembrance during a religious service scheduled for the following day.
styled: I hope you are well. I've tried a number of times to start this card; now its 10:15 P.M. Was just talking with Mary. She is in great hopes that you will succeed in getting "Mother and Dad Jim" for a trip East. I think it would give (Jim at least) them another lease of ten yrs. Be sure and write them I said so. I've been wanting to write them so long. Have about sixty letters ahead to answer. Well! Well: so Annie O Brien is to celebrate her golden Wed'g. I remember her quite well - knew before she was married. I surely will remember them in Mass tomorrow

neutral: Mrs. James Casey needs speedy health improvement. This is an urgent matter concerning a special member. February 18th, 1948. From Emma Casey. Courage is a significant factor in overcoming difficulties. Maintain your efforts. Cultivating confidence greatly strengthens courage and should always be encouraged; it is essential for inner strength.
styled: Mrs. James Casey - for speedy health improvement, God willing - emergency - special - member. February 18th 1948 God bless you Sister, Emma Casey "Courage is half the battle" Keep it up. Confidence in God is courage infinitely reinforced by God's grace to be always fostered - the very soul of prayer.

neutral:
This will be the final sermon we can deliver, and its topic is patience and resignation. He received the news without any visible change in his expression and has consistently demonstrated patience and resignation since then, serving as a genuine lesson and inspiration for the 30 novices and everyone else. He never complained.

I hope you will forgive me for not writing. I have intended to do so many times, but honestly, more often, there are so many tasks I feel I should complete, yet I lack the time, which makes me feel unproductive and as if I accomplish nothing. I am sure Father Edward has written about Father E.J.'s peaceful and dignified passing and the truly joyful, solemn service and funeral. Everyone seemed content. As we followed the Bishop from the cemetery, one of the fifteen priests remarked, "This feels more like a wedding than a funeral."

Maintain your courage; or rather, maintain confidence, which is courage strengthened by a higher power.
styled: its the last sermon any of us will be able to give and its on patience and holy resignation." Thanks be to God; he received the announcement without the least change of countenance and has been an esample of patience and resignation ever since - a real sermon and edification to the 30 novices and to us all. Never a complaint! I hope Dear Sister that you will forgive me for not writing you. I hav stated a number of times to do so; but honestly more friquently there are so many things it seems I ought to do and do not get time that I feel I get no where and do seemingly nothing. .... I am sure Fr. Edw'd has written of Fr.E.J.'s peaceful and beautiful death and really joyful, solem Mass and funeral. Every one seemed happy. As we followed His Excellency the Bishop from the cemetery one of the fifteen priest half-exclaimd-"This is more like a bridal affair than a funeral." ... Keep courage; rather confidence in God, which is courage divinely reenforced.

neutral: The purpose of my existence is to understand a higher power. This understanding is intrinsically linked to cherishing and acting in accordance with its principles, which represents a profound objective. For those who embrace this path, it brings a state of ultimate fulfillment, representing the highest possible value.
styled: - for God's holy guidance God made me to know him O what a Bless'd aim! To love Him and serve Him Sure rests in the same. It's Heaven begun For the grateful on earth To treasure aright ! ? ! Highest Heaven its worth.

neutral: After reading your letters last night, I began writing to both of you and your cousin Mary Eileen Clare. I intended to finish the letters, but it was almost 11 p.m., and I was too tired to continue writing. I wrote to your mother a few months ago when she was quite unwell. I understand she has improved somewhat since then. She seemed to recover significantly two years ago at the happy reunion and a special ceremony. Life's joys and sorrows are brief. The religious training program currently has 23 new members, who are promising young men. We could assign fifty clergy members tomorrow if we had them for domestic and international outreach. There is a great need for more workers. Solanus
styled: After finishing your letters for the 1st time last night I started to write both of you and your cousin Sister Mary Eileen Clare. I meant to get them done but it was nearing 11 p.m. and my eyes threatened a strike if I continues. I wrote your dear mother a few months ago when she was quite low. Thank God, I understand she improved some since. . · She seemed to pick up wonderfully two years ago at the happy reunion and Solemn 1st holy Mass. . . But how short the joys of earth! - and the sorrows too! Deo Gr. Clerical Novitiate - at present 23 novices, promising young men. We could place fifty priests tomorrow if we had them for the home and foriegn missions. Pray the Lord of the vineyard that He send laborers. Fr. Solanus

neutral: After leaving Betzel's, the group traveled several blocks to attend a prayer service for a young Bower boy, a distant in-law who had drowned in Chicago a few days prior. The child's mother, Kathleen, was a niece of John's first wife, Nellie O'Brien. Maurice led the service. Upon leaving, a decision was made to drive to Diamond Bluff. The author supported this idea. The author was unsure if a copy of the current letter had been sent some years ago. This letter, combined with the previous one, forms a double letter, which was considered worthwhile.
styled: From Betzel's we went over several blocks and prayed the rosary at the wake of a little Bower boy, a distant in-law drowned in Chicago a few days before. The child's mother, Kathleen, was a niece of John's first Wife Nellie (O"Brien); May their dear souls rest in peace! Fr. Maurice led the rosary. On our leaving there, it was de- cided that we take a "spin" down to Diamond Bluff. Of course I favored the proposition, because while "the Bluff" I am not sure if I sent you a copy of this letter some years ago or not. At all events I hope you like it. With my own it makes a double letter - worth while I hope.

neutral: We enjoyed our visit to Portland and your well-located main house in Marylhurst, which was on our route to San Francisco and Los Angeles. Booklets regarding the Seraphic Mass Association are being sent separately. Your Mother is also being enrolled in the Emergence list, with the hope that she will quickly improve physically, mentally, and emotionally. We hope her recovery exceeds the doctors' expectations. Yesterday, a letter was received from Maurice E. Joachim, and today, one from E'd. Both appear to be feeling well.
styled: You and your community. Yes we quite enjoyed our visit to Portland and out to your ideally located Mother house in Marylhurst - on our way to San Francisco and Los Angeles. .We are sending in separate cover book- lets pertaining to wonderful source of blessings, the Seraphic Mass Association. I am enrolling your dear Mother too in the Emergence list for the intention that she speedily improve in health - physically, mentally, spiritually. I hope she give the doctors a surprise. P.S. Yesterday received letter from Fr. Maurice E. Joachim and To-day one from Fr. E'd. Both seem feel- ing well. Deo Gratias!

neutral: I hope you are well, as I am. I don't know when I last wrote to you or how long I've wanted to write, but I think of you almost every day. However, your son, Father John McCloskey, a Jesuit priest, visited us yesterday. This prompted me to write you a few lines without further delay. Only a week or two ago, I learned from our friends, the O'Donnells, that Father John was nearby, even in Chicago. They had been planning to drive down since early June. At that time, they were very kind to me and our nephew, Bernard Maurice, when we traveled to St. Paul and then visited Father Maurice Joachim in Gracefille. Our visit to Maurice had to be short due to the circumstances, but I think we all quite enjoyed it. Both Father Maurice and Father Edward are quite well.
styled: God bless you and all yours. I hope this finds you well -- as, than is be to God it leaves me. I really do not know when I've written you last or how long I've been wanting to write you, though I hardly think there is a day passes that I do not remember you. However, your son John now our promising, young Jesuite Father Mc Closkey gave us the pleasure of a visit here yesterday; and so, I determined on writing you at least a few lines before letting it linger longer. Only a week or two ago I learned from some good friends of ours - O'Donnells - of Father John's presence so near, even in Chicago. The had been figuering on driving down ever since early in June, when they were very kind to myself and our Nep- hew Bernard Maurice, when we went out to St. Paul and from there visited Fr. Maurice Joachim in Gracefille. Our visit to poor, dear Maurice had to be short under the circumstances but I think we all quite enjoyed it. Both Fa- thers Maurice and Edward are quite well. Thanks be to God.

neutral:
A religious service had been planned to commemorate M's 36th anniversary of becoming a priest. However, the chapel was very small and temporary. Therefore, I assisted him during his service, and he, surprisingly, was able to assist during mine. The service took place on Wednesday, marking the anniversary of his first religious service as a priest, rather than Monday, his ordination anniversary. I had committed to the community leader, who was unwell at the time, that I would make every effort to return by Sunday.

I had an important visit to make to a sick individual in Royal Oak, near Detroit. This visit added approximately 375 miles or more to my return journey. A person who had converted from Judaism drove me from Detroit. We had a pleasant visit yesterday and Saturday evening. Everyone appeared to enjoy it. John had to return this morning for his classes, so they departed around 5 p.m. yesterday.

I am also sending two letters that may be of interest, along with a photo taken a little over a year ago. The photo depicts the subject at a younger age.
styled: We had planned on a solemn Mass on the 36th anniversary of M's ord- ination but the chapel is very small - just temporary; so I ser- ved his Mass and he surprised me how well he was able and served mine. It was Wednesday, the anniversary of his First Holy Mass instead of Monday of ordination and I had promissed the Father Guardian who at the time was not well, that I'd try hard to be back for Sunday. I had quite an important sick-call to make in Detroit - Royal Oak rather - on returning whic added about 375 miles or more of a trip. One of our convert Jews -- very clever who we hope will be a priest some day - drove me down from Detroit. We had quite a nice little visit yesterday and Saturday- evening. They all seemed to have enjoyed it. Fr. John had to be back this morning for his classes. So they left about 5 p. m. yesterday. I am sending you a couple of letters I think will interest you; as also a photo taken a little over a year ago. Of course its younger than the original.

neutral: It is challenging to fully comprehend the profound opportunity available to individuals to contribute to a significant cause, thereby ensuring a positive outcome for their own future. This reflects immense wisdom and knowledge. The reader may be wondering about the purpose of this discussion. There is a vast amount of information to convey, more than can be covered in a single communication. This extensive topic brings to mind the recipient's mother, known as Nell or Ellie, who, many decades ago, made significant efforts to ensure the contentment and happiness of family members. These events occurred in locations such as Prescott, Trimbelle, St. Croix County, and Superior, Wisconsin. The author believes the recipient was an infant when their mother wrote a significant letter describing a 500-mile journey to attend a religious service. This letter was given to the recipient in November.
styled: For who can fully appreciate the privilege that Almighty God has given each one of us in just this possibility of our helping Him in the work of Redemption and thus saving our own "destiny for eternal glory?" "O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!" You will be wondering what all this may be coming to; and there is so much that I would write you that a whole book would not exhaust it. So much, when I think of your dear Mother, Sister Nell or Ellie, as we used to call her in her mother-like efforts to make the rest of us contented and happy in the long decads back in our family history, in Prescott, in Trimbelle, in St. Croix Co. in Superior, Wis. I think you must have been the baby when she - your dear Mother - wrote that notable letter describing the 500 mile-trip to Christmas Mass, that I gave you last Nov- ember.

neutral:
The sender addresses Dorothy, conveying good wishes for her and her family on a particular significant day.

The sender states a long-standing desire to write to Dorothy, noting that Dorothy has been in their thoughts frequently since a memorable day spent with her and her family on the "mount," with a view of the majestic "old Ranier." The sender expresses surprise that nearly three years have passed since that day.

The sender then reflects on the passage of time and their own mortality, contemplating how much more time will pass before they, too, die and join those who have already passed away, including those who have died more recently. Among those who have passed, the sender specifically mentions Brother Guss as a significant individual.

The sender indicates a desire to dwell on past memories but states that time prevents them from doing so, as past events are fleeting and transient, regardless of their perceived importance or splendor. Such reflection is deemed valuable only if it contributes to a deeper understanding of fundamental principles or a higher, ultimate purpose.
styled: My Dear Niece Dorothy: - God bless you this dear, beautiful Feast of the most priviliged Spouse of Mary. May be too be watching over you and yours! I've been wanting to write you these many months. Indeed you have been on my mind quite a little ever since that memorable day we conclude with you and your little family on the "mount" in view of the majestic "old Ranier. Who would believe that nearly three years has passed since that day? How many more-times three, till we follow so many of our dear ones gone ahead of that land-mark event, and join even those who have followed since? -- poor, dear Brother Guss, (at least for me), one of the notables. I would like to continue playing with memories but time forbids me to waste it on events that have passed and do pass like soap-bubles, no matter how grand and gaudy, unless they pertain to the one thing necessary - knowing God better so as to love Him and serve Him better and save our immortal souls.

neutral: Regardless, I had intended to have a serious discussion with you at that time, but your brief visit and the circumstances made it impossible to address what I believed you and Charlie needed. It was evident from the beginning that he was troubled; he expressed his concerns during a brief private conversation we had. I met Charlie for the first time on that specific day at the Mouth, and then again a day or two later at Aurelia's residence on Lake Washington. I was compelled to commend you on having such a husband and on the good fortune of your marriage, particularly regarding your children. I will omit many details that I believe would be of interest, but you can easily infer what would logically follow if I were to elaborate further. Therefore, I want to emphasize one aspect of mutual harmony between spouses, which I believe is paramount in married and family life. What is it?
styled: At all events I wanted to have a heart-to-heart talk with you on that occasion but the shortness of your stay and circumstances made that impracticable for what I felt you and poor, dear Charlie needed. I could see from the start that he had something on his mind. He could not resis- Lamenting it in a little personal interview we had together. I'd never met Charlie before that refered-day on the Mouth and then a day or two afterwards out at aurelia's place on Lake Washington and I surely felt like congratulating you on such a husband and on the blessing God had be- stowed on your union - such dear children. I am going to skipp a whole lot that I am sure would interest us but you will be easily able to guess all about what would naturally follow if I had time to continue. So I would like just now to stress one feature of mutual harmony between man and wife that it seems to me must next to everything in matrimonial and family-life. What is it? ? ?

neutral: It is hoped that Mary will bestow particular benefits upon individuals and their families, especially on a significant day honoring her. To ensure such a benefit, one should seek ways to particularly please her. An effective way to do this is by studying her life and striving to emulate her exceptional adherence to virtues such as charity, patience, purity, humility, and temperance. It is widely held by prominent religious scholars and theologians that from the very beginning of her existence, Mary received more extensive divine favor than all other beings combined. This is often illustrated by comparing her to the brightest moon outshining all stars. Furthermore, it is believed that even the most exalted celestial beings can only distantly approximate her exemplary adherence to virtues, which she demonstrated as she matured in understanding and spiritual favor.
styled: God bless you this most cherished feast of our Blessed Mother Mary. I do hope she may bless you specially - you and yours. However, to insure such a booned favor, we ought on our part try to find some way whereby specially to please her our so gracious blessed Mother. This we can hardly do better than by studying her life and trying to imitate her peerless practice of the Christian virtues - or any one of them - charity. pat- ience, purity, humility, temperance, etc. Of course if we remember and keep in mind that the greates doctors of the Church and theologians are unanimous in their conviction that even at the very first instant of Mary's soul's conception she received greater and more abundent graces than all other creatures taken together -- as the brightest moon outshines all the stars -- and that even the highest seraphim can follow only at a shadowy distance her Christ-like practice of the virtues as she grew in wisdom and grace before god and men

neutral:
A recent report about your family, specifically concerning D. and C., indicated that the entire family situation had significantly improved.

It is supremely important for family peace that spouses adjust their preferences and ideals to align with each other's, thereby revitalizing their initial affection. This also sets a positive example for children and neighbors, and helps demonstrate that the potential for achieving profound and lasting success is worth far more than the relatively minor sacrifices required.

Around 1904, the press, both Catholic and general, appeared to give disproportionate attention to Tolstoy, who was widely regarded as the preeminent genius of the era.
styled: I almost forgot to tell you first that a recent letter concerning your family - rather just a few lines of a report about you - took a tear from my eye: D. and C. and the whole family situation immeasurably improved." Pardor brevity. Now what I wanted to stress is this: The supreme importance for PEACE sake in a family that the husband or the mother, adjust their likes - their ideals - so as to harmonize with those of the other "life- partner", thus renewing and reenforcing their "courting-days affection" for oneanother, edifying the children and neighbors and, in this "vale of tears" helping to convince all concerned that after all the very possibility of our making the grade and gaining the eternal goal is worth infinitely more that the comparatively trifling sacrifices demanded. Just a little example that I now remember ought to make what I want to say, interestingly clear and per- tinent. About the time I was ordained ( 1904), the whole current press - Catholic as well as general - seemed to focus almost dangerously undue attention on a certain Tolstoi as the outstanding general genius of the hour and of the age.

neutral: Wishing peace for you and your family, both now and in the future, as life is seen as a temporary stage. I am once again beginning a response to your letter of April 24th. I hope this message finds you as healthy and hopeful as it leaves us here. The world's processes, though often mysterious, are considered remarkable, and are believed to ultimately result in a positive outcome for appreciative, grateful, and sincere individuals. History provides numerous examples supporting this claim, particularly from the medieval and modern eras, which are seen as demonstrating a higher standard of noble conduct and inspiring greater loyalty to enduring principles than the ancient world, with superior recognition and reward always being evident.
styled: 4 - you and yours. And may the peace of the saints be ours, here and beyond the hopeful borders of this solemn pilgrimage - afterall but a momentary "vestibule to eternal realities". For the severalth time I am starting again a response to your pathetic plaint of April 24th. I do hope this finds you in every way as healthy and hopeful as it leaves us all here at the Friary. Deo Gr. How wonderful, even tho' full of mystery at every turn, are not His - God's own - works and ways! always in the final - never failing in the turning to the Glory of God and the happiness of the faithful, the appreciative, the grateful, and true. History abounds with examples most telling of this happy contention; mediaeval and modern as well as . nay, infinitely surpassing anything- in the ancient world, for real, "excelsior chivalry" and for inspiring loyalty to faith and eternal principle; - divine appreciation, remeration always infinit- ely in the leade.

neutral: Examples that inspire and demonstrate quiet confidence, unquestioning adherence to authority, and unwavering commitment to one's principles, even when challenged, are consistently found. This is presented as the sole discipline that provides purpose to all other disciplines, described as 'The Science of our beneficial interconnectedness with others.' Alternatively, it is characterized as 'The Science of our beneficial relationships and our fortunate reliance on others.' This perspective offers a hopeful outlook on life's journey.
styled: Beautifully romantic and hope-inspiring at once are always the examples of humble confidence, of unhesitationg obedience to God and authority, of persevering loyalty in the face of contradic- tion to faith and principles of RELIGION, -after all and in reality the only science that gives purpose to every other science, "The Science of our happy dependence on God and our neighbor." Or; if you will: "Religion, the Science of our happy relationship with and our providential depencence on God and our neighbor. Hopeful borders of this solemn pilgrimage

neutral: Thank you for your communication of July 19, which I received and recorded. I wish you lasting happiness. Warm wishes to you, Grandma Plunkett. Please maintain a youthful spirit and keep all of us younger generations, down to the youngest great-grandchild, in your thoughts.
styled: Thank you for your kind favor of July 19, received and duly recorded. May the good Lord always give you true interior joy. Yes God bless you Grandma Plunkett. Keep young in heart and pray for us youngsters - clear down to youngest great-grandchild.

neutral: I am just now reading your letter from December 190, after 11 p.m. Time seems to pass very quickly. Your cousin Mildred called from Chicago about a week ago, and I spoke briefly with several of them, including Captain Florence Casey, who was being transferred to Detroit, Michigan at that time. They all appear to be well, including your Aunt, "Grandma Grace." In fact, Grace gave me a pleasant surprise: a 'congratulations' on my 83rd birthday. Your Uncles Pat and Owen also wrote, as did Monsignor Edward. This letter is being sent to you two months later than intended. Late last night, while looking for something else entirely, I was embarrassed to discover these cards still buried under other correspondence. I intend to mail this letter today.
styled: Only now I come to your letter of Dec. 190 - after Il p.m. God help us! I hardly know how the time slips by. Your cousin Mildred called from Chicago a week or so back and I had a little word with several of them including Captain Florence Casey was just then being transerred to Detroit Mich. Thanks be to God they all seem to be well - including even your Aunt - "Grandma Grace". In fact Grace gave me a pleasant surprise - a "congratu- lations ... " on my 83rd birthday. Your Uncles Pat and Owen also wrote and Mgr. Edw'd. All well Dec Gr .! Blessed be the Most Holy Trinity in every tick of time ! God bless you Eileen again - two months after this was supposed to be yours. Looking for something quite dif- fierent late last night I felt ashamed of myself to find these cards still "just snowed under" (all kinds of let- ters, etc) Please God I'll get it off today.

neutral: In the peacefulness of old age, we gather once more with you. Our hearts will forever hold deep respect and love for you, our parents. With a little practice, singing this will be beneficial to its listeners. Solanus Casey. Please excuse the haste. P.S. To Mrs. Plunket: This will accomplish more than my personal presence there.
styled: And now in the calmness of life's sunset glow, We are gathered once more round your knee, Fore'er in our hearts will burn homage and love, For you, Daddy and Mother Machree. I am sure with a little practic this sung as above ... will edify its hearers. Fr. Solanus Casey, OM Cap. Pl. Pardon Haste P.S. Please Mrs Plunket: This will be more than would be my going thither.

neutral: I have been thinking about you often recently. I intended to write, but settling into a new location has been quite demanding.
