Well now Good Bye for the present from Yonkers. My new address will be: P.S. Please Margaret could you send me a copy of Fr. Edward's "Jubilee Poem"? I lost the one I had .... lent it to ..

neutral: The narrator recalled Mother's death three years prior, which they perceived as beautiful, occurring at noon. The narrator's internal response was one of complete acceptance of the situation. The narrator now understood the perceived beauty of Mother's death with unprecedented clarity. This act of acceptance led the narrator to a state of profound unconsciousness, which they described as "perfect darkness and death." This state, however, was incredibly brief. It ended with extreme suddenness, replaced by feelings of profound peace and solemnity. Fundamental principles of wisdom and truth became apparent, including concepts like "To the pure everything is pure" and "Charity knows no evil... is not suspicious." Around 12:15 PM, the narrator heard Dr. K. urgently telling Dr. E. to "Hurry up!" and had a sensation of seeing Dr. E. cutting away remaining tissue, an action the narrator physically felt without any pain. The narrator responded with profound gratitude and wonder. The chaplain granted permission for the narrator to perform a religious service, but the Superior was incredulous the next morning.
styled: The des- cription of Mother's beautiful death three years ago at the 2nd ring- ing of the Angelus flashed on my memory and my heart was only able to respond: Behold - be it done to me acording to Thy holy Will." I can realize now as never before how beautiful in the sight of heaven Mother's death must have been. With the above act of resignation I came to "perfect darkness and death". A shorter instant, however, than that death lasted could not be imagined. With electric quickness the bubble broke and O, what peace! What solemnity! !!...... The very breath of existence seemed to be principles of wisdom and truth, e.g. "To the pure everything is pure". "Charity knows no evil .... is not suspicious," etc. At about 12:15 (P.M.) hearing Dr. K. urging Dr. E. "Hurry up! Hurry up!" and seeming to see the latter cutting away the last flesh- rags, as I actually felt him without the slightest pain. I could only weep out with joyous wonder: "Deo Gratias! Deo Gratias! Thanks be to God!" -.. ... The Rev. Chaplin, gave his consent to my saying holy Mass, but Sr. Superior could not believe next A.M.

neutral:
A note was sent to Maurice, and a short note will now be prepared for dispatch in the morning mail. Upon returning from the hospital, it was realized that an incorrect meter had likely been provided for the verses about the Angelus. If that is the case, a correction is desired immediately.

The proposed opening and its meter are as follows:
God's angel message / Mary received - uu - - -u u --
(His Breath over shading her / Virgin conceived Blest among women / Hail Mary : Hail - uu - - - uu -- Ave Maria : Ave -
The final line matches the German version and is acceptable. This arrangement would be satisfactory for the first section, except for the perceived weakness of the second parenthetical line. Improvement by rephrasing is permitted.

A request was also sent to E.F. for a song about Louis, who is considered the patron of the Third Order.
styled: I just got a note off to Fr. Maurice, and now please God I'll get a little one ready for the mornings mail to yourself. I found when I cam back from the hospital that I had probably given you the wrong meter in regard to those verses on the Angelus - the Angelus in verse. If I did I want to correct it now. Here's how we started it and the measure : God's angel message / Mary received - uu - - -u u -- (His Breath over shading her / Virgin conceived Blest among women / Hail Mary : Hail - uu - - - uu -- Ave Maria : Ave - This last line is exactly how the German ends & is O.K. This would be quite satisfactory for the 1st part were it not for the weakness of the 2nd ( ) line. If you can improve it by turning it around anyway, you'r at liberty to do so. We sent also a request to Rev. E.F. for a song on St. Louis - Patron of the Third Order.

neutral: The sender received your letter some weeks ago and is always pleased to learn of the prevailing hopeful situation. The sender recently contacted The Irish World, which is in press today. The sender has not seen your "From Generation to Gen." Dr. Kain, the poet editor, stated a week or two ago that he had not seen it either. It should be sent to him at #49 Walker St. (Irish World Office). The sender hopes that your current circumstances, and those of the entire "family tree," are much improved compared to last year, making last year's situation a pleasant memory. The sender finds the memory of past trials pleasant. Sending best wishes to all, including Lois and Maurice, Edwin and Teresa, Marion, Francis and Laurence, Clemmie, Papa Frank, and M.C.
styled: I received your welcome letter some weeks ago, and am always pleased to learn of the hopeful situation that seems to prevail. Thanks be to God! I've just phoned a little word to the Irish World - in press today. I have not seen your "From Generation to Gen." Dr. Kain - poet editor - had seen nothing of it a week or two ago, he told me. Send it to him #49 Walker St. (I.W. Office.) I trust your circum- stances, and that, of course of the whole "family tree" is such this year as to make of last years situation a pleasant memory .. . The memory of past trials is pleasant! How pleasant the glorified mem- ory of the saints in Heaven must be! who have finally triumphed - and forever over the world, the flesh and the devil! Well, Well, the day is coming fast when by God's mercy we'l all be withem and then: O then ! ! ! Now with love and God's blessing to all - as on the photo - Lois and Maurice & Edwin and Teresa, Marion, Francis and Laurence, and Clemmie, too, with Papa Frank and finally M.C.

neutral: I hope you and your family are well. Since January 1st, I have made several attempts to write a comprehensive letter. Today, 19 letters were processed, a personal record, with some mail from last week remaining unprocessed. I attended a week-long retreat in Huntington with M.E. in early October. M.E. is well and has been transferred to 226 E. 113th St., New York City, with his departure from his previous location occurring on the 15th. Mary Casey visited last evening and is well. Frances Malloy and her family are all well. Ed. Sampson and the Noonan family are all well.
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope you are all well -"Granma" Granpa" and all. I started half a dozen times since January 1st to write a let- ter worth while ..... 19 letters broke my record To-day - with a few bunches untouched since last week. . I was for a week's retreat down with Fr. M.E. in Huntington early in Oct. He is well and was trans- ferred to 226 E. 113th St. , N.Y. City. leaving here 15th. Mary Casey was here last evening is well. Frances Malloy's are all well. Ed. Sampson and Noonans are all well. Love and God's blessing to all.

neutral: A national convention for members of the Third Order of St. Francis is scheduled for October in Chicago. The parents were members of the Third Order of St. Francis for over 20 years before their deaths. M.C. and E.F. are also members of the Third Order of St. Francis. Margaret and Frank may also be members. I plan to be in Yonkers this week for a period of focused reflection. Best wishes to all, both older and younger. B. Francis Solanus.
styled: You probably have heard about the national convention to be held in October at Chicago by the members of the Third Order of St. Francis. Of course you know the dear Father and Mother were tertiaries for over 20 yrs. before they died. Rev. M.C. & Rev. E. F. also belong to the same. Perhaps Margaret and Frank too belong to it. They ought to be such ..... God willing I'll be in Yonkers for retreat this week. With love and God's blessing to all - the elders and youngsters, I remain sincerely your Brother B. Francis Solanus O.M.C.

neutral: I completed the religious service despite the significant anticipated difficulty. Around 11 o'clock, Parker informed me that an urgent appendicitis case had arrived, and that they were almost ready for me, requesting a short wait. By this time, I had begun writing a couple of cards to my colleagues, and my pain seemed to have lessened. My most frequent internal thought was a plea for help, occasionally one of thanks. When writing to Edward, I intended to fulfill the Superior's proposal: that I have him compose a specific devotional text to a particular piece of music we possess, with lyrical German words, potentially titled 'The [a specific prayer] on at Sea.' This is how I began it:
styled: Thank God I said holy Mass with the great dif- ficulty anticipated. At about 11 oclock "Parker" came in to tell me that an urgent case of appendicitis had come in as they were about ready for me and -- "have a little patience". I had started a couple cards to our Rev Brothers by this time and my pain had become less acute, I think. My most fre- quently repeated prayer was "God help us!" - sometimes, "Deo Gratias!". In writing Fr. Edward I wanted to comply with Father Superior's proposition, That I get him to write the Angelus according to a certain beautiful little music we have, with sweet words in German, whose title might be: "The Ave Maria on at Sea" - Here is how I started it:

neutral: The item will be found soon. It is not available to be returned with this correspondence. A request is being sent to Maurice for the item, if he has it. The item is believed to have been misplaced. Upon opening an older letter dated December 18, 1926, found in a similar envelope, there was disappointment as it was not the expected item. Nevertheless, the 1926 letter, which included verses titled 'THANKSGIVING,' was also found to be interesting. It is hoped that the referenced story will be located and returned soon. There is confidence that the item will appear. An answer to the recipient's letter was intended, but due to the misplacement, this message will be sent as is, with an enclosed sample of letters received daily at this location. The enclosed sample will demonstrate that the recipient is not alone in experiencing difficulties. Other interesting letters were previously kept but are no longer available.
styled: At all events I'll find it before long. I am sorry I haven't it to send back with this. I am writing to Fr. Maurice that if he has it we want it. I think I just mislaid it and seeing your other letter of Dec. 18, 1926 in a similar envelope I was just disapointed as opened it to read it again. However, I found the one of '26 interesting too - with your verses : "THANKSGIVING". Please God I'll find your story re- ferred to and you shall have it back before long. Just say a little prayer with me to Saint Anthony and it must show up from some quarters. . I was intending to write a sort of answer to your letter but since I have mislaid, I'll simply let this go as it is and inclose a sample of the letters we get here almost every day. You will see that you are not the only one favored with trials and crosses. I was keeping some others very interesting but they've gone somewhere else.

neutral: It is important to remember that our true home is not in this world. Life in this world is brief, and what comes after is eternal; therefore, current circumstances should not cause significant distress. However, various influences often present negative portrayals and unrealistic assurances, which aim to induce worry and discouragement. In contrast, other perspectives promote trust and confidence, advising against worry. They suggest focusing on present challenges rather than future uncertainties, drawing parallels to how nature sustains itself without apparent anxiety. Often, significant worries concern events that ultimately do not occur.
styled: Remember my dear sister that you - we all - must keep in mind the fact that we are all exiles, not from Ireland as our dear parents were, but from Heaven. The thing the world calls "life," is so short after all and the hereafter so eternal that nothing here ought to really disturb us. But the "allied" enemies of our souls -- world, flesh & devil are always ready with their dark pictures on the one hand and impossible promises on the other: anything to lead us to worry and discouragement. . Jesus, on the contrary, always inspires with trust and confidence ... "Behold the birds of the air . . . Behold the lillies of the field.". .. "Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof. . . " In other words do not worry. As I have often observed our biggest worries are always about something that never happens. ·

neutral:
It is difficult to execute plans exactly as intended. A month has passed since this document was started. Several attempts to complete it were made, but each time something prevented its completion, illustrating how plans can be thwarted.

The writer anticipates disappointing the recipient. The recipient's letter, received on the aforementioned date, arrived with other correspondence from the recipient and additional items. After reading the recipient's "prize story," a decision was made to have a copy typed. This typing request may have contributed to the delay in providing a response. The recipient's letter and paid story were given to niece Mary to read. Their current whereabouts are unknown, though it is believed they were sent to Father Maurice, Joachim.
styled: How little we can really plan and carry out as intended! Think of it: a whole month has slipped by since I started the above. Quite a number of times I wanted to start and finish it and then came along something to prevent me doing so. Only another example of how: "Man proposes but God dis- poses". Blest be His ways and all His plans, so unsearchable so incom- prehensible! !! Blest forever be His will and His Holy name !! ! I rather fear now that I am going to disappoint you. I had your letter, received on the above date, together with one or two others of your own and some besides. After reading your "prize story" I deter- mined to have a copy of it typed. That was perhaps one reason why I failed to get an answer to you before. I let our niece Mary read your letter and your paid story and now I am not just sure what has become of them. I think I must have sent them to Father Maurice, Joachim.

neutral: It is easy to forget the teachings from the Sermon on the Mount, such as "Blessed are the poor in spirit," found in Matthew chapters 5 and 6. The Sermon on the Mount also includes the teaching, after referencing birds and flowers, "Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself." A significant error is often made when, instead of attributing positive outcomes to divine goodness and providence, people act as though everything depends on luck or chance. Miss McEvily, a prominent supporter of charitable work, became anemic approximately five years ago and was admitted to the state hospital at Eloise, Michigan. She particularly regretted that she could only participate in a specific religious observance once a week.
styled: How easily we for- get the beautiful words of Our Dear Lord' in His sermon on the mount; -- "Blessed are the poor in spirit ... etc" as in Matt. V & VI. The conclusion of all, after calling attention to the bird of the air and the flowers of the field, etc: "Be not solicituous for the morrow for the morrow will be solicitus for itself". I sometimes think we make a great blunder in the fact that, instead of thanking God for His goodness and kindness on every side and making acts of confidence in His loving providence, we just act as though everything depended on luck or on fortune etc. Is it not true? And what a mistake! ... One of our best promoters of mis- sion work - a certain Miss McEvily - became enemic about five years ago and had to go the state hospital at Eloise Michigan. She lamented the fact most especially that she could receive now only once a week.

neutral: I hope you are feeling better today than when you wrote that letter on the 11th. It was quite a letter! I had planned on answering a letter from a new religious leader this morning, but found it difficult to finish reading yours before starting a reply. Continuing to read, I found it improved in tone and I enjoyed it considerably. However, I observe that you, like many people including myself whom I encounter frequently, are prone to worrying about the future, as if there were no consistent evidence or philosophical basis to trust that things will ultimately be fine. Consider past experiences and agree with me that most significant worries are almost always about hypothetical future events that never materialize. I have long believed that these worries, often concerning imagined problems, are a significant source of harm and are ultimately counterproductive.
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope you are feeling better this beau- tiful feast of Mt. Carmel-and of our Blessed Mother-than when you wrote that letter of the 11th. Sure some letter! I had planned on answer- a letter of our new Archbishop this morning, but found it hard to fin- ish reading yours before starting an answer. After reading on I found it took a brighter turn and I quite en- joyed it. However, dear Margaret, I see that you are just another piece of humanity like myself and like I meet with every hour of the day - inclined to worry and fret about the morrow as though Our Dear Lord had never spoken a word about His divine providence or proved His loving so- licitude for each of us a thousand times a day. Just think back a lit- tle and be convinced with me that our biggist worries are almost invar- iably about things that have never happened. For my part I've long been convinced that these worries - mostly about phanthoms of some kind - must/ a big source of toll for the enemy of salvation. .....

neutral:
When asked if she would exchange her life and opportunities with Henry Ford, despite his immense wealth, she appeared to value her spiritual well-being more than ever. She expresses daily gratitude for her ability to perform missionary work. As an expert stenographer and typist, she diligently maintains her diary.

July 17 marked the seventeenth anniversary of an operation the narrator underwent at St. Francis' Hospital in New York City. The operation was scheduled for 10 a.m. on a Sunday to address a rupture, but it was delayed when an urgent appendicitis case arrived just as the orderly was about to summon the narrator. The narrator had been in severe pain for at least forty hours, unnoticed by others. Despite attempts to find gratitude, his primary and frequently repeated plea was for help. The operation commenced at noon. The previous night, the narrator had committed to a nun to conduct a religious service at 6 o'clock.
styled: When I wrote back and asked her if she would swap places and chances with poor Henry Ford, with all his billions, she seemed disposed to appreciate more than ever something of the wealth of her faith. Now she thanks God every day that she can do good missionary work. An expert stenographer & typist she keep her diary, hardly ever missing. July 17 - seventeenth anniversary of an operation this poor son of Adam underwent in St. Francis' Hospital, N.Y.C. It was Sunday, plan- ned for 10 a.m. ( just a little rupture) but "an urgent case of append- icitis" came in just as the orderly was to call me and so, I was put back. ... I had been in agony for at least forty hours, though no one else seemed to know it, and while I tried to thank God for it all, my principal prayer - at least a thousand times repeated - was: "God help us!" Well the operation took place just as the noon Angelus was ring- ing. I had promised the sister the night before to say holy Mass at 6 o'clock - "Please God" I said.

neutral: I conducted a religious service and administered communion to the sisters and patients. It was one of the most positive and memorable experiences I have had. I would not have missed it, despite any personal cost or effort. The fact that I missed only one religious service was almost considered inappropriate by the doctor and sisters. This was due to an error on my part and an unintentional deviation from instructions. Alternatively, one might say it was due to a fortunate turn of events. However, I've digressed. I hope to improve my consistency, conciseness, and prudence. You know we are expected in Superior for Edward's anniversary celebration. He was here about three weeks ago and shared some general plans, but I haven't heard from him since. I know his responsibilities keep him very busy, so I am not concerned about the details. I have plenty to keep myself busy for at least eighteen hours a day.
styled: Thank God I did say holy Mass and gave Holy Communion to the sisters and patients. .... It was certain- ly one of the most beautiful and happy experiences I have ever remem- bered, Thanks be to God! I certainly would not 've missed it for all it cost me. Something that almost was a scandal to Doc- tor and sisters was the fact that I missed only one holy Mass. This was due to happy mistake on my part and an accidental disobedience to orders. Ha Ha! We ought rather to say it was due to a beautiful dis- position of the merciful providence of our divine Sweetheart. But Dear Sister, What a diversion! Whither am I going? Please pray that I learn consistency and conciseness and something more of prudence, etc, etc. Of course you know we are expected in Superior for Fr. Edward's jubilee. He was here about three weeks ago and told us of some gen- eral plans; but since that I've had no word from him. I know his affairs keep him hustling I am not anxious about particulars. I have plenty to keep me busy myself for at least eighteen hours a day. ..

neutral: Given the billions of dollars requested and spent by this individual, if he genuinely supported laborers and the poor, those groups would likely experience stable and adequate employment. The speaker's assessment is that this individual primarily serves the interests of financial institutions. Separately, the author expresses a belief that their fundamental purpose is to comprehend and engage with a supreme entity. They consider this objective, encompassing devotion and service, to be immensely valuable and fulfilling. This pursuit is described as bringing a profound sense of ultimate reward and significance, particularly for those who appreciate its value, equating it to the highest possible state of existence.
styled: If he were a practical friend of the laborer or of the poor, considering the billions he's been demanding and having spent, you and your class would hardly need worry for a decent employment. It seems to me he is simply of the bankers. P.S. II But after all .... God made me to know Him. O what a bless'd aim! To love Him and serve Him sure rests in the same. It's heaven begun - for the grateful - on earth - To treasure aright !!!!!.... Highest Heaven its worth.

neutral: The enclosed Christmas card was found late this evening, almost 11 P.M., but was sent regardless. A phone conversation took place earlier today with M. Casey, who is mentioned in the card. She is well and expects Mildred to visit this week. She also mentioned plans to go to California soon. Mrs. E. Sampson visited last Sunday. E.D. Senior, E.D. Junior, and E.D. III are also well. Mr. Doonan visited some time ago and appears to be in good health. Christmas dinner was had at Molloys. James is doing well; he is in his second year at Sacred Heart Seminary. Father Coughlin resumed his broadcasts last Sunday, delivering a tribute to Bishop Gallagher. Father M. E. Joachim is well.
styled: God bless you. I hope you are well. Strange ... the herewith enclosed Xmas card! I only just came across it Tonight - now almost 11 P.M. I just thought I'd send it anyway. I was talking to-night (by phone) to same M. Casey therin mentioned. She is well, expecting Mildred here this week .... - tells me she expects to go to California before long .... Mrs. E. Sampson was in last Sunday. E'd - Sr. & Jr. are well also E'd III. Old Mr. Doonan was in some time ago and seems pretty well. I had dinner Xmas at Molloys. James is doing well - 2nd yr. in Sacred Heart Seminary. Our prophet, Father Coughlin, started again last Sunday on the air in a touching tribute to Bishop Gallagher. Fr. M. E. Joachim is well.

neutral: The author occasionally finds comfort in the thought that eventually, Father S. will die. The author hopes that their own struggle for existence will then be over. The author hopes that by that time, they will strongly desire death, similar to the sentiment attributed to St. Paul shortly before his death, which expressed a desire for an end to life and a transition to a perceived better state. The author believes this will happen soon, considering fifty years of suffering insignificant compared to the eternal happiness they believe awaits them after death. The author concludes by sending good wishes to Margaret, her family, and other loved ones in the W., as well as to Owen, Grace, Martha, Bernard, and their respective families. Regarding Roosevelt, the author expresses good wishes for him, noting that their enthusiasm for him is significantly diminished or rapidly fading.
styled: I console myself occasionally with the thought that sooner or later the day will come when they will say of poor Fr. S. " ... He's gone." Please God the struggle for existence will then be over. I just hope that by that time I'll be able to exclaim with St. Paul when shortly before he died - a martyr - : "I (desire) long to be desolved and to be with Christ." O well it will not be long. "What are fifty years of pain to the endless joys awaiting us above?" Now I'll say Good Night and God bless you Margaret - you and yours and all dear ones in the W. With love and God's blessing to Owen and Grace and of course to Martha and Bernard and their whole families. God bless you all! Praised be Jesus Christ !!!! P.S. As for being for Roosevelt: Well, I say God bless him too, though my enthusiasm for him is almost - or fast becoming - ancient history .

neutral: I hope you and your family are well. This morning, I had planned to work on 'Appreciation of the Little Flower' and open some of the 50 or more letters accumulated here. However, after finishing your letter last evening around 11 PM, I feel I must at least begin a reply. Sending a response as long as yours would be impossible. This is one reason I seldom write to loved ones, unless otherwise compelled. The time needed to complete such a lengthy, personal letter is equivalent to writing a dozen others and, in my view, provides less benefit. Naturally, I attempt to make all my correspondence personal and caring. I am certain they would be so if we could achieve a state of ideal devotion to the highest good and extend that same level of care to others. Naturally, the latter would follow from the former if that devotion were truly genuine. Greetings to Margaret Therese, repeating the well-wishes conveyed a month ago.
styled: I hope you are well - you and yours. I wanted to do some work on "Appreciation of the Little Flower" this a.m. and open a few of the 50 or more letters piled up here for me, but feel, since reading your let- ter last evening (finished about 11 o'clock), that I must make at least a little start on an answer. That I should send you a response corre- spondingly long as yours I am sure you will smile at as out of the question. That is one reason why I so seldomly write dear ones - except when motived otherwise - the time taken to finish such a "love letter" re- quires as much as a dozen others, and (I sometimes feel at least) brings less good. Of course I try to have all my letters and responses be more or less "love letters". I am sure they would be such if we could only love God as we ought and our neighbor as ourselves. Quite naturally the latter follows the former if really genuine. Well! Well Dear Margaret Therese :- Greetings once more as a month ago in the words above.

neutral:
Maurice Joachim appears to be considering returning to the Order. I received a good letter from him today. His letter is normal.

On October 24th, I just received your address. I had thought I would have been home much earlier. I am still confined here, but hope to be released soon. Tomorrow will mark six weeks, the longest I have ever been incapacitated. However, I believe I can discern a beneficial and comforting influence in these circumstances. The initial weeks were extremely difficult, particularly the nights, but I found the experience to be valuable.

I just received a good letter from our niece, Mary Casey; it seems James is recovering. How is your other son? I started to write to him on a few occasions but never sent a letter. I keep them all in my thoughts. Best wishes to you all.
styled: Maurice Joachim seems figuering on coming back to the Order. I received a really fine letter from him To- day Deo Gr. His letter is perfectly normal. God be praised! Oct. 24th I just got your address -- Thought I'd be home long ago. Praised be Jesus !... am still here on one foot, but hope to be re- leased soon - 6 weeks Tomorrow, the longest I've ever been laid up. Thank God, however I think I see His merciful and gentle hand in it all. First weeks were days of real penance and nights doubly so -wonderful! - Just received good letter from Mary Casey, our Niece. Deo Gr. it seems James is recovering. How is that other son of yours. I started to write him a couple of times but never sent him a letter. I hope I pray for them all. . God bless you again, Every one of you

neutral:
I hope you and your family are well and coping with the recent bereavement. I am sorry to hear about Frank Junior. He was fortunate in many respects and is now at peace.

Last week, I received a call from the Monastery, prompted by your telegram, informing me that Frank Jr. was very ill and in poor condition. My thoughts were with him. I remember his close call several years ago. He is now at peace.

You may wonder about my being here in St. Mary's. I have not conducted religious services for five weeks as of tomorrow. Fortunately, I hope to conduct a service soon. I was brought here by ambulance, despite my objections. Although it has been a significant hardship, I have enjoyed the change. I have received daily religious communion every morning, and as soon as I was able to use a wheelchair, I was taken to the chapel. This started happening in the last few days, when a second service was held at 7:15. You will be pleased that the priest
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope this finds you all in good health and resigned to the cross - the recent bereavement God has seen fit to visit you with. Poor dear Frank Junior. In so many ways fortunate these days. 'R.I.P.' A week tomorrow they phoned me from the Monastery of the telegram you sent, that Frank Jr. was sick - very low etc. Well, about all I could do was to pray for him. I remember his close call several years ago .... May he rest in peace! You may wonder about my being here in St. Mary's. I have not said holy Mass since five weeks Tomorrow. Thanks be to God I hope to say holy Mass soon. They brought me here in an amubulance, though I rather objected .... Notwithstanding the real penance it has meant, I've really enjoyed the change. They have brought me holy Communion every morning and as soon as I was able to go in a wheel chair they wheeled me over to the chapel. This latter the last few days when we had a 2nd holy Mass at 7:15. You will be pleased that Fr.

neutral: I have just read your letter from two weeks ago. I was in the hospital for nine weeks. I had been ill with influenza for about five days when, on September 13, I awoke feeling severely unwell. This was due to having forgotten the previous night to apply ointment to my feet after using electric light therapy for varicose eczema around my ankles. I resumed my duties on November 10, which was exactly one week prior to the current date. I returned to St. Bonaventure's after conducting the 8 o'clock service, which I had announced was for all benefactors, especially those in the hospital: religious sisters, nurses, orderlies, patients, and myself. This occurred last Sunday, November 15th. I had to move with a limp during the service, but I completed it without any serious difficulty. My foot is still stiff, but keeping it elevated and rested results in very little pain. I am currently resting it on the bed. Although sitting in one position becomes tiresome, individuals over sixty often experience discomfort from prolonged sitting.
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope you and all the folks are well. I just finished your letter of two weeks ago - was in the hospital just a novena of weeks. I had been fighting grip(p)e for about five days when on September 13 I awoke "doublly downed", having forgotten the night before to apply ointment or salve to feet after using electric light on vericose eczima around ankels. I started to say holy Mass Nov. 10 - just a week To-day. Came back to St. Bonaventure's after offering the 8 o'clock Mass, as I an- nounced for all benefactors - especially for "all in the Hospital - sisters, nurses, orderlies, patients, etc including my poor self". That was last Sunday, Nov. 15th. Of course I had to limp around on the Altar pretty much, but thanks be to God got through without any serious difficulty. The old foot is still stiff but by keeping it raised and rested it causes very little pain. I'm resting it on the bed now and though it gets tire- some sitting in one position - well anyone over sixty need not be told how the "rear fenders" cry for better padding.

neutral: After dinner, having agreed to meet them at the old spring, I left them to unpack their belongings. I headed for the old "Big-Ravine," intending to revisit the places where, over sixty years ago, we had herded cattle, studied our lessons, picked nuts and wild fruits, and been chased by all sorts of wild animals—even imaginary ones. I was disappointed. None of the old landmarks remained, except the ravine itself. The small bushes had grown into tall trees, obscuring the view of the beautiful old hills. Little Mary Hupert and I ducked under the fence to gather some wild plums, but the area had become too much of a dense thicket to attempt following the ravine. So we ducked back and followed the pasture fence up over what we used to call the "birch-burned-hill," which had been a picturesque prominence sixty-five years prior, featuring a beautiful cluster of white birch trees resembling a beard on its face, and about half a dozen enormous boulders that seemed to protect them.
styled: After dinner, with an understanding that I'd meet them over at the old spring, I left them to go and pitch their bundles - not that I would not have enjoyed same myself - I started for the old "Big-Ravine", thinking, I'd visit the scenes where we had sixty and more years herded the cattle, studdied our catechism, picked nuts and wild fruits and were chased by all kinds of wild animals-even imaginary ones. . . I was disapointed. Nothing of the old land-marks remained, except the ravine itself. The little bushes had become tall trees so that one could not see any of the beautiful old hills. We dodged under the fence to get some wild plums - little Mary Hupert and I - but it was too much of a real jungle to attempt to follow the ravine. So we dodged back and followed the pasture fence up over what we used to call the "burch-burned-hill," - a picturesque prominence sixty-five years ago with a beautiful bunch of white burch trees like a beard on its nose and about a half dozen enor- mous boulders to kinda protect them.

neutral: I am somewhat disappointed that this long letter contains many words but little substance. My intention was to add a brief postscript, but the message has become unexpectedly long. Nevertheless, before I finish, I want to suggest a potential solution for young Edward. For years, during times when other approaches appeared unsuccessful, I have recommended reading the biography of Mary, titled "The Mystical City of God". It is considered to be Mary's own work, as she is believed to have guided the writer, leading me and others to refer to it as Mary's autobiography. Recently, I have attempted to read only after seeking insight and direction, and before going to sleep, often in a kneeling position. I am not, if I told Mary Casey about that when her brother James, Jr.
styled: Dear Margaret; I am almost disapointed at this long letter because of the many words and hardly anything said. I just meant to type a sort of P.S. and now look where we are! However, before I close, let me tell you a possible remedy for young Edward. For years, when Seraphic Mass Association and everything seemed fu- tile - unavailing - I have been recomending the reading of the life of our Blessed Mother Mary, - "The Mystical City of God". It is so much the dear Blessed Virgin's own work - having coached the actual writer - that I and others have been refering to it as the autobiography of our Blessed Mother herself. Of late I have been trying to read only after praying to the Holy Spirit for enlightenment and guidance, and before my late "(k)nock out", on my knees. I am not, if I told Mary casey about that when her brother James, Jr.

neutral: A 13-year-old named Mary soon outpaced me while climbing. Wearing my heavy outer garment over my other clothes, I was breathing heavily, and she smiled at my exertion when I reached the top. The former boulders have been overgrown by birch trees, which have transformed them into numerous small mounds. We then proceeded to the open field, which had remained largely unchanged since 1881. We descended the hill, passing the car others had parked near your birthplace, and continued to the spring, which was now only a small puddle. Feeling I had climbed sufficiently, I waited at the spring until their voices ascended from deep within the wooded ravine. I then gave a loud whistle, and they responded. Realizing the challenging, overgrown terrain I would have faced had I attempted to descend that short quarter of a mile, they had just completed a series of prayers for my appearance. We then returned to the car where I had left Mary and took a final look at the old building site.
styled: Mary about 13, soon left me behind climbing - with my heavy habit over my other clothes and was smiling at my puffing when I reached the top. The one-time bolders have been taken over by the burch-family that has converted them into as many little mounds . We then made for the open field which had not grown much or changed since 1881. Down over the hill we went past the auto the others had left near the sight where you were born to the spring - just a little pud- dle now. I felt that I had climbed enough; so waited at the spring till Their voices reached up from away down in the woody ravine. Then I whist- led on my thumbs and they answered. Seeing the jungle-like proposition I would have been up against had I attempted to come down that short quarter of a mile, they had just finished three Patres and Aves in honor of the Little Flower that their Rev. associate might some how appear. We climbed back to the auto where I had left Mary and then took a last view of the old building-sight.

neutral: Only the caved-in cellar remained, from which a thirty-foot sprout grew from an easily visible acorn. Six individuals, including Mary's brother and the driver, returned across the field. After dropping the children off at the house, they departed for Saint Paul via River Falls, stopping in River Falls to visit Mrs. Cath. Manion Lowe, 83, a woman who held a significant, long-standing role in the speaker's life. She was pleased by their visit. Her father-in-law had moved the speaker's family from their River-bank home when the speaker was approximately three years old. The speaker perceived him as an old man at the time, though he was likely not more than in his fifties. The ease of traveling to St. Paul as a casual evening drive would have been unimaginable sixty years prior.
styled: All was left was the caved-in cellar, with an acorn that we did not have to look for. Its sprout upwards was thirty feet. Six of us - Mary's brother and the driver - started back over the field. Having dropped the children off at the house we started via River Falls for Saint Paul - stopping in the former to visit my God-mother, Mrs. Cath. Manion Lowe, 83. Needless to say she was pleased that we called. It was her rough and ready, big-hearted father-in-law who moved us from the River-bank home when I was about three years old. It seemed to me even then that he was an old man though he probably was not more than in his fifties. How wonderful is memory and all the gifts of God that He blesses us with! Who would ever have dreamed it possible sixty years ago that we'd be able some day to get to St. Paul just as an evening drive? Thanks be to God for all His blessings and mercies. Thanks also to our Blessed Mother Mary, next to Jesus for having given Him to us.

neutral: The person addressed was 61 years old on September 23rd and was the only family member born in the "new house" in Trimbelle. Five years prior, Maurice, Edward, and the narrator visited the old Trimbelle farm and unintentionally passed the old log-house-knoll. The previous evening, the day of the Celebration in Prescott, they had arranged with a neighbor, Alex Hupret (then 83), to have dinner with him the next day. This was conditional on Edward being allowed to help with farm work, specifically pitching bundles, for an hour. The farm is now Hupret's. A man named Weldel had previously purchased it from the family. Weldel cried upon meeting them, having waited at St. Mary's in "Big-river" (now dried up). Maurice and the narrator had planned to stay there overnight before returning for the funeral of a family in-law, a young nephew of Nellie (O'Brien) Casey. They retraced their path and located their host across the road, approximately 50 meters west of the previously mentioned location.
styled: If I remember rightly you were 61 on September 23rd. You were the only one of the family borne in the "new house" in Trimbelle. When we - Fr. Maurice, Edward and myself - visited the old Trim- belle - farm five years ago we ran past the old log-house-knoll before we knew it. We had made an agreement the night before - the day of the Celebration in Prescott - with an old neighbor, Alex Hupret (83 at the time), that we would take dinner with him next day on condition, as Fr. E'd put it: "that you allow me to pitch bundles for an hour". Its Hupert's farm now. A man by name Weldel bought it from us. Poor, dear, old man wept when he met us, having waited for us out at dear, old St. Mary's in "Big-river" (now dried up) where Fr. M. and I were to stay over night and go back for the funeral of an in-law of ours - a little nephew of Nellie (O'Brien) Casey's We retraced our wheeling and found our host across the road and only about ten rods West of the said old place.

neutral: On October 16th, I completed the second book and received the most encouraging letter from him to date. Consequently, I requested that everyone make a significant effort for Edward and his family to reunite. I also expressed gratitude for the photographs and noted that the 22 grandchildren were not present in the group.
styled: On October 16th I finished the second book and that day I received about the most encouraging letter from him of any yet. · So Have them all get on the job and storm Heaven for poor young Edward and his family that they get back together as we would all like to see our friends to do. P.S. Many thanks for fine photographs. Too bad you would not have had the 22 grandchildren along in the crowd.

neutral: The individual was in St. Paul until Thursday at 10:30 AM. Religious services were conducted on Friday in St. Paul, Saturday in Chicago, Sunday in Detroit, Monday in New York City, and Tuesday in Brooklyn. Two religious services scheduled for Los Angeles were not conducted. Greetings were extended to Frank, identified as the supervisor. The sender expressed regret that time was limited and indicated a preference for a career as a plumber.
styled: till Thursday 10:30 in St. Paul; said holy Mass Friday in St. Paul, Saturday in Chicago, Sunday in Detroit, Monday in N.Y.C., Tuesday in Brooklyn. Missed 2 Masses from Los Angeles. P.S. Best regards to my "boss Frank". Too bad time was so short ... I'd come back a plumber.

neutral:
An operation for osteomyelitis was anticipated. It is known that a promise was made at the time: if the operation proved unnecessary, fifty enrollments would be made in the Mass Association. There have been notable cases, and this particular one is presented as noteworthy.

Around New Year's Day 1941, due to discouragement regarding Fr. M. Joachim's condition, a decision was made to undertake a specific devotional practice. This involved four books previously completed over nearly eight years: "The Conception" (610 pages), "The Incarnation" (608 pages), "The Transfixion" (790 pages), and "The Coronation" (610 pages). The practice would be performed while kneeling.

Shortly after the practice began, Fr. M.J. wrote a letter to Fr. Edw'd. This letter was later received from the Philippine Isles, accompanied by the comment: "This is the best letter received from him in years." Before the first book of the devotional practice was completed, Fr. M.J. was performing religious services, specifically on Saint Patrick's Day and four additional services that week.
styled: was expecting to have an operation for ostemalitis I am not certain, but I know she made a promise to the Poor souls at the time that if there were no operation necessary she'd enroll them fifty times in the said Mass Association. I have known of very remarkable cases. This one I am sure will in- terest you. About New Years 1941, inclined to be discouraged in regard to Fr. M. Joachim's condition, I made up my mind, notwithstanding the fact that it had taken me nearly eight years to finish the four books before - the "Conception" 610 pages, the "Incarnation 608 pages, the "Transfixion" 790 pages and the "Coronation" 610 pages - that I'd pray them this time on my knees. I had hardly started when Fr. M.J. wrote the letter to Fr. Edw'd which I received back from the Phil. Isles with comment: "this is the best letter I've received from him in years". And before I was { through with the first book he was saying Holy Mass - i.e. on Saint Patrick's Day and four other Masses that week. Deo Gratias!

neutral:
I recently discovered your letter of July 16, noting it as another instance of oversight. I am approximately fifty letters behind, with many still unopened. I hope to establish a system to manage my correspondence. Despite initial concerns about completing the 9000-mile-plus journey to Seattle and back to Detroit, my health has remained good since I began traveling.

A certificate for John and Edith is being sent in a separate envelope. I hope it is satisfactory. I have not heard from Edward since I left him on the bus for Mt. Angel. We had arrived from Los Angeles the previous night, attended a religious service at the Cathedral, and held a meeting with a senior church official. On Saturday at 1:30 P.M., Owen saw me off on the train to Seattle.

On Sunday and Monday, I attended a religious service at the Convent, with M. Joachim assisting. I then departed for Spokane on Monday the 16th, around 9 P.M. I stopped in Spokane for 24 hours, and on Wednesday, I was on the train all day, beginning at 7:20 a.m.
styled: God bless you and yours. I just came across your letter of July 16 and I thought: "God help us, another negligence"! I must be about fifty letters behind - quite some not opened. Pray the dear Lord give some system or other whereby I keep up. Thanks be to God, however, my health has been good ever since I started on my 9000 or more miles - even though it was feared I'd not be able to make it to Seattle and back to Detroit. Yes Deo gratias. I am sending you a certificate for John and Edith in separate Enve- lope. I hope it be OK. I've not heard from Msgr. Edw'd since I left him on the bus for Mt. Angel. We'd come in from Los Angeles the night before and offered Holy Mass in the Cathedral - and had a nice conference with the Archbishop. At 1:30 P.M. Owen left me on the train for Seattle. That was Saturday. Sunday and Monday I had holy (Mass) at the Convent. Fr. M. Joachim serving, and left for Spokane Monday 16 about 9 P.M. Stopped over 24 hours in Spokane; on train all day Wednesday from 7:20 a.m.

neutral: A message was sent to Edwin a few days ago and should arrive soon, possibly before this letter. I have often regretted not having his address and forgetting the name of the hospital where we visited the patient. It is almost time for the daily mail collection, so I must conclude this overdue note. I almost forgot to thank you for your recent interesting letter. You are likely accustomed to such delays from this sender. My apologies. Grace also mentioned her senior Bernard is coming from the East and that she might visit here. Please extend best regards to her, to my many namesakes, and to all our loved ones.
styled: I sent a little message to your Edwin a few days ago which ought (to) reach you very shortly, if not ahead of this. I have often regretted that I had not his address and that I forgot the name of the hospital in which we visited the poor dear invalid. May it please the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary to turn his long illness to have been a manifest blessing of some kind! It is nearing time for the daily letter collection. So I'll have to finish this already tardy note. Almost forgot to thank you for your in- teresting letter recently. I guess you must be more or less accustomed to such neglect from these quarters. Please pardon. Grace also tells me of her senior Bernard coming from the East and of her possible visit hither. Please ... best regards to her and to my many namesakes out there and all our dear ones.

neutral: F.F. Maurice and Edward visited two weeks ago. They traveled from St. Paul with Joe O'Brien (the writer's brother-in-law), Aunt Mary, and Uncle Pat Murphy's wife, after an overnight stop in Chicago with Dean and Mildred Conley. The Monsignor continued to Boston a day or two later. M.J. stayed for ten days, appearing to enjoy the location where he had spent approximately ten months in a training period fifteen years prior. Although somewhat restless, he appears to be in good health and performs a daily service. Helena arrived a few days before the group of men referred to as the Brothers. This concludes the task the writer set yesterday morning to send a card to each of their siblings in the West.
styled: I wanted to tell you just briefly of F.F. Maurice and Edward's visit here two weeks ago. They came down from St. Paul with Joe O'Brien - Brother-in-law, Aunt Mary, Uncle Pat Murphy's Wife, having stopped over night with Dean and Mildred Conley in Chicago. Msgr. went on to Boston a day or two after. Fr. M.J. stayed ten days - seemingly enjoying where as a novice he put in about ten months fif- teen years ago. Thanks be to God, tho a little restless he seems doing pretty well, saying holy Mass every day. Helena was here a few days ahead of the Rev. Brothers. This is the end of a purpose I made yesterday a.m. of writing a card to each of my brothers and sisters in the West." .Man purposes but God disposes"

neutral: Edward expressed the view that fifty years of suffering were minor compared to the ultimate future happiness. Upon reading this, I was strongly tempted to discard it, as it did not reflect my intended message. My intention was to describe our months of planning before Guss's death, aimed at resolving the conflict between him and another individual, and how the situation was favorably resolved. I had always believed it was merely a misunderstanding between them, which proved to be the case. They both sent me positive letters regarding the matter. Months before Guss became ill, he wrote to me requesting support for the other individual. Later, shortly after his first operation and following their complete understanding, he wrote to me again, expressing acceptance of his probable fate and finding his only hope in spiritual matters. He died on a significant religious observance. This marked another significant passing within the community, which was considered a cause for gratitude.
styled: Edw'd puts it "What is 50 years of pain to the endless Joys awaiting us above!" When I read the above I almost tore it up. It is not what was in my mind to write ..... I wanted to tell you our planning for months before poor, dear Br. Guss died in some way to smoothe off the "friction" between him and some one else and about how beautifully the dear Lord took care of that for us ... I felt all along that it was nothing more than a misunderstanding be- tween them. Such it turned out to be, Deo Gratias. They both wrote me beautiful letters about it. In fact months before Guss got sick he wrote me asking prayers for the other party. Later on, shortly after his first oper- ation and after the really beautiful understanding between them he wrote me again .... quite resigned to the probability of what actually came and appeal- ing to the Sacred as his only source of hope of rescue. How beautiful, ... He died on the Feast Itself .... Well, thank God for another beautiful deathe in the Family. te- ful we ought to be!

neutral:
Wishing you a happy holiday season and a prosperous new year, from someone mostly confined to bed.

I began writing several days ago but was unable to send the message in time for the 51st anniversary of my first full day in the organization. My work has been interrupted by weeping eczema. However, I was able to attend a midnight service and conduct an additional service. My feet are improving, and otherwise I am quite well.

January 18th: I am still mostly confined to bed, though I conduct a daily service. I missed conducting four daily services, including two on Christmas Day. I hope my condition improves soon. I hope this message, though delayed, is not too late. I received a nice letter from M. Cleopha.
styled: Requested with best wishes for a Merry Christmas and a Happy and blessed New Year, by one in bed most of the day -- God bless you this Bl. Feast. I started to write you several days ago but something thwarted my success in reaching you for this 51st anniv'y of my first full day in the Order Deo Gr. I've been checqued in my rush of work by weeping eczema; Thanks be to God for each and all of His designs. Was able however to attend Sol .- mid- ngt Mass and offer one holy Mass besides ... Deo Gr .! Feet are im- proving ... and otherwise am quite well. Jan. 18th Am still mostly on the matress, tho saying holy Mass every day. I lost four daily Masses including two on Xmas. I am hoping things brighten soon. Hope this even so tardily coming may be not too late. Had a nice letter from Sister M. Cleopha

neutral: Recently, thoughts have repeatedly turned to you and Frank, with your large family and everyday challenges, and your resilience to continue despite many difficulties. Such resilience is often underestimated. This morning, I walked through the orchard and vineyard, which were abundantly fruitful, and knelt in the small Capuchin cemetery located behind this monastery. I was moved by the sound of the chimes from the tower of Saints Peter and Paul, less than two miles away, which brought many pleasant thoughts of the past to mind. However, the past seems somewhat somber when compared to the prospect of ultimate, lasting well-being, which is believed to be assured. Ultimately, the true value of the past lies in its role in cultivating an appreciation for our fundamental connection to a benevolent, guiding origin.
styled: Rememberances of late, have been whispering again & again of you and poor dear Frank with your big family and prosaic handicaps - and with all - nevertheless your God-given faith to carry on in face of so many diffi- culties! O the Faith! How little it is possible for us in this world to appreciate it! I was strolling in the orchard and vineyard this a.m. bountifully loaded. Deo Gr. and kneeling in the little Capuchin cemetery - all behind this ideal monastery, - I was thrilled by the chimes of SS. Peter and Paul in their tower smiling at me less ( than) two miles away - thoughts multiplied of the wonderful past. Wonderful indeed to muse over! Thanks be to God. Still how Comparatively melancoly when, anchored in holy faith, we turn to the spring of Eternal blessedness assured our per- severence ...... Indeed: what is all the past, aside from the privilege that ought to be our supreme aim, to have fostered and to foster - appreciation of our being children of our Heavenly Father and of our Blessed Mother Mary? As Fr.

neutral: I recently received a letter from your Mother, my sister Margaret, who informed me that you are finally showing slow improvement. This is welcome news. I have often intended to write to you, as I understand you may frequently experience loneliness and discouragement. Despite this, it is widely observed that individuals who are highly regarded often experience difficulties. If we could overcome our limited perspective and comprehend the vastness of eternity, along with the potential rewards for those who endure suffering patiently and with acceptance, then the temporary joys and sorrows of the present would seem inconsequential. It is likely because we reflect so infrequently and superficially on the profound concepts of time and eternity. I am sending you some leaflets that I believe you will find beneficial and enjoyable to read.
styled: God bless you and yours. I just received a letter from your dear Mother -- my Sister Margaret, who tells me you are at last slowly improving. Thanks be to God for the favorable report! I have often wanted to write you; for I know you must often get lonely and discouraged. And yet, we see in such inumerable cases and are assured on every page of Holy Scripture that: "Those whom God loves He tries." If our short sightedness would only let us get a peep into the infinite depths of eternity and even a shadow of the glory there reserved for those who suffer patiently and at least resignedly O! how like nothing would seem all the momentary joys of time and the sorrows alike. No doubt it is because we think so lightly and perhaps to seldomly about the great mysteries in connection with this phenomenon - time -- eternity! I am sending you a few little leaflets that I am sure you will profit by reading and will like.

neutral: The sender expresses hope for the recipient's physical, mental, and inner well-being. The sender reports being well in these areas, with the exception of some self-admitted neglect concerning their inner well-being. The sender is preparing for an appointment with a chiropractor, described as highly skilled. However, for several years, this individual has been separated from his family and from religious observances. Efforts are being made to encourage him to change his current behavior or perspective. There is concern that his intelligence may be detrimental to him, leading to excessive pride. The sender requests support for Dr. Jake Young to return to religious observance. His wife, who converted to the faith, demonstrates considerable patience with him. His animosity towards her is identified as a significant issue, despite their three respectable children, six grandchildren, and his age in the mid-sixties.
styled: God bless you these wonderful days - of our wonderful Patron of St. Therese, yesterday and of the holy Rosary. I hope you keep well in body, mind and in soul. Thanks be to God I can not complain in these regards, - save of course some neglect on my part regarding the last. I am just getting ready to go to my doctor - a chiropractor - and a very clever one. Sad to say, however, he has been for several years away from his family and from the holy Sacraments. We are trying hard to bring him back to his senses, as I tell him. We just fear that he is too clever for his own good - too much savoring of the big head. So you can help us by a prayer now and then for the conversion of Dr. Jake Young. His poor wife is a convert and keeps up great patience with him. His bitterness to her is his trouble, though they have three very creditable children, six grand-children and he is in his middle sixties.

neutral: We have thirty promising novices, nearly all 18 years old this year. If enough were available, we could place 100 priests in missions. There is a great need for workers, but few are available. The enclosed item was returned yesterday. Initially, this was a surprise until 'Los Angeles' was seen instead of 'Ok'. Grace A. and Bernard departed yesterday afternoon (around 3:30 PM) for Mildred and Dean's, following an approximately 21-hour visit. Both appeared to have enjoyed their meeting and related activities in New York, and their return journey thus far. They were vaguely planning to visit Burkhardt, Hudson, St. Paul, Superior, S. Paul, and Graceville. It is good news that Clem's child recovered so fortunately.
styled: Thanks be to God: We have thirty promising novice -- nearly all 18 yrs. old this year, if available we could place 100 priests in the missions. "The harvest . . great ... laborers are few." Bles'd be God! The herewith enclosed came back yesterday. At first it was a surprise, - till I saw "Los Angeles" instead of Ok .- Well Grace A. and Bernard left last - p.m. (about 3:30), for Mildred and Dean's after about a 21 hours visit. Both seemed to hav enjoyed their meeting, etc, in New York and return so far. They were figuering (vaguely) on seeing too Burkhardt, Hudson, St. Paul, Superior and S. Paul and Graceville. .God bless you each and all. Glad "Clem's little one rallied so fortunately.

neutral: A visit to Wisconsin occurred last week. Something was discovered. The province was divided this year. This location now functions as a house of studies, with 53 individuals studying philosophy. The total community numbers close to 70. The novitiate has returned to St. Bonaventure's in Detroit, Michigan.
styled: I was up in Wisconsin last week. Some one Kindly "unearthed" ... We divided our province this year. This is now a house of studies - 53 studying philosophy - close to 70 in family. Deo Gr. The noviciate is back in St. Bonaventure's. Detroit, Mich.

neutral: I hope Margaret Therese and Frank are all in good health and have a positive outlook. I am thankful for all positive things. I received your telegram. This morning, I performed a religious service for you, especially for Edwin, who recently passed away. I hope he is in a peaceful afterlife. I understand you miss him greatly, perhaps more than others. I have often thought of him since our visit to him in the hospital exactly five years ago, and of you all as well. It seems that five years have passed quickly. I was recently hospitalized at St. Joseph Hospital in Fort Wayne for a couple of weeks. I am grateful for my recovery and doubly thankful to have returned to St. Felix since last Friday. It is quiet here, approximately a mile from town. I am listening to the simple calls of the turtle dove and quail, sounds that have been familiar to me for over seventy-five years, along with other birds. The quail's 'bob white' call is pleasant to hear.
styled: My dear Sister Margaret Therese and Brother Frank. I do hope this finds you all in good health and hopeful outlook. Thanks be to God for all his mercies to us and for everything. I received your wire. I offered my holy Mass this Morning for your intentions and especially for your lately-deceased Edwin. I hope he is already in Heaven praying for the rest of us. No doubt you miss him as much as you would any of the others, probably more. I have often thought of him since our little visit to him in the hospital five years yesterday, and of you all of course. What a short five years! Glory be to God! I was in St. Joseph Hospital, Fort Wayne a couple weeks myself recently. Thanks be to God for the same and thank Him doublly I am back to St. Felix since last Friday. It is quiet here just about a mile from Town and with other birds that entertain, I am listening to the simple call of the turtle dove and the quail, so familiar more than seventy-five years back. Their old "bob white" call is musical now.

neutral: The speaker expressed disappointment at not having contacted Grace before her death. The speaker believes Grace understood the reason for this failure and did not blame them. The speaker, Grace's brother, who is currently significantly incapacitated, is requesting Grace's assistance. The speaker had previously intended to send a letter to Grace's older sister, anticipating that the sister would experience greater grief due to their close geographical proximity for several years. However, based on a suggestion from Rosemary, the speaker now considers an alternative approach more practical, provided it can be completed.
styled: Yes I was disapointed at not having reached poor, dear, little "Granma Grace" before, as we can confidently hope she did, gently sigh her weary soul to heaven. ... I think she knows now why I failed and I hardly think she blames me. Rather I am asking her to come and help me her poor, cloding stupid brother - just at present a stumbling 3/4s invalid. Deo Gratias I was really figuering on sending that letter to her older Sister who I am sure will miss dear Grace more than any of the rest of us; having been these several years from each other literly "just across the Golden Gate". At your suggestion and from your letter I think it would be more practical Rosemary. - if I can get it finished.

neutral: The author frequently recalled a notable visit with an individual five years prior and expressed a strong desire for further visits. The author believed that continued engagement with the individual could still be effective, possibly because the individual had not yet reached a final, ultimate destination. Therefore, it was considered a primary responsibility to maintain and increase these efforts, at least for a period. The author committed to this course of action. The author reflected on memory as a valuable attribute but considered hope to be even more significant. These two concepts were seen as working together, alongside two other virtues, faith and charity, to achieve a greater good. The author expressed a sentiment of profound reverence and a wish for peace among people of goodwill. The author questioned the extent of current appreciation and gratitude. The author hoped that a benevolent force would compensate for this lack until a final, ultimate state of perfection and happiness was achieved. This text, dated December 22nd, was found on an unfinished card.
styled: How often I have remembered our privileged little visit with him five years ago and wished I could visit him again and again! Well, though I think we can pray to him with good results yet because it is easily possible too that he is still detained from the great, final Goal of the saints, it is no doubt our first duty to keep up our prayers for him and rather multiply them at least for a time. This I at least pur- pose to do, with the help of our Guardian Angels and the grace of Almighty God. What a wonderful gift of God is memory! But what is it to compare with hope! .. Ah! They cooperate together to glorify God, with the other two of the triune virtue, faith and charity. Glory to God in the highest! And on earth peace, to men of good will." How appreciate? Where is our gratitude? May the merciful providence of God supply our deficiency here- in till our Heavenly Father call us Home by the light of the Holy, the Infant Jesus perfect us in these shades of eternal happiness! Dec. 22nd Just came across this unfinished card.

neutral: The author has not been well recently, but began to feel better starting yesterday (Monday morning). The doctor found the author's temperature to be normal, and improvement continued last night when the author started but then stopped typing. The author had a particularly sleepless night. However, the author performed a religious service this morning with little difficulty, the first time since an unspecified date. The author expects to leave the infirmary tomorrow. The author is aware of a large amount of work awaiting at least an initial review, but believes that with the help of others, despite potential mistakes and oversights, it will be managed. There has been another death in the family. The deceased was characterized by a strong acceptance of their fate, endured severe pain for 20 months, and displayed consistent, cheerful humility. These qualities are considered admirable.
styled: I hope this finds you better than I have been - rather say I was - these past few days. Glory be to God, however, the improvement I feel started yesterday ( Monday-morning). When the Doctor came my tempera- ture was normal - was still improved last night when I started typing to you but simply gave it up. Had a peculiarly sleepless night Glory be to God! But offered Holy Mass this Morning with little difficulty - first time since . Please God I'll be leaving the infirmary Tomorrow. I know there is abundance work waiting for at least a glance of inspecti but with God's grace and help of others - and no doubt plenty of mistake and oversights - we'll get thru. Glory be to God for another death in the Family, whose outstanding features - confident resignation to God's will that bordered close to the heroic acceptance of soul - chissiling pains for 20 mons. grace and never-failing, mirthful humility - Ah! traits of sanctified character that stand out in the lives of those whose death the Holy Ghost glori- fies as precious in the sight of the Lord. .. ..

neutral: An idea quickly formed: if a single act of support could benefit a legitimate cause, then a much larger, daily effort, particularly one associated with charitable missions, should be even more effective. The narrator assented, and John agreed to contribute fifty cents. That same night, the company received a significant order. Two nights later, McK. enthusiastically reported that the company had worked overtime for two days and had just received an order for 45,000 machines, to be delivered within thirty days. It was believed that this order saved the company from bankruptcy.
styled: 20 times quicker than I could tell it, however, so that it seemed absurd to hesitate, flashed on my mind: "If a single Holy Mass must help any legitimate cause, why should not five hundred Masses dayly in connection with the holy foreign Missions help?" "Alright John, " I answered. "yes Father; I'll give them fifty cents. . . . That same night the Com- pany received an astounding order. Two nights later McK. waved in tri- umphantly: "Father! we had over-time yesterday and To-Day and we heard this after-noon: the Co. has an order for 45000 machines, wanted in thirty days". ... It was believed: that order saved Det. itself from bankruptcy. P1. Pardon such patchwork - longer than intended.

neutral: I received your telegram regarding Edwin, who had suffered for a long time. I am confident that his passing was a favorable transition rather than a death in the usual sense. I therefore view it as a fortunate event for your family to have had such a special individual, and that he may now serve as an advocate for the rest of you, potentially as a second family member to do so. I nevertheless sympathize with you on the loss and separation you must for some time expect to experience in his regard. You will likely miss him, especially when you can no longer make your customary visits to the hospital. You will indeed miss him, perhaps more intensely and for a longer period than you might have missed others, had someone else passed instead.
styled: God bless you and guide you and yours. I hope this finds you in the holy joy and calmness of the Resurection and the Ascension that filled the souls of Mary our Blessed Mother and her little Family - the nucleus of the Church - as they waited and pleaded for the coming on the Holy Ghost. I received your telegram of poor, long-suffering little Edwin. Confident that his was a happy transition rather than a death in the usual sense, I rather congratulate you on having such a chosen one to give to God; and consequently, on having one of your Family - in God's mercy we hope the second one - to make intercession for the rest of us, still, "viatores". Of course I nevertheless sympathize with you on the temporal loss and separation you must for some time expect to experience in his regard. You will possibly miss him at least when forced to aban- don your wanted visits to your friendly little hospital. Miss him? Indeed; and for a time and in a way perhaps more than you'd miss any of the others had someone else gone instead. Poor, dear Edwin!

This was a significant source of hope for millions. Other automotive companies followed slowly, with most operating only one or two days per week. Chevrolet appeared to be one of the slowest; it was later revealed (a year or two later) that the company had already begun bankruptcy negotiations.

On Thursday, February 12th, around 9 p.m., John McKenna came to the office. He had developed enthusiasm for a particular association in the months following August 1st, 1924. He was clearly discouraged, despite his usual strong convictions.

He expressed his distress, stating he did not know what to do and could not support his wife and family with his current work schedule. He reported not having worked a full day in two weeks, and on that particular day, he had only worked two hours. He added that the company was constantly finding excuses to send workers home.

Suddenly, as if inspired, McKenna suggested, "Enroll the Company!" This was considered a novel idea.
styled: That was quite a "beam of hope" for perhaps millions. The other auto-companies followed lingerlingly, but most of them just one and two days each week - one of the slowest seemingly, the Chevrolet, which as we learned only a year or two later, had already started negotiations to- wards bankruptcy. ... On the 12th of February, Thursday about 9 p.m., John McKenna who had become enthusiastic about the Ser. Mass Asso'n the first months after my arrival back from New York, August 1st, 1924, came to the Office. He was evidently discouraged, notwithstanding his other- wise wonderful Faith. "Father", he began, "I don't know what to do; I can't support a wife and family the ( ) I've been working. I haven't had a full day now in two weeks; and To-Day I had only two hours. ... They'er always finding an alibi to send the men home." ... , All at once as tho by in- spiration: "Father! Enroll the Company! ? " "That's new", thought I.

neutral: To Margaret, Frank, and your loved ones, I just found the enclosed item and thought it might interest you. I presume my silence sometimes makes it seem as though I have forgotten my friends. As years and decades pass, I seem to make no progress with my correspondence. However, with hardly any exception, my old friends seem earnest about their spiritual well-being, which many unfortunately seem indifferent about. Our brothers, E'dand and O.B.J., attended our jubilee celebration, which marked two 25-year anniversaries and one 50-year anniversary. Everyone present seemed very pleased. Owen was not well but maintained good spirits.
styled: God bless you My Dear Sister Margaret - with Brother Frank and all your dear ones, I just came across the herewith inclosed and tho't it might interest you. I presume my silence sometimes seems as tho' I had forgotten my friends. ... Ah! God help us! As years and decads pass I seem to get no - where with my correspon- dence. Thank God, however, with hardly a positive exception my old friends seem earnest about saving their souls - which so unfortunally many seem to be indifferenct about ...... Our dear brothers, Fr. E'dand O.B.J. came to our jubilee - 2 Silver one golden - Every one present seemed more than pleased. Glory be! Poor dear Owen was not well but kept up good spirits.

neutral: Return to your task. Stop worrying. Come here so we can discuss this. I feel compelled to help you with this challenging situation. However, the best resolution will occur. Understood.
styled: "Get on the job" again Come, shake off that worry. ... and come over till I pull your ears for .... as Patron of Lost Things must do something to get you St. Anthony, However, the dear Good God always knows best .. O.K.

neutral:
Several notable instances were associated with the Seraphic Mass Association. Margaret and Frank had been enrolled in the association approximately a week prior, following receipt of a letter. The enrollment of companies and projects in the Seraphic Mass Association had not been previously mentioned. The subsequent case was the first of several similar instances.

The economic downturn of late 1925 and early 1926 severely impacted residents of Detroit. Every automobile factory in the city ceased operations for at least a week during Christmas, with no indication of when operations would resume. Approximately one or two days before New Year's, it was announced that Ford would resume operations on a specified date after New Year's and would operate three days a week until further notice.
styled: Dear Margaret I wanted to tell you of at least a few other remarkable cases - answers to prayers especially in conection with the wonderful Seraphic Mass Association. Incidently, in which we enrolled you and Frank after receiving your letter about a week ago. I hoped to get this off to you before the middle of the week, and here it (is) Satur- day night just striking ten. Glory be to God! October 26, 9:20 P.M. According to the baptismal certificate ... I was 84 yesterday. Deo Gr! ... Deo Grt! Dear Margaret: I hardly think I ever told you about our enrolling companys and projects in the Seraphic Mass As'n. The following - first in several similar to it since - I am sure will please you. The slump of 1926-25-Winter was tough one on Detroiters. Every Auto factory in the city shut down for at least a week at Christmas, without a word when they would start up again. Only a day or two before New Years was it announced that Ford would start up again, such and such a day after New Years and would continue at three days a week till further no- tice.
